buildings.description: Metropol Palace, Belgrade's first modern post-war hotel, was created by Dragiša Brašovan by converting the unfinished House of the Central Committee of the Youth of Yugoslavia. He conceived the building as an autonomous volume, independent of its urban surroundings.
buildings.history: The structure began as the House of the Central Committee of the Youth of Yugoslavia, designed by Dragiša Brašovan, and was never finished. Between 1954 and 1958 the shell was adapted into a hotel, the first post-war Belgrade hotel built to contemporary standards. The commission fell in the third phase of Brašovan's career, when he was rethinking his stylistic bearings.

buildings.description: The Society of Saint Sava building on Cara Dušana street was designed by Petar Bajalović, for many years a professor at the architecture department of Belgrade's Technical Faculty. The society's name is inscribed on the corner tower, and the house ranks among his finest residential works from before the First World War.
buildings.history: Bajalović's design dates from 1914, but the house was finished only in 1924, with the First World War lying between the drawing and the completed building. The Society of Saint Sava received a monumental academic building with two portals and a square corner tower carrying its inscription.

buildings.description: "Serbian Crown" is the only surviving representative of Belgrade's first hotels of the European type, opened in 1869 as the most modern and most prestigious in the city. Its plan still follows the old han tradition, with the whole building grouped around an inner courtyard.
buildings.history: The hotel went up in 1869, and already in 1870 the owner Milija Pavlović opened a tavern inside, moving onto it the sign with the Serbian crown emblem taken from the tavern of the same name in Uzun-Mirkova street. After the bombing of Belgrade on 6 April 1941 destroyed the National Library, the tavern closed and the house began to gather a new library collection. The Belgrade City Library is there today.

buildings.description: The seat of Serbia's National Assembly since 2006, built over nearly thirty years, and in 1961 the venue of the first conference of the Non-Aligned Movement.
buildings.history: Jovan Ilkić won the 1901 competition, but work began only in 1907, when King Petar I laid the foundation stone; the First World War stopped construction. After Ilkić's death in 1917 his son Pavle oversaw the resumption, and the final phase from 1935 was led by the Russian architect Nikolai Krasnov, who designed the interiors. The first session was held on 21 October 1936. In 1961 the building hosted the first conference of the Non-Aligned Movement, and since 2006 it has officially served Serbia's parliament.

buildings.description: The Palace of the Ministry of Finance of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, today the seat of the Serbian government, is the work of Nikola Krasnov, the foremost of the Russian architects active in interwar Belgrade. A bronze personification of Yugoslavia crowns the dome over the corner.
buildings.history: The palace was built between 1926 and 1928, and Krasnov added a third storey in 1938. The sculptures on the facades — allegories of Fruitfulness, Craft, Industry and Mercury, together with the bronze Yugoslavia on the dome — were made by the sculptor Đorđe Jovanović. The subjects were chosen to reflect the work of the ministry the building served.

buildings.description: The Patriarchate of the Serbian Orthodox Church was built between 1933 and 1935 to a design by the Russian architect Viktor Lukomsky, on the site of the 1863 metropolitanate. Its purpose shaped the style: a modernised version of the Serbian-Byzantine, with old models freely reinterpreted.
buildings.history: Work ran from 1933 to 1935 on the site of the 1863 metropolitanate, and Lukomsky gave the building a modernised Serbian-Byzantine form. The compound also holds a chapel dedicated to Saint Simeon Mirotočivi, the Patriarchate Library and the Museum of the Serbian Orthodox Church. A mosaic of Saint John the Baptist, made after a design by the painter Vladimir Predojević, sits above the main entrance.

buildings.description: The Air Force Command building in Zemun is one of Dragiša Brašovan's most original works: he placed it on the site of the former Military Command and tied it into a single urban ensemble with the Zemun Military Command house in Glavna Street. It remains one of the dominant landmarks of Zemun's Old Core.
buildings.history: The headquarters went up in 1935 to a design by Brašovan. After the war the building turned into the cradle of Serbian aviation medicine: in 1945 the first medical commission for pilots began working here, a forerunner of the Air Force Medical Institute, and on 15 February 1957 the Air Force Museum was founded in the same building. On 5 April 1999 at 04:18 two missiles struck it during the NATO bombing, hitting the central section from Glavna Street and the tower from the courtyard side. That June a plaque honouring the airmen and air-defence crews who died in the strikes went up beside the right-hand projection of the main facade, and the building was rebuilt to the original design in 2000–2001.

buildings.description: The Military Geographical Institute is one of Serbia's oldest state and military institutions, working without interruption since 1876; for it Milorad Macura designed, in the early 1950s, the first monumental public building of post-war Belgrade, deliberately conceived outside the canons of socialist realism.
buildings.history: The building went up between 1950 and 1954, and the institute moved in in 1956. Macura began the design at the Projektantski zavod NO Beograd and finished it at the Atelje arhitektura i urbanizam; a single volume holds two wings for two users — a printing house facing the park and the institute itself on Mije Kovačevića street. The scheme introduced brise-soleil screens and a consistent modular system to domestic post-war practice, both on the facades and inside.

buildings.description: The Palace of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts houses the country's highest scientific institution, which traces its descent to the Society of Serbian Letters of 1841 and took its present name after the Second World War. The design by Andra Stevanović and Dragutin Đorđević was ready as early as 1912; the palace itself was completed in 1924.
buildings.history: The academy was founded on 1 November 1886 as the Royal Academy, building on the Society of Serbian Letters (1841–1864) and the Serbian Learned Society (1864–1892); from 1892 it was the Serbian Royal Academy, and after the Second World War it took its present name. Stevanović and Đorđević drew up the palace in 1912, but the design was carried out only in 1924; a mezzanine was inserted into the scheme along the way, bringing the number of levels to four. Its facades face three streets.

buildings.description: The Royal Palace in Dedinje is the official residence that King Alexander I commissioned in 1924 and received by 1929. With the chapel of Saint Andrew the First-Called and the White Palace it forms a royal compound on the hill above Belgrade. The architects were Živojin Nikolić and the Russian émigré academician Nikolai Krasnov; until 1941 the Karađorđević dynasty lived here, and today the palace is again home to the family of its head, Prince Alexander.
buildings.history: The palace went up between 1924 and 1929, commissioned by King Alexander I as the official royal residence. Until 1941 it remained the home of the Karađorđević dynasty, and during the Second World War it was damaged in air raids. The post-war restoration changed the facade completely. In the years of socialist Yugoslavia various state bodies occupied its halls. Today it houses the present head of the Karađorđević house, Prince Alexander, grandson of King Alexander I, together with his family.

buildings.description: The house of the Belgrade merchant Nikola Spasić on Kneza Mihaila street was built in 1889 to a design by Konstantin Jovanović: shops occupied the ground floor, while each of the two upper storeys held a single large flat. Its facades are counted the most successful exercise in the academic style in Belgrade.
buildings.history: The house belonged to the well-known Belgrade merchant Nikola Spasić and was built in 1889 to Konstantin Jovanović's design as a two-storey residential and commercial building. Each of the two upper floors held one large flat of complex layout, a statement of the bourgeois taste for representation, while the ground floor was given over to shops. Inside, stucco panels with painted landscapes and round medallions with portraits in grisaille survive — a rarity in Belgrade architecture at the end of the 19th century.

buildings.description: The Special Hospital Saint Sava is a highly specialised institution for cerebrovascular disease and a teaching base of Belgrade's Medical Faculty. It occupies a building in the city centre, put up between 1930 and 1932 for the Belgrade branch of a Zagreb workers' insurance office and converted into a clinic in 1946. The hospital stands on the Sava plateau near the Appellate Court and the intercity bus station, among republican institutions.
buildings.history: The hospital as an institution was founded in 1930, while its present building went up between 6 October 1930 and 29 September 1932. Lavoslav Horvat's scheme won first prize in the 1929 competition because it managed to combine institutions of quite different purposes under one roof. After serious disagreements with the contractor Horvat walked away from the job, and the documentation was signed by Petar Gačić, whose later drawings substantially altered the original design. The facade was eventually built as a mirror image of the competition project, so the first appearance — an example of monumental neoclassicism of the late 1920s — was lost for good. Straight after the Second World War, in 1946, the building was adapted for hospital use and has served that purpose ever since. In May 1992 a chapel of Saint Luke the Apostle and Evangelist was consecrated in the hospital, the first hospital chapel in Serbia.

buildings.description: A hotel opened in 1908 as the Rossiya Palace, the Belgrade office of a St Petersburg insurance company; its arrival marked a turning point in Belgrade Art Nouveau.
buildings.history: The Rossiya Palace was built in 1905–1907 to a design by Jovan Ilkić and a group of St Petersburg architects: the 1904 competition's first prize went to Viktor Kovačić, but the company chose Ilkić's entry. The site's owner, Svetozar Vukadinović, found an insurance company in Russia whose director accepted his plan, and on 14 January 1908 King Petar I opened the palace with the Moskva hotel. It was then the largest private building in the Kingdom of Serbia and the biggest hotel in Belgrade. In April 1941 it was badly damaged in the bombing, and a renovation was completed in 2013.

buildings.description: The Ministry of Transport building on Nemanjina street is one of the supreme achievements of high academicism in interwar Belgrade: Svetozar Jovanović designed it in 1927–1931, and the stone sculpture ensembles on its facades were made by Toma Rosandić, Dragomir Arambašić, Živojin Lukić, Lojze Dolinar and Risto Stijović. The Railway Museum, founded in 1950, is housed here today.
buildings.history: The building went up between 1927 and 1931 to Svetozar Jovanović's design, its whole interior subordinated to a specialised purpose: offices, studies and the main ceremonial hall lined the long corridors. A clock tower rises above the central pediment of the main facade, flanked by figures of Atlantes, and the sculptural ensembles in stone were carved by the leading sculptors of the generation. Part of the building now holds the Railway Museum, founded in 1950.

buildings.description: The palace built for the Ministry of Forestry and Mining and the Ministry of Agriculture and Waterworks now houses the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Its 1923 design came from Dragiša Brašovan and Nikola Nestorović, and Nikola Krasnov saw the building through to completion.
buildings.history: Construction ran in stages from 1923 to 1929: by 1926 the building had risen only to the first floor, and the job of finishing it was handed to the architect Nikola Krasnov, who kept the basic form and drew up the facades and interiors. The palace was completed in 1928. Two ministries moved in, and today it is the seat of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

buildings.description: The administrative palace of the National Bank is the most important work of the architect Konstantin A. Jovanović and one of the purest examples of academic style in Serbian architecture. The older wing dates from 1889, while the extension with its teller hall was added in 1922–1925.
buildings.history: The building went up in 1889 as the head office of the National Bank of the Kingdom of Serbia and was extended between 1922 and 1925 to a design by Konstantin A. Jovanović. The addition closed the block around an inner courtyard: the original hall with its monumental double staircase was kept, and a new teller hall was built alongside. Though nearly four decades separate the two phases, the interiors were drawn by the same architect and finished in a consistent manner.

buildings.description: The student residence of the University of Belgrade was designed by the Russian architect Georgij Pavlovič Kovaljevski, one of the group of Russian architects who helped shape Belgrade into a European capital in the post-war years. Its purpose has not changed since.
buildings.history: The dormitory was built in 1927/1928 for students of the University of Belgrade. It took a significant urban position in the shaping of the city centre, and the specific purpose it was given has survived to this day.

buildings.description: The palace built in 1935–1938 to house the Postal Savings Bank, the Main Post Office and the Main Telegraph under one roof — the central postal institution of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. Its appearance was shaped by Vasilije Androsov after the winning 1930 competition entry by Josip Pičman and Andrija Baranji was set aside in favour of a more monumental academic design.
buildings.history: The corner plot at Takovska and Bulevar kralja Aleksandra was bought in 1928 from the church of St. Mark for 13 million dinars; an all-Yugoslav competition for a palace of the Postal Savings Bank and Main Post Office followed in 1930 and drew fifteen entries. The first prize went to Josip Pičman and Andrija Baranji, but their scheme was dropped during the economic crisis and because the authorities wanted a more monumental image; new plans were drawn up under Dimitrije M. Leko and the façades were entrusted to Vasilije Androsov. Work began on 10 March 1935, the cornerstone was consecrated that August, and the palace was consecrated on 10 October 1938, with the post office opening on 28 November. After the war the wing along the boulevard, built for the Postal Savings Bank, housed the National Bank from 1946 until 2006, then government ministries, and since 2013 the Constitutional Court of Serbia, while the Takovska wing has remained a post office.

buildings.description: A building on Studentski trg, given by Captain Miša Anastasijević to his country for schools and learned institutions; today it houses the Rectorate of the University of Belgrade. It was built in 1857–1863 to plans by the Czech architect Jan Nevole.
buildings.history: The house was intended as a palace for the captain's daughter Sara and Đorđe Karađorđević, but the St Andrew's Assembly of 1859, which restored Prince Miloš to the throne, put an end to those plans. Construction ran from 1857 to 1863 to plans by the Czech architect Jan Nevole, with Josif Steinlechner as builder; in 1863 Miša Anastasijević handed the building over to the state and the Great School moved in. Later it housed the gymnasium, the ministry of education, the National Library and the National Museum, while its ceremonial hall hosted sittings of the assembly and the first exhibition of copies of Serbian frescoes organised by Mihailo Valtrović and Dragutin Milutinović. Half of the building now belongs to the Rectorate of the University of Belgrade.

buildings.description: The old building of the Faculty of Agriculture in Zemun was designed by the architect Vojin Petrović on the site of the former Kontumac. For Zemun it documents the years of economic, social and educational rise and the growth of higher education.
buildings.history: The two-storey building went up in 1932 to plans by Vojin Petrović on the ground of the former Kontumac and housed the Faculty of Agriculture. A third floor was added in 1947/48, and in the 1970s an extension was built that formed a single whole with the older part.

buildings.description: The first building in Belgrade purpose-built for technical faculties, and still home to the schools of electrical engineering, civil engineering and architecture. It was designed by Nikola Nestorović and Branko Tanazević.
buildings.history: The building was erected in 1925–1931 to a design by Nikola Nestorović and Branko Tanazević; until then the Technical Faculty occupied premises in Vasina Street. Its foundation stone was consecrated on 3 June 1926, when the walls already stood high above ground. After the Second World War a third storey was added to a design by Mihailo Radovanović. The original purpose has survived: three technical faculties still work here.

buildings.description: One of Belgrade's first large modern hotels: the house was built for the Insurance and Credit Society of the Belgrade Cooperative to a design by Nikola Nestorović, one of the leading Serbian architects of the day.
buildings.history: The hotel was built between 1910 and 1912 as the home of the Insurance and Credit Society of the Belgrade Cooperative. Nikola Nestorović designed it, and the Secessionist treatment places it in the mature phase of the Belgrade Secession. It is counted among the first large modern hotels in the city and as an anthology piece of Serbian architecture.

buildings.description: The building of the Second Women's Gymnasium, today the Nikola Tesla Electrotechnical School, was put up in 1933 to a design by the architect Milica Krstić-Čolak-Antić on the site of the Higher Women's School and the State Council. Here generations of Serbia's most accomplished women were educated, carrying literacy and culture into the country's towns, and the school itself became one of the engines of its cultural and technical advance. An academic frame filled with motifs of traditional Serbian-Byzantine building, set in a strong position in central Belgrade, makes the house a telling example of the city's architecture of its day.
buildings.history: The gymnasium received its own building in 1933: the architect Milica Krstić-Čolak-Antić drew the plans, and the plot had previously held the Higher Women's School and the State Council. The house was designed in the academic manner with motifs of traditional Serbian-Byzantine architecture, and its position in the centre alone made the school a marked element of the city fabric. As an educational institution it carried the schooling of its pupils and directly shaped the high achievements of Serbia in culture and technical development. It taught, first of all, generations of the country's most gifted women, who spread literacy and culture through these lands. Later the same walls housed the electrotechnical school, and more than a century of continuous teaching on one site remains an important record of Belgrade's educational history.

buildings.description: The Ministry of Posts building is one of the most successful surviving works of Momir Korunović and a representative example of the modern national style in Serbian architecture. When it was finished in 1930, it was one of the largest buildings in Belgrade.
buildings.history: The foundation stone was consecrated in December 1926, and the building went up between 1926 and 1930 to Korunović's design; at the time it was one of the biggest buildings in Belgrade. Korunović fused motifs from Serbian medieval building, European Romanticism and the Secession into an original expressionist whole.

buildings.description: A church on the Tašmajdan plateau, conceived as the metropolitan church of the Yugoslav capital and the largest Orthodox church in the country at the time. It was built between 1931 and 1940 to a design by the architects Petar and Branko Krstić.
buildings.history: The church was built between 1931 and 1940 beside a small cemetery chapel of 1835, on the spot where the sultan's decree on Serbian autonomy was read out in 1830. The Krstić brothers modelled it on the Gračanica monastery and sized it for its role as the metropolitan church of the royal capital; work on the interior was cut short by the war. The crypt holds King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga together with other members of the dynasty, and in 1968 the relics of Tsar Dušan were transferred here from the Monastery of the Holy Archangels near Prizren.

buildings.description: The library grew out of the book collection of the University of Belgrade, and its building was paid for by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace after Mabel and Slavko Grujić, the Kingdom's envoys in Washington, appealed to it. The design is by Dragutin Đorđević and Nikola Nestorović.
buildings.history: The collection began at the start of the 20th century, when the Velika škola became a university and received the books of the Serbian Seminar of the Faculty of Philosophy. Construction took four full years, and the library opened with ceremony in 1926. Dragutin Đorđević and Nikola Nestorović designed the palace, and a bust of Andrew Carnegie presented by his endowment stands in the vestibule.

buildings.description: The Museum of Science and Technology was founded in 1989 on the initiative of the academician Aleksandar Despić, the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts and twelve industrial organisations. Since 2005 it has been housed in the old thermal power station in Dorćol, at Skender-begova 51.
buildings.history: The museum was conceived as a keeper of the country’s technical heritage, yet it began with no collection at all: from the first inventory number onwards the curators assembled the holdings themselves, mostly through gifts. At the end of 2005 the Serbian government assigned it the building of the first public thermal power station in Dorćol, and the reconstruction and extension were designed by the architect Boris Podreka, who presented the scheme in May 2007. As the project stalled, the museum opened its doors on 28 August 2009 with an exhibition on Serbia’s technical heritage, followed by “Second Circle”, more than 400 objects from 25 collections on 1,600 square metres.

buildings.description: A Romanian Orthodox church in Ovča, in Belgrade’s Palilula municipality, built between 1921 and 1933 to a design by the architect Radivoje Predić with money from the parish and the villagers. It counts among the few surviving examples of the Serbian-Byzantine manner in the Banat.
buildings.history: An older nineteenth-century church, a small chapel of rammed earth, stood on the site before the present one, and four icons of 1837 from its iconostasis were kept and are attributed to the circle of Konstantin Danil, most likely to his pupil Jovan Popović. The works were entrusted to the builder Stevan Katinić of Zemun, and the church and the believers of Ovča paid for them. In 1989 the icon painter Boško Kovačev decorated the interior.

buildings.description: Saint Sava Seminary in Belgrade is an educational institution of the Serbian Orthodox Church that trains clergy and teachers. Its history reaches back to the first seminary in Serbia, founded by Dositej Obradović, which worked for three years and closed after the defeat of the First Serbian Uprising. In 1896 the school was reorganised and named after Saint Sava, and since the 1957/58 academic year it has occupied its present building in Karaburma.
buildings.history: The first seminary in Serbia, founded by Dositej Obradović and run by Vikentije Raić, abbot of the Fenek monastery, lasted three years and closed after the First Serbian Uprising was defeated in 1813. In 1826 Metropolitan Petar Jovanović opened a school for clergy in the Prince's Residence in Kragujevac, where the course ran one year, then two, three from 1838 and four from 1844. In 1896 the seminary was reorganised as the Seminary of Saint Sava, admitting pupils who had finished primary school, with a nine-year course, and it began work in that form in 1900. In 1920, when all seminaries were reformed, Saint Sava's moved to Sremski Karlovci, and from 1928/29 the course lasted six years. Teaching stopped when the Second World War began; in 1943 an improvised seminary with classes II to VI ran in Niš, and in 1949 the school reopened at the Rakovica monastery. Since 1957/58 it has occupied the present building in Karaburma.

buildings.description: The Faculty of Orthodox Theology is the part of the University of Belgrade that trains specialists in Orthodox theology. The idea of a higher school of theology for the Serbian Church was discussed from the 1860s, and the 1905 university law already provided for such a faculty, yet work began only in the autumn of 1920. The faculty sits in Palilula, and its library and theological journal became the backbone of its research.
buildings.history: In 1892 came a proposal to turn the capital's theological seminary into a faculty of the Higher School, and in 1899 a commission on the transformation of that school and a church delegation agreed to open a theological faculty within the future university. The Serbian Church then reformed its secondary theological schools so that their graduates could continue their studies. The 1905 law on the University of Belgrade already included the faculty, but a shortage of teachers and the strains of the Balkan wars and the First World War pushed its opening to the autumn of 1920. Its academic council met for the first time on 6 September 1920 and chose as dean the protopriest Stefan Dimitrijević, a historian of the Serbian Orthodox Church, while classes began on 15 December. The library became the base of research: its first book arrived on 12 December 1920, when the fund already held 3,075 publications, by 1930 it counted 9,700 titles, and in 1926 the faculty launched its theological journal.

buildings.description: The Ukrainian embassy in Belgrade is the country's diplomatic mission in Serbia, working from a building on Paje Adamova Street that the government bought for the mission in 2009. Relations between the two states reached embassy level on 15 April 1994, and the first Ukrainian mission opened in 1995. Today the chancery represents Ukrainian interests, carries out consular work and keeps up political, economic and cultural contacts with Serbia.
buildings.history: Embassy-level relations with the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia date from 15 April 1994. Vadym Prymachenko became the first Ukrainian ambassador in August 1996, after serving as general consul and then as chargé d'affaires. The first Ukrainian embassy was inaugurated in 1995 and later moved to other premises; in December 2009 the government bought a house on Paje Adamova Street 4 for the mission. By 2018 the two countries had signed 73 bilateral documents, among them interstate, intergovernmental and regional agreements. That July the embassy reacted to protests in Serbia over Ukrainian political questions, asking that the country's internal affairs not be interfered with, and in December it examined the case of a confiscated consignment of artefacts — Bronze Age, Byzantine, medieval, ancient Slavic and Celtic — on their way from Ukraine to Serbia.

buildings.description: The Royal Chapel of Saint Andrew the First-Called is a small Orthodox church beside the Royal Palace in the Dedinje compound, dedicated to the apostle whom the Karađorđević family honours as its patron saint. Building began in 1924 together with the palace, following the model of the King's Church at Studenica and the monastery of Saint Andrew on the Treska. Živojin Nikolić designed it with the Russian émigré architect Viktor Lukomsky, and its walls were laid in white stone from the island of Hvar. Services are still rare, usually held for occasions in the Karađorđević family.
buildings.history: The chapel was founded in 1924, at the same time as the Royal Palace, while the furnishings for worship arrived only in 1936. Until the April War of 1941 it guarded precious Christian relics — the right hand of John the Baptist, the icon of the Mother of God known as Filerimos and a particle of the True Cross — which King Peter II carried away to Ostrog monastery. After the liberation of Belgrade in 1944 a partisan entered and fired at the face of Christ Pantocrator, and the mark is visible to this day. No liturgy was held there until 2001, when Patriarch Pavle consecrated it after Alexander Karađorđević and his family moved into the Royal Palace. The frescoes were painted by Russian masters Boris Obraskov, Baron Nikolai Mayendorff, Vladimir Bichkovski and Yevgeny Varun-Secret.

buildings.description: A winter garden built for Josip Broz Tito and later turned into his burial place; it is now part of the Museum of Yugoslavia. It was built in 1975 to a design by the architect Stjepan Kralj.
buildings.history: The pavilion was built in 1975 as a winter garden for Tito's residence in Užička Street and was then called the Flower House; the architect was Stjepan Kralj. Tito spent much time there, especially after his final break with his wife Jovanka in August 1977, and before his death he asked to be buried in this winter garden. After he died on 4 May 1980 the fountain in the centre was removed and within days, before the funeral on 8 May, the space was rebuilt as a tomb; the site then became a place of pilgrimage and in 1982 was included in the Josip Broz Tito Memorial Centre, reorganised in 1996 as the Museum of Yugoslavia. In 2013 Tito's wife Jovanka was buried beside him.

buildings.description: The türbeh of Damat Ali Pasha is an Ottoman mausoleum of 1784 in Belgrade Fortress's Upper Town. It holds the body of Silahdar Damat Ali Pasha, the Ottoman general and grand vizier, and together with Sheik Mustafa's Tomb it is one of the last surviving examples of Islamic funerary architecture in the city. The small domed building survived bombardment and decades of changing use, and remains a rare physical trace of Ottoman Belgrade.
buildings.history: When the Turkish army left in 1867, the building became a store, then housed a collection of old weapons and captured trophies. The 1915 bombardment of Belgrade destroyed the portal and part of the niche holding the original inscription; the Austrians started repairs that same year, and Belgrade's city municipality finished the reconstruction in the 1930s, when a new plaque was set above the entrance. Research and restoration in 1936–1937, led by Mehmed Delić, uncovered two graves beneath the brick floor and a broken nişan inscribed in 1818/19. The marble plaque had been taken to Budapest during the First World War and was returned in 1958 through the restitution of cultural property, later passing to the türbeh. Marko Popović's 1991 study established the 1784 date that underpins the building's present attribution.

buildings.description: The house takes its name from its owner, the merchant Manak Mihailović, and remains the rarest kind of old Belgrade town house from the first half of the 19th century. It is now part of the Ethnographic Museum and holds the Hristifor Crnilović collection.
buildings.history: The house was built around 1830, when the efforts of the renewed Serbian state were focused on turning Belgrade into a Serbian town and preparing it for the role of capital. It marks the old line linking the Varoš kapija gate with the Topčider road, and the medieval route between the Sava bank and Zeleni venac. Today it forms part of the Ethnographic Museum.

buildings.description: The family house of Jovan Cvijić was built in 1905 on Kopitareva gradina, and together with the collection preserved inside it remains an authentic testimony to the life and work of the scholar. Cvijić was not only a geographer and a connoisseur of the lands and peoples of the Balkans but also president of the Serbian Academy of Sciences, professor and rector of Belgrade University, and an honorary doctor of the Sorbonne and of Prague University. Today the house is a museum devoted to him, and its interior is prized above all for the painted decoration of walls and ceilings by Dragutin Inkiostri Medenjak, inspired by the landscapes of Bosnia, Šumadija and Herzegovina.
buildings.history: The family house of Jovan Cvijić was built in 1905 on Kopitareva gradina. The collection of objects preserved in it remains an authentic testimony to the life and work of the scholar, one of the finest connoisseurs of the lands and peoples of the Balkan Peninsula. Cvijić was president of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and a corresponding member of the Yugoslav Academy, professor and rector of Belgrade University, and an honorary doctor of the Sorbonne and of Prague University. For his services to geography and geology he was awarded gold and silver medals by the geographical societies of London, New York and Paris. The house, a pronounced example of early twentieth-century academism, is today a museum devoted to him. Its interior is distinguished above all by the painted decoration of walls and ceilings by Dragutin Inkiostri Medenjak, whose themes were inspired by the landscapes of Bosnia, Šumadija and Herzegovina.

buildings.description: The house of the merchant Miloje Božić, raised in 1836 over the remains of an older Turkish building. Since 1951 it has held the Museum of Theatre Arts of Serbia and ranks among the oldest homes still standing in Belgrade.
buildings.history: Miloje Božić, a merchant from the village of Čumić near Kragujevac, built the house in 1836 and had his initials and the year carved above the entrance. It stayed purely residential through the nineteenth century; after the Božić family it belonged to Rista Hadži-Popović, an exporter from Skopje, until 1920. Between 1920 and 1924 the sculptor Toma Rosandić kept his studio and flat there, and the house was then turned into a painters’ house where Belgrade artists lived and worked. In 1951 the Museum of Theatre Arts of Serbia moved in.

buildings.description: The first building designed specifically for the First Belgrade Gymnasium, a school founded back in 1839 as the second grammar school in the Principality of Serbia. Its architect was Milica Krstić.
buildings.history: Founded in 1839 as the second grammar school in the Principality of Serbia, the gymnasium spent almost a century without premises of its own. The house on Cara Dušana Street was finally built in 1938 to a design by Milica Krstić, in the unornamented modernist manner then current in Belgrade. Generations of its pupils went on to become statesmen, military commanders, politicians, artists, scholars and professors.

buildings.description: The “King Petar I” school on Kralja Petra Street rose in 1905–1906 on the site of an older elementary school at Varoš kapija, and when it opened it was called the most modern building for primary teaching in Serbia. Jelisaveta Načić, the country's first woman architect, drew the plans, and the school is counted her most important work. Standing in the main čaršija beside the cathedral, the Metropolitanate and the Princess Ljubica residence, it records the social and cultural climate of Belgrade at the start of the twentieth century.
buildings.history: The building went up on the site of the earlier school at Varoš kapija at the start of the twentieth century, when Belgrade needed new school houses. Jelisaveta Načić produced the design and combined an academic composition with elements of the Secession, more visible inside than on the facades. The corner single-storey house, with three street facades and a representative entrance, received the ceremonial air expected of a school in the middle of the čaršija. For its functional and artistic qualities the building is held to be the architect's finest work and a notable achievement in Belgrade architecture.

buildings.description: The only survivor of the palace complex of Prince Miloš Obrenović’s sons: a hammam of 1836–37, laid out on the principles of Turkish public baths and now run as a catering venue.
buildings.history: Work on the bath began in 1836–37, while the modern Serbian state was still taking shape, yet it followed the conventions of Turkish public baths. It formed part of the palace complex of the prince’s sons and was later used by the Ministry of Finance, the hammam being all that remains of the ensemble. Hadži Nikola Živković, Prince Miloš’s court builder, is thought to have conceived it; the Topčider residence and Princess Ljubica’s residence are also credited to him. In 1948 the hammam was listed as a cultural monument, though later alterations have largely erased its authenticity.

buildings.description: Palilula Elementary School on Takovska Street opened in 1894, only a year after the school in Dorcol, and it marks the point at which Belgrade finally took up the most advanced European ideas about school design. Milan Antonovic drew the plans in the academic spirit of the nineteenth century. The building took a corner where three streets meet and was given a spacious yard, while its symmetrical block, with a raised central section and two equal entrances, sets out a clear school plan. Beside it stands the Skolska trpeza, an endowment of Nikola Spasic built in 1905.
buildings.history: The school was built in 1894 to a design by Milan Antonovic. A year earlier the Dorcol school had appeared in the city, and Palilula took the next step, adopting the most advanced European solutions of the day for school buildings. A plot at the corner of three streets allowed the building to be surrounded by a spacious yard, and the plan was made single-tract, with corridors facing the yard and classrooms facing the street. Symmetry is stressed by a raised central section, which holds two staircases on the courtyard side and is matched by two equal entrances on the main facade. As early as 1894 the building had a full set of services, including central heating and ventilation ducts. In 1905 the Skolska trpeza, the endowment of Nikola Spasic, was built on the same site.

buildings.description: Vuk Karadžić Elementary School is one of the oldest schools in Serbia, founded in 1838 and known as the Palilula School until 1931. Its main building on Takovska Street was designed by Milan Antonović and completed in 1894 on land given by the Serbian commander Toma Vučić Perišić. The school counts poets Vojislav Ilić and Milutin Bojić among its former pupils.
buildings.history: Teaching began in 1838 with 35 pupils under the first teacher, Milutin Popović, followed by Živko Stefanović. The old building nearest Takovska Street was built in 1894 to Milan Antonović's design, and a small building followed in 1905, paid for by the benefactor Nikola Spasić. That small building initially housed the city's first pupils' boarding canteen, the oldest school institution in Belgrade for poor and travelling pupils. A middle building linked to the old school by a passage was added in 1956, and the large gymnasium in 1963. The school marks its day on 6 November, the birthday of Vuk Karadžić.

buildings.description: The Belgrade Philharmonic is the oldest symphony orchestra in Serbia, founded in 1923 by the composer and conductor Stevan Hristić. Its hall stands in central Belgrade and hosts many of the orchestra's concerts. In 2023 the ensemble received the Sretenje Order, first class.
buildings.history: The orchestra gave its first concert in 1923, drawing on players from the National Theatre opera, Belgrade music schools and a few amateurs, with Hristić as founder, artistic director and chief conductor. Under Hristić, until 1936, it established a subscription concert system and took on the classical and contemporary repertoire of the day. After a first international tour to Sofia in 1936, Lovro Matačić took over and raised the ensemble's performing level until the Second World War. In the post-war years Oskar Danon led the orchestra, which played its first post-war concert on 7 November 1944 and gained official autonomy in 1951. The 1960s brought its peak, with a fifth-place ranking among European orchestras under Živojin Zdravković, while the 1990s brought a ban on international performances and the loss of many players. After 2000 the orchestra was revived, and a support foundation appeared in 2004.

buildings.description: The Press House at Knez Mihailova 6 was raised in 1958–1961 from Ratomir Bogojević's competition-winning design — one of the few of his works that were built, and by common account his finest. The eight-storey prism was meant to hold the Cultural Centre of Belgrade and the Union of Journalists of Yugoslavia, bringing editorial rooms, halls and exhibition spaces under one roof. Set on the edge of a block destroyed in the war, it completed the ensemble of Trg republike and gave the square a new anchor.
buildings.history: Ratomir Bogojević won the competition, and building ran from 1958 to 1961; during the works the number of investors and users grew, and the architect had to change the spatial and functional organisation. A freely treated plan let the various cultural and business contents find their own levels, while the facade was assembled from a modular system of windows that produced a polychrome grid. The eight-storey block, with two recessed storeys forming its fifth facade, holds the square and answers the neighbouring Albania Palace, reading with it as a single urban entity. For the younger generation of Belgrade architects the house became a model, and Bogojević, who died in 1962, left it as his most important work.

buildings.description: Belgrade's first skyscraper, the Mortgage Bank of the Trade Fund palace at the corner of Knez Mihailova and Kolarčeva. Built on the site of the 1860 Albanija kafana, it long set the height marker for the city centre.
buildings.history: The palace was built in 1938–1939 for the Mortgage Bank of the Trade Fund to a competition design by Branko Bon and Milan Grakalić, and completed to designs by Miladin Prljević and engineer Đorđe Lazarević; on completion it was the second-tallest skyscraper in South-East Europe. The site had held the 1860 Albanija kafana, demolished in the night of 17 October 1936. In 1944 it withstood a half-tonne bomb, and on 20 October 1944 the Yugoslav flag was raised on it to mark Belgrade's liberation.

buildings.description: At Knez Mihailova 12 stands the house from which Geca Kon ran the largest publishing business in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. Kon had opened Belgrade's first bookshop in 1901; in 1932 he moved his own shop into this building, which he had bought from Petar and Milovan Matić and which the architect Radoslav Todorović designed in 1928. The shop turned into a meeting place for the writers and intellectuals of interwar Belgrade.
buildings.history: Geca Kon began with a bookshop and soon added publishing: law, social sciences, literature, university and school textbooks. He printed the collected works of the best-known writers of his day, among them Konstantin Jireček's history of the Serbs, Dvorniković's characterology of the Yugoslavs, Jovan Cvijić's 'Balkan Peninsula' and the encyclopaedic 'Serbian People in the Nineteenth Century'. By the interwar decades his list had passed five thousand titles, which made him the Kingdom of Yugoslavia's largest publisher. In 1932 he opened his bookshop at Knez Mihailova 12, in a house bought from Petar and Milovan Matić and built in 1928 to Radoslav Todorović's design. The shop quickly became the haunt of leading writers and intellectuals. Kon worked for four decades, until his tragic death in 1941, pulling Serbian bookselling and publishing toward European practice.

buildings.description: The House of the Association of Yugoslav Engineers and Architects on Kneza Miloša Street went up between 1933 and 1935 to a design by Milan Manojlović and Isak Azriel, for a professional society founded in 1919. The building was meant to make the ideology of integral Yugoslavism visible, the political doctrine the association and the state treated as dominant. Plain walls without ornament, and windows sized to the rooms behind them, made it one of the purest functionalist statements in prewar Belgrade.
buildings.history: The association that commissioned the house had been formed in 1919 as a body of engineers and architects for the new state, and a building of its own was to secure its public standing. Work ran from 1933 to 1935: the range towards Kneza Miloša rose four storeys high, while on the Lazarevićeva side the volume was broken up and set back from the building line. Above the ground-floor mass an L-shaped structure appeared with a flat roof terrace, and the glass plane on the projecting part marked the staircase. Uniform windows on the floors suggested identical offices behind them, while the large openings of the lower zone pointed to public and representative rooms for meetings; the single concession to tradition was the stone cladding of that lower zone.

buildings.description: Serbia’s oldest and foremost museum, founded in 1844, has occupied the former Fund Administration palace on Republic Square since 1952. The 1903 building was designed by Nikola Nestorović and Andra Stevanović.
buildings.history: The museum opened in 1844 and has moved several times since: from Kapetan Miša’s building to Princess Ljubica’s residence and the New Palace, before settling on Republic Square in 1952. The building itself went up in 1903 as the palace of the Fund Administration and later housed the Mortgage Bank, making it one of the country’s earliest banking houses after the National Bank of 1889. It gained an atrium and a wing towards Laze Paču Street in 1930, and in 1964–66 the museum was rebuilt to drawings by Aleksandar Deroko, Petar Anagnosti and Zoran Petrović.

buildings.description: A rental building on Knez Mihailova, put up in 1922–26 to a concept by Petar Popović with Dragiša Brašovan. Its ground-floor kafana, Russian Tsar, inherited the name of the old single-storey house on the site and counted Branislav Nušić among its regulars.
buildings.history: The house went up between 1922 and 1926: Petar Popović supplied the concept, Dragiša Brašovan developed it, and the architect Milan Sekulić acted as contractor. The name Russian Tsar came from the old single-storey building that had stood on the plot before. In the interwar years the kafana had the air of a smart Belgrade establishment, with the painter Mihajlo Petrov, the writer Veljko Petrović and Branislav Nušić as regulars. Its original interior was destroyed in the early 1960s, when the first self-service restaurant, Zagreb, opened in the space.

buildings.description: Founded in Belgrade in 1896, Prometna banka put money directly into industry, and by 1912 it had outgrown its cramped quarters in Uskočka Street and began building its own house on Knez Mihailova. The design came from the architect Danilo Vladisavljević together with the engineer Miloš Savčić, chairman of the board: shops filled the ground floor, the bank's offices took the first floor, and the Srbija insurance company the second. A Secession building of large glass surfaces, a corner dome and sculpture above the cornice, it was bolder than most of its neighbours, and the painted vestibule windows showed Serbia sheltering trade, industry, technology and agriculture.
buildings.history: Prometna banka was set up in Belgrade in 1896 and, beyond ordinary banking, put capital straight into industrial ventures. Its earlier address was a single-storey house at Uskočka 6, and only the bank's growth and the drive of its board chairman, the engineer Miloš Savčić, made the move to Knez Mihailova possible, with work starting in 1912. Vladisavljević and Savčić produced the design, and by 1914 the building was complete: shops at street level kept the commercial character of the street, the bank occupied the floor above, and the Srbija insurance company the one above that. Bold structure, broad glazing and the introduction of a mezzanine new to Belgrade set it apart from the Secession around it. The bank stayed until it closed in 1949.

buildings.description: The station from which the first train left for Zemun on 1 September 1884, carrying King Milan I and Queen Natalija. After its reconstruction in 2020 the building has been earmarked for the Historical Museum of Serbia.
buildings.history: The station building went up in 1882–85 alongside Serbia’s first railway, the Belgrade–Niš line completed in 1884; the Austrian von Flattich supplied the concept, which the architect Dragiša Milutinović developed. The first train left for Zemun on 1 September 1884 amid palace ceremony, carrying King Milan I, Queen Natalija and the heir Alexander, with more than two hundred foreign guests at the opening. The station handled both passengers and freight until those roles passed to new yards at Makiš and Prokop, and after the 2020 reconstruction the building is meant to receive the Historical Museum of Serbia.

buildings.description: A pavilion built in 1928 by the Association of Friends of Art in Belgrade to a design by Branislav Kojić. Until the Second World War it remained the city’s only exhibition venue, hosting every show of domestic and foreign art.
buildings.history: The Association of Friends of Art commissioned the building, and Branislav Kojić compressed painting galleries, an exhibition hall and a concert hall into a single structure. Živorad Nastasijević painted the vestibule ceiling with allegories of the arts, and Vasa Pomorišac made the stained glass above the main entrance. Among the first events held here were the Salon of Architecture and two large exhibitions of Yugoslav modern architecture, in 1931 and 1933.

buildings.description: The Grujić family villa, built in 1896 to a design by Milan Kapetanović. Its treasure is a family collection assembled over generations, tied to Jevrem Grujić, founder of the Liberal Party, and General Kosta Protić.
buildings.history: The villa went up in 1896 as a free-standing town house, unusual in Belgrade for its painted façades: the decoration imitating sgraffito was done by the Italian master Domenico d’Andrea. Over the generations the family gathered a precious collection of objects, mostly of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries — paintings, sculpture, applied art, old weapons, archives and books. It is bound up with Teodor Herbez, finance minister to Prince Miloš, with Jevrem Grujić himself, General Kosta Protić and the journalist Stevan Ćurčić.

buildings.description: The Museum of Aviation stands inside the Nikola Tesla airport complex near Belgrade, a free-standing rotunda begun in 1969 and completed twenty years later to a design by Ivan Štraus. Its circular torus was conceived as an emblem of the institution itself, and the glazed skin lets the exhibits read against the airfield beyond. The lower ring acts as a podium carrying the museum's working core, while the exhibition level is handled on a monumental, representative scale. In 1989 the building received the federal Borba award for the best architectural work of the year.
buildings.history: The museum was planned as part of Belgrade's main airport, and the setting shaped it: aircraft could be seen both inside the display and out on the apron through the glass. Work stretched across two decades, from 1969 to 1989, with structural design entrusted to Belgrade engineers. Ivan Štraus split the programme in two — a service podium below and a ceremonial exhibition tier above — and wrapped both into a single torus. Almost from the day it opened, the museum ranked among the country's leading institutions, and its holdings, backed by a large archive, became the standard reference for aviation in the region from 1911 onward. In 1989 the building won the federal Borba award for architecture.

buildings.description: The Spanish House in Belgrade's Savamala is a once-representative palace raised around 1880 in the spirit of nineteenth-century academic architecture. It served the river port as a customs house, later became a warehouse and premises of the Serbian Shipping Company, and after the First World War housed the Museum of River Navigation. By the early twenty-first century the half-ruined building had become one of Savamala's symbols and a stage for art projects and repeated rebuilding plans.
buildings.history: The Spanish House was raised around 1880 as a palace with a basement, ground floor and one upper storey. In its port years it served as a customs house and then as a warehouse, and the Serbian Shipping Company also used it; after the war the Museum of River Navigation moved in. From the middle of the twentieth century the building changed several tenants and almost as many reconstruction schemes, most of which stalled for lack of money. Yugoslav River Shipping rented offices there for about a decade until 2003, hoping to restore a museum use, but instead created its river navigation museum in its own office building in Kneza Miloša Street. A later investor planned a hotel, stripped the interior down to the outer walls and added new elements, yet that attempt also collapsed over finances. In 2012 the near-ruin, by then without roof or windows, became the base of the Goethe-Institut's Urban Incubator: Belgrade project for Savamala; the temporary-architecture works stopped two years later, after an art pavilion had opened there in 2013.

buildings.description: One of the first modern barracks in Serbia: the home of the 7th Regiment, raised at the close of the nineteenth century to plans by Dragutin Đorđević. It took a corner site among the other military buildings of the quarter, and its heraldry — the arms of the Kingdom of Serbia, shields and armour — announced the soldier's trade to the street. It remains among the most representative military buildings preserved in Belgrade.
buildings.history: The barracks for the 7th Regiment went up at the end of the nineteenth century, when purpose-built modern military housing was still a novelty in Serbia. Dragutin Đorđević's design provided two storeys over a basement and a semi-basement. In 1927 Božidar Vukićević added a third floor, giving the block its present height. It still stands among the other military buildings of the quarter, as it was meant to.

buildings.description: The House of the Workers' Chamber on Nemanjina Street was raised in a single season, between 1 May and 24 November 1928, to a design by Svetislav Putnik. It was conceived as a monumental public building that would hold the chamber's offices, its representative halls and rooms for overnight stays. At its heart lay a theatre auditorium shaped as an atrium on the ground floor, and with it the house entered the history of the Serbian stage.
buildings.history: The contractor Tuner i Vagner built it from Svetislav Putnik's drawings, with a basement, a semi-basement, a high ground floor and four storeys above. The chamber received a symmetrical academic facade whose central arched portal was flanked by two monumental figures of workers, a reminder of whom the institution served. The entrance has since been walled up and the sculptures removed, their trace lost. Inside, little of the original finish survives; the present appearance of the rooms is the work of later reconstructions.

buildings.description: The only garrison church in Belgrade and Serbia, raised in 1863 primarily for the army at the initiative of Metropolitan Mihailo and Prince Mihailo Obrenović, to plans by Pavle Stanišić and Jovan Ristić.
buildings.history: The church rose in 1863, in the age of romanticism and in reference to the traditions of Serbian medieval church building. Two church houses and a new bell tower followed in the churchyard in 1865, 1891 and 1939; the older house sheltered the First Belgrade Gymnasium from 1865 to 1906. Stevan Todorović painted the iconostasis in 1881, and among the bells kept here is the small one from the cathedral, the first to ring after the Hatt-i Sharif of 1830.

buildings.description: The Faculty of Teacher Education is a member of the University of Belgrade, housed in the former Women's Teacher School building. Its foundation stone was laid in 1933, and the design came from Jovanka Bončić-Katerinić, one of the most experienced engineers and architects of the Ministry of Buildings' architectural department. She combined classical academic principles with modern ideas, producing a restrained building without ornament whose clear spatial structure still serves teacher training.
buildings.history: In 1933 the foundation stone was laid for the new building of the Women's Teacher School. The design came from Jovanka Bončić-Katerinić of the Ministry of Buildings' architectural department, which after the First World War was responsible for all state buildings. The house is a synthesis of classical academic and modern construction: restrained, without stylistic elements or decoration, with a coherent spatial structure. Today it accommodates the Faculty of Teacher Education of the University of Belgrade.

buildings.description: Beli dvor, the White Palace, is one of the two residences of the Karađorđević royal compound on the Dedinje hill in Belgrade. King Alexander I commissioned it with his own funds as a home for his three sons, and Prince Regent Paul oversaw its completion and was the only member of the family to live there before the war. Later it became a stage for state ceremonies and receptions, and it now holds a notable collection of European painting.
buildings.history: Construction began in 1934, the year Alexander I was assassinated in Marseille, and the palace was finished in 1937 under Prince Paul's supervision. Aleksandar Đorđević designed it in a Neo-Palladian manner drawing on English country houses of the 18th century, among them Ditchley Park, while the French firm Maison Jansen decorated the interiors. A kitchen and garage were linked to the main building by an underground tunnel, and a shelter was added before the war. After 1945 the communist government seized the royal family's property, and the palace was used by Tito and later by Slobodan Milošević for official functions. Milošević received the US envoy Richard Holbrooke there before the NATO bombing and later resigned in front of the fireplace of the Main Hall, and much of the original inventory was sold off, with only a small part returned. Today Prince Alexander and his family use the palace, which is owned by the Republic of Serbia.

buildings.description: The home of the Belgrade Cooperative for Mutual Aid and Savings, a society founded in 1882 that grew into one of the capital's leading banks and the first domestic insurance institution in Serbia. The palace was built to the joint design of Nikola Nestorović and Andra Stevanović — their most important shared work and a benchmark of Belgrade architecture at the turn of the 20th century.
buildings.history: The cooperative was founded in 1882 on the initiative of a group of Belgrade merchants, became a joint-stock company in 1890 and opened an insurance department in 1897 — the first domestic insurer in the country — operating until 1944. In 1897 the shareholders resolved to build a new headquarters and bought plots near the former Small Market on the Sava; construction ran from spring 1905 to 1907. The commission went to Nikola Nestorović, who worked out the plans and interiors, and Andra Stevanović, responsible for the structural system; on waterlogged ground by the Sava the foundations were made of reinforced concrete for the first time in Belgrade. Damaged in the 1941 and 1944 bombings, the building was later taken over by the Geological-Geophysical Institute "Jovan Žujović", which added extra floors in 1956/57 and 1958/59.

buildings.description: The house that the architect and university professor Nikola Nestorović designed for himself in 1903, and where he lived and worked. A rare surviving family house, it reflects the high standard of domestic culture in Serbian middle-class life around 1900.
buildings.history: Built in 1903, the villa was designed by Nikola Nestorović, a prominent architect and university professor, who also lived and worked in it. Its central three-part plan, with basement, ground floor and attic, forms a single composition with the symmetrically laid-out garden. The baroque ornament of the main façade was carved by Franja Valdman.

buildings.description: The British Embassy in Belgrade is the United Kingdom's chief diplomatic mission in Serbia and also represents the British Overseas Territories. It works from a building on Resavska Street, while the ambassador's residence carries the name Elsie Inglis House. The name honours Elsie Inglis, the Scottish doctor and suffragist who organised Scottish Women's Hospital units in Serbia.
buildings.history: The first British legation stood at 22 Gračanička Street, but as consular and commercial business grew the mission outgrew the house and in the mid-1930s moved into leased premises at number 42 in the same street. After the Second World War that building was again overcrowded; in 1951 the Serbian government sold the neighbouring plot at number 44 to the mission. The lease on number 42 ended in the late 1970s, and the embassy is now at Resavska 46. When Tito visited Britain in 1953, Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden raised the embassy's accommodation needs with him, and in 1955 the Yugoslav authorities offered land for a new residence, an offer accepted that year. The residence took the name Elsie Inglis House in 2015, at a ceremony held on International Women's Day and led by President Tomislav Nikolić and Ambassador Denis Keefe.

buildings.description: The Belgrade Drama Theatre began in August 1947 as the City Theatre, the first company founded in the Serbian capital after the Second World War. A theatre at Crveni Krst had already been foreseen by the city's 1923 master plan, yet its own stage opened only in the 1948/49 season. Fame came with productions of contemporary American drama around 1960, and after the 2003 reconstruction the auditorium seats 495.
buildings.history: Petar Petrović staged Boris Gorbatov's «Mladost otaca» in the hall of the National Theatre on 20 February 1948, and that premiere opened the company's history. Its own house at Crveni Krst received audiences in the 1948/49 season, starting with Nušić's «Sumnjivo lice» directed by Salko Repak on 20 March 1949. From 1959 to 1975 the company was merged with Belgrade Comedy into a single house called «Savremeno pozorište», then separated again in December 1975 and returned to its present name. In the mid-1950s and early 1960s it staged «Death of a Salesman», «Cat on a Hot Tin Roof», «The Glass Menagerie» and «A View from the Bridge», performances that stayed in the memory of generations. A thorough reconstruction completed in spring 2003 brought the building up to high European standards.

buildings.description: The villa where King Peter I of Serbia spent the last years of his life. It was built in 1896 for the Belgrade merchant Đorđe Pavlović, and in 1919 the house was rented and adapted for the monarch on his return to Belgrade. The interiors of this royal residence were deliberately modest, in keeping with the king's own character.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1896 for the merchant Đorđe Pavlović as a free-standing villa with a large garden. After the king died in 1921, the government of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes bought the property in 1924 with the intention of opening a museum of King Peter I there. A monumental gate was added at the garden entrance, its portal modelled on those of the court complex at Terazije. Three key dates from the king's life, the arms of the Kingdom of Serbia and his monogram were carved on the gate, because the villa itself carried no mark that a great ruler had lived in it.

buildings.description: The Third Boys' Gymnasium got its own house on Njegoševa in 1906, built to a design by Dragutin Đorđević and Dušan Živanović as a representative school modelled on the most advanced institutions of its kind in Europe. Among the pupils the source lists are Stevan Sremac, Simo Matavulj and Živojin Mišić.
buildings.history: The house went up in 1906: Vasa Tešić carried out the building work, Franja Valdman carved the architectural sculpture, and Dragutin Inkiostri Medenjak and Paško Vučetić painted the interiors. Its desks, the source notes, were occupied by Todor Mijušković, Vladimir Titelbah, Nikola Vulić and Marko Murat.

buildings.description: The Church of Saint Alexander Nevsky, whose cult was brought to Belgrade by soldiers of the Russian Volunteer Corps of General Chernayev. Construction began to a design by Jelislaveta Načić and was finished with the help of Vasilije Androsov; the north choir holds a marble altar to the fallen of the liberation wars of 1876–1878, 1912–1913 and 1914–1918.
buildings.history: The church was begun in 1912 to Jelislaveta Načić's design, but the First World War stretched the work to 1929, and the architect Vasilije Androsov had a large part in finishing it. The iconostasis was installed in 1930 after being made for the Karađorđević endowment at Oplenac, with icons painted in the workshop of Boris Seljanak. In the same year the north choir received a marble altar to the fallen, designed by Mihailo Milojković, and the south choir a monument to Tsar Nicholas II of Russia and King Alexander I Karađorđević.

buildings.description: Prince Miloš's residence in Topčider is the work of Janja Mihailović and Nikola Đorđević, who built it under the supervision of the prince's chief builder, Hadži Nikola Živković. With its parks and buildings of various purposes it formed the Obrenović court complex — then the political, church and cultural centre of the Principality of Serbia.
buildings.history: The residence was built between 1831 and 1833, when the Topčider estate was laid out on European lines, with buildings of different purposes set among parks and the natural landscape. For many years it served as the ruler's court, and in 1966 it became part of the Historical Museum of Serbia.

buildings.description: The birthplace of Vojvoda Stepa Stepanović in Kumodraž is a modest rural house of the mid-nineteenth century, in which one of Serbia's most prominent military commanders was born in 1856. Preserved houses of this popular-architecture type are few in the Belgrade area, and their architectural and ethnographic value has only grown with time. The house stands as a monument to a man whose name is woven into modern Serbian history, from the wars of 1876–1918 to the breakthrough of the Salonika Front.
buildings.history: The house was built in the middle of the nineteenth century, and in 1856 Stepa Stepanović, one of the most prominent Serbian military commanders, was born in it. His long military service mirrors the history of the development and strengthening of the Serbian army: he earned the rank of vojvoda through the skill he showed in the wars of 1876–1918, and twice served as minister of the army. After Radomir Putnik he was largely responsible for establishing and implementing the organisational basis of the Serbian armed forces. His greatest success was the breakthrough of the Salonika Front, which placed him among the foremost commanders of the First World War. A year after the war ended he retired from active service and lived withdrawn in Čačak until his death. As an example of vernacular architecture the house has architectural and ethnographic value, the greater for the small number of preserved houses of this type near Belgrade.

buildings.description: Belgrade's first town hospital, built to a design by Jovan Frencl at the initiative of Prince Mihailo Obrenović, with money raised from contributions across Serbian society. Alongside the Kapetan-Mišino building it is the most significant example of romanticism in Belgrade's architecture.
buildings.history: The building went up in 1868 as the first town hospital; the funds came from contributions, and Prince Mihailo Obrenović was the driving force behind it. Many foreign and Serbian doctors who shaped the country's medical science and practice worked here, which makes the building a monument to the history of healthcare.

buildings.description: The building of the "Vladimir Perić-Valter" School of Economics in Cetinjska Street was raised in 1929 to a design by Josif Najman for the commercial school founded on 23 September 1844 as the Posleno-trgovačko učilište. It was paid for by the endowment fund of the Belgrade merchants Vasa and Nikola Radojković. The School of Economics, earlier the Commercial Academy, marks the high point of a long development of secondary commercial education in Serbia, which peaked in the 1930s with this very building.
buildings.history: The commercial school began in 1844 as the Posleno-trgovačko učilište and trained generations for Serbian trade. In 1929 it received this new building, designed by Josif Najman and paid for by the endowment fund of the Radojković brothers. By then the school had become the Commercial Academy, and the house itself came to stand for the summit of secondary commercial education in Serbia, a path begun by the first semi-private business schools and completed here in the 1930s. It was built for a single purpose, and its whole arrangement answers that purpose.

buildings.description: The Belgrade City Museum grew out of a private collection: the merchant Samuilo Stefanović offered the city his weapons, jewels and paintings as early as 1894, and the purchase went through in 1902. In 2006 the museum was assigned the former Military Academy building in Resavska Street, meant to become its permanent home.
buildings.history: The museum dates its foundation to 1903, when the city was given a room in the National Museum for what was called the Municipal Museum; the move to Princess Ljubica’s Residence, ordered in 1911, was prevented by the First World War, in which a large part of the city’s archives was lost. The holdings grew slowly: 155 items at the end of 1929, 1062 five years later; during the war the museum closed after a bomb hit its roof and upper floor. The Museum of 4 July joined it in 1954 and Princess Ljubica’s Residence in 1980. Since 2015 the museum has hosted a concert season called “Musical Vaults of Belgrade”.

buildings.description: The General Staff and Ministry of Defence ensemble on Kneza Miloša Street is Nikola Dobrović's key work: two stepped blocks, conceived as the State Secretariat for National Defence, step down towards Nemanjina and read as a city gate.
buildings.history: The complex was built between 1955 and 1965 to a design by the architect Nikola Dobrović; at the time of construction it was called the State Secretariat for National Defence. The two monumental blocks stand slightly back from the street line of Kneza Miloša, and each is entered through a monumental portico. Placed at the crossing of the busiest city arteries, the ensemble became one of Belgrade's most striking architectural images and a major work of post-war Serbian and Yugoslav architecture.

buildings.description: One of the few old houses of Savamala to survive the regulation of that part of the city in 1834. A tavern occupied the ground floor, and it was there that Petar Kočić wrote his first literary works; the Najdanović family bought the house in 1893.
buildings.history: The house was probably built before 1830 and belongs to the rare surviving examples of Belgrade town dwellings from the first half of the nineteenth century. Its upper floor served as living quarters while a tavern occupied the ground floor, and that tavern is linked with the name of Petar Kočić, who wrote his first literary works there. In 1893 the house was bought by the Najdanović family. For Savamala it remains one of the reference points of the district where the beginnings of modern urbanisation are visible.

buildings.description: One of the earliest works of contemporary architecture on Terazije: the Hempro building went up in 1956–1957 to a design by Aleksej Brkić, announcing both his personal artistic manner and a new, unconventional architecture. It is inserted into the historic fabric of Belgrade's commercial centre.
buildings.history: The building was put up in 1956–1957 to a design by Aleksej Brkić and ranks among the pioneering works of post-war Belgrade architecture. It is read as a departure from socialist-realist norms and a shift towards Western European influence, while its form owes much to Mies van der Rohe and the International Style without embracing strict functionalism. The house is also seen as a skilful modern insertion into the inherited urban matrix of Terazije and as a basis for the further development of authored architecture.

buildings.description: The Military Hospital in Vračar was built between 1904 and 1909 to a design by Danilo Vladisavljević, and its contemporaries called it the most modern hospital in the Balkans. Its pavilions, linked by parkland, were laid out so that architecture served treatment, meeting the strictest sanitary demands of the day. As a teaching centre it became the nucleus from which the Medical Faculty of the University of Belgrade grew.
buildings.history: The hospital went up between 1904 and 1909, and already then it was spoken of as the most modern in the Balkans. Vladisavljević spread the pavilions through a park and tied them together with greenery and paths, a scheme praised by foreign as well as Serbian experts. The buildings share one romantic idiom, with the administration block the most emphatic of them. The hospital served through the Balkan Wars and the First World War, and a long line of distinguished doctors worked within it. It also became the seedbed of medical teaching, from which the university faculty later grew.

buildings.description: The house of the Society of the Serbian Red Cross in Simina Street was built by Aleksandar Bugarski in 1879 for the society's offices and stores, which were turned into a hospital in wartime. For more than a century it has housed one of the country's central humanitarian institutions.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1879 to a design by Aleksandar Bugarski, one of the greatest Serbian architects of the nineteenth century. The client was the Society of the Serbian Red Cross, founded in 1876 as part of the International Red Cross to help wounded, sick, captive and interned soldiers and civilians in wartime and to assist stricken populations during disasters and epidemics. The society's offices and stores were converted into a hospital in wartime. In 1925–1927 two more floors and a mansard were added.

buildings.description: The Archive of Serbia on Karnegijeva Street was built in 1928 to a design by Nikolai Krasnov, and it is one of the few public buildings put up expressly as an archive. Its stacks hold the records of the principality and kingdom up to 1918, the papers of interwar Yugoslavia and of the occupation, and private collections besides. Today it is the principal source for the study of Serbian history from the emergence of the state to 1941.
buildings.history: The archive acquired a building of its own in 1928, a rare case in a city where most public edifices were adapted to institutional needs after the fact. The design was Nikolai Krasnov's, and he gave the building the air of monumental academism with a richly worked main facade. The stacks hold the records of institutions that operated in the Principality and Kingdom of Serbia up to 1918, those of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and of the wartime occupation, and private papers as well. Besides the files of the central ministries — internal affairs and justice, foreign affairs, education and culture, finance and the economy — the archive keeps the records of individual bodies in science, art and schooling. Personal and family collections are especially prized: the papers and correspondence of statesmen, politicians, scientists, writers and public figures illuminate the social life of their age.

buildings.description: The Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary stands on Veliki trg, the oldest square in Zemun, laid out when the Lower Town was being built up in earnest. Its foundation stone was laid in 1785, the roof went on nine years later, and in 1795 the bell tower was finished and the church consecrated. The single-nave building, with a barrel vault, an apse and sacristy to the east and a tower over the west entrance, joins a classical scheme to Baroque detail. For Zemun it remains a record of a town whose population was confessionally mixed.
buildings.history: The church was begun in 1785 and stood under roof by 1794; the following year the bell tower was raised and the building consecrated. It was renewed in 1817 and thoroughly restored in the middle of the 19th century, when the tower received a new dome. The square it faces is the oldest in Zemun, laid out to a plan during the busier building of the Lower Town, following the idea of the supreme comital inspector Tadeus Esterhazy. In its forms a classical scheme meets Baroque elements, and the building itself testifies to the several confessions that made up the town's population.

buildings.description: The Hristić-Mijušković house on Dobračina dates from 1930, designed by an engineer named Mijušković on land that had belonged to Filip Hristić, a diplomat, foreign minister and later education minister in the government of Prince Mihailo Obrenović. A two-storey house replaced the earlier single-storey one, and it has stayed with the family, whose descendants still live there. With its furnishings and family archive, it stands as a characteristic home of its period and a defining presence on Dobračina and in Belgrade's historic centre.
buildings.history: The plot on Dobračina had belonged to Filip Hristić, a diplomat, foreign minister and later minister of education in the government of Prince Mihailo Obrenović. In 1930 a two-storey house designed by the engineer Mijušković replaced the single-storey building that stood there. The author worked in late academism, with symmetry stressed both in the plan and in the treatment of the walls. The house never left the family — Hristić's descendants live in it today — and with its furnishings and family archive it preserves the character of a home of its day. That is why it is read as a typical residential building of the period and as an important element in the ambience of Dobračina and the wider historic centre.

buildings.description: The town villa of the lawyer Milan Milovanović in Dobračina: he bought the house in 1900 and in 1927 added an upper floor to a design by Đura Bajalović. Its first owner was Colonel Đorđe Marković, who built the house in 1884.
buildings.history: The house was built by Colonel Đorđe Marković in 1884. In 1900 it was bought by the lawyer Milan Milovanović, and in 1927 a further floor was added to a design by the architect Đura Bajalović. The extension cost the building its original layout, in which living and service rooms were grouped around a central hall entered from a covered porch.
