The two phases still read as one stylistic whole, with only a barely visible difference in the treatment of the facade on the oldest and the added part.

buildings.description: The house where the poet Stevan Kaćanski (1830–1900) lived, a native of Srbobran who fought in the 1848 revolution and in the Serbo-Turkish war of 1876–77. A single-family home of the 1880s, it is a characteristic example of Belgrade residential architecture at the close of the nineteenth century.
buildings.history: The house was raised in the 1880s for a single family and became the home of the poet Stevan Kaćanski, born in Srbobran in 1830. He fought in the 1848 revolution against the Hungarians, raised a volunteer legion during the bombardment of Belgrade in 1862, and served in the Serbo-Turkish war of 1876–77. In the mid-1850s he was the first to bring romantic pathos into Serbian poetry, and his arrival marked a new departure for the literature.

buildings.description: The monumental house King Alexander I Karađorđević built as a boarding school for gymnasium pupils was handed over to the Archives of Yugoslavia in 1969. The architect was Vojin Petrović.
buildings.history: The house went up between 1930 and 1933 to a design by Vojin Petrović as the Home of King Alexander I for pupils of secondary schools, boarding pupils of the Men’s Gymnasium of King Alexander I Karađorđević. It offered a library, a hall for music and drawing, sports rooms with a swimming pool and laid-out playing fields. In the Second World War the home ceased to operate and the Gestapo and the German military command moved in; afterwards higher military and political schools occupied it until 1953, then the federal ministry of the interior until 1970. In 1969 it was handed over to the Archives of Yugoslavia, which has kept the records of the Yugoslav state from 1918 to 2006 since 1950.

buildings.description: A baroque church raised in Surčin in 1777 on the site of an older wooden one. Its carved iconostasis, the work of a Novi Sad master, and thirty-seven icons by a Karlovac painter rank among the valuable monuments of Serbian art of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
buildings.history: The church replaced an older wooden building in 1777 and was built in the baroque manner, with a high bell tower and a semicircular apse. Its gilded iconostasis was carved in 1801 by Marko Vujatović, a master from Novi Sad; the thirty-seven icons were painted in 1807–09 by Stefan Gavrilović of Karlovac, and Konstantin Pantelić executed the wall compositions in 1811. The church archive keeps documents from 1785 to 1859 and parish registers from 1766 onwards, and the church remains one of the settlement’s main urban landmarks.

buildings.description: Madlenianum became the first privately owned opera and theatre house in Serbia and in Southeast Europe. Madlena Zepter, wife of the businessman Philip Zepter, founded it and gave it her name. The company moved into a Zemun building that had once served as the National Theatre’s second stage, in the old town core, and since 1999 has presented opera, ballet, concerts and drama.
buildings.history: The theatre was founded on 25 December 1997, and the building opened to the public on 26 January 1999 with Cimarosa's «Il matrimonio segreto». A thorough reconstruction and extension followed, carried out in several stages. The fully refurbished and enlarged house, equipped with modern stage technology, reopened on 19 April 2005. Conceived as an opera house, Madlenianum gradually widened its repertoire to musicals, ballet, concerts and drama.

buildings.description: The Museum of Contemporary Art, built in 1962–65 from the competition entry by Ivan Antić and Ivanka Raspopović. A landmark of New Belgrade, it can be seen from the Belgrade Fortress, the new Sava bridge and the river.
buildings.history: The museum was built between 1962 and 1965 on the strength of a competition design by Ivan Antić and Ivanka Raspopović submitted in 1960. Inside, the architects let different levels interpenetrate through broadly cantilevered slabs and tied the interior to the exterior. In 1965 the authors received the City of Belgrade’s October Prize, and the building was then ranked among the finest and most modern museum houses in Yugoslavia.

buildings.description: The home of the State Printing House, an institution founded in 1831, built in 1936–40 to a design by Dragiša Brašovan. It was the first building in Belgrade with a reinforced-concrete skeleton, and it has since become a centre of the city’s art life.
buildings.history: The state press, one of the oldest institutions of the Principality of Serbia, was founded in 1831 in Kragujevac and moved to Belgrade four years later. Its new house was begun in 1936 and finished in 1940, but the German bombardment of April 1941, which badly damaged the building, prevented the presses from starting. Printing resumed in the surviving parts in 1944; the works were renamed Jugoštampa in 1946 and BIGZ in 1970. In 1992 the building was placed under state protection as a cultural monument.

buildings.description: Hall 1 is the centrepiece of the Belgrade Fair, the exhibition ground raised between 1954 and 1957 by the architect Milorad Pantović with the engineers Branko Žeželj and Milan Krstić. Three domed pavilions linked by walkways were composed as a single urban gesture, and the hall was immediately ranked beside the best structures of its kind anywhere. The Fair remains one of the strongest works of Serbian postwar architecture and a witness to the technical, scientific and creative confidence of the late 1950s.
buildings.history: The Fair took shape between 1954 and 1957, designed by a team in which the architect Milorad Pantović worked alongside the engineers Branko Žeželj and Milan Krstić. The plan relied on a rhythm of repeating masses, a single family of materials, and large glazed surfaces that let inside and outside flow into each other. Three domed exhibition halls became the accent of the composition, joined by walkways, and the first of them was greeted as an engineering feat on a par with the famous examples abroad. For postwar Serbia the Fair became evidence of a society's technical, technological, scientific and creative ascent at the turn of the 1960s. Its scale and coherence still place it among the most accomplished works of domestic architecture.

buildings.description: The Stone Palace, known as the Old General Staff Building, was raised in 1924–1928 for the army of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia to a design by the Russian émigré architect Vasily Baumgarten. In 1937 it was proclaimed the most beautiful building in Belgrade, and after the war it housed the General Staff of the Yugoslav People’s Army.
buildings.history: The palace rose with the wave of ministry buildings along Kneza Miloša Street, each of them larger and more expensive than the one before. It was one of the most modern buildings in Europe for a military headquarters, and in April 1941 it survived the German bombing of Belgrade, when one of the first bombs fell only metres away, on the former Ministry of War. After the war the General Staff of the Yugoslav People’s Army sat here, and between 2008 and 2010 the Cultural Heritage Protection Institute of the City of Belgrade restored the facades and the interiors, primarily the Great War Hall.

buildings.description: Belgrade’s cathedral church, tied to the central events of Serbian history: it keeps the relics of Tsar Uroš and despot Stefan Štiljanović and the tombs of Prince Miloš and Prince Mihailo Obrenović, while Dositej Obradović and Vuk Karadžić lie buried before its entrance. It is one of the largest church buildings raised in the Principality of Serbia.
buildings.history: The church went up between 1837 and 1840 on the site of a church of 1728, following plans by A. F. Kverfeld, a builder from Pančevo. The interior was furnished and decorated between 1841 and 1845: the sculptor and medallist Dimitrije Petrović drew the designs for the woodcarving, while the paintings were entrusted to Dimitrije Avramović, one of the most important Serbian painters of the nineteenth century, formed under the influence of the Vienna Academy. As the city’s cathedral it became the setting of many events in the history of Belgrade and Serbia; its wall paintings and iconostasis were restored in 1993–96.

buildings.description: Built in 1933 for the Ministry of Social Policy and Public Health to a design by Dimitrije M. Leka, one of Serbia’s leading architects. The heritage register treats it as Leka’s most important work, the fullest statement of his understanding of academism.
buildings.history: The house was erected in 1933 to designs by Dimitrije M. Leka, conceived entirely on academist principles with strict symmetry of plan and façades. The two sculptural groups at the ends of the street façade, on the level of the first floor above ground, are the work of the sculptor Lojze Dolinar. The heritage register ranks the building among the anthology pieces of Belgrade’s interwar monumental architecture; today it houses the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia.

buildings.description: The Church of Saint Basil of Ostrog in the Bežanijska Kosa neighbourhood was the first church raised in New Belgrade after the Second World War. Its architect, Mihajlo Mitrović, chose the plan of an early Christian rotunda and reinterpreted it with modern means. Construction began in 1996 and was paid for by donations from the saint’s devotees.
buildings.history: Work began in 1996, and on 12 May 2001 the completed church was consecrated by Patriarch Pavle. Mitrović drew on the tradition of old Serbian builders, placing a rotunda at the heart of the plan while modern structural methods gave the ancient image a contemporary form. The church belongs to the Serbian Orthodox Church and stands in the Bežanijska Kosa neighbourhood.

buildings.description: A corner house in Zemun’s old core that passed in 1870 to Stevan Marković, mayor of Zemun, and has stayed with the Marković family ever since. It is one of the town’s rich burgher houses from the turn of the nineteenth century.
buildings.history: The house was raised in the eighteenth century and reconstructed in 1801. It was built by the Greek merchant Dima, from whom it was bought by the well-known trader Miloš Urošević; in 1870 his heirs sold it to Stevan Marković, mayor of Zemun. Bombing in the Second World War damaged the building, so its original closed composition around an inner courtyard is partly lost.

buildings.description: The home of the Zemun magistrate, the town administration whose history reaches back to 1751; the building went up between 1823 and 1832 to plans by the Zemun builder Josef Felber. It is considered the purest example of classicism in the architecture of Zemun’s old core.
buildings.history: The Zemun magistrate was founded in 1751, and in 1755 the town acquired its first town hall — a low baroque building with a mansard that served the magistrate until 1832 and then housed its officials; it burned down in 1867. Beside it a new magistrate building in the spirit of classicism was put up between 1823 and 1832 to plans by the Zemun builder Josef Felber, and in 1836 it was extended on the site of Miloš Urošević’s house under plans signed by the town clerk Križanić, which disturbed the original purity of the classicist design. The magistrate occupied the building until 1871, when it was handed over to the court that sat there for many years.

buildings.description: The post office in the old core of Zemun, built in 1896 to plans signed by the city engineer Dragutin Kapus on the site of an eighteenth-century post building that had been torn down. Interior refits in 1961 and at the end of the twentieth century left it among the principal public buildings of historic Zemun.
buildings.history: The post office went up in 1896 on the site of an eighteenth-century building that had been demolished; the works were carried out by the contractor Franja Jenč, and the plans were signed by the city engineer Dragutin Kapus. The building has two ranges of rooms with a corridor between them, a layout developed for postal needs, and its façades follow the neo-Renaissance with northern Baroque touches on the roof. The interior was modernised in 1961 and again at the end of the twentieth century. It is counted among the most important public buildings documenting the historical and urban character of Zemun’s old core.

buildings.description: The house of the Belgrade lawyer Jakov Čelebonović, built in 1927–29 and occupied since 1950 by the Museum of Applied Arts. The façades were designed by the architect Nikola Krasnov, the layout is attributed to the engineer Mihailo Belić, the interiors to the Dutch architect Neregar.
buildings.history: The house was built for the lawyer Jakov Čelebonović between 1927 and 1929; the drawings were signed by the engineer Mihailo Belić, probably responsible for the layout, the architect Nikola Krasnov, author of the façades, and the Dutch architect Neregar, who designed the interiors. Jakov, Marko and Aleksa Čelebonović all lived here, each leaving a deep mark on Belgrade’s cultural history, and their art collection was kept in the house. Since 1950 it has housed the Museum of Applied Arts, whose holdings are of exceptional importance for Belgrade and Serbian art.

buildings.description: The Đorđe Jovanović Library is the central library of Belgrade's Stari Grad municipality and part of the city library network. It opened in 1945 as the Library of the First District and later took the name of the Serbian writer and critic, one of the founders of Belgrade surrealism. Its collection holds around 65,000 items, and the library works with schools, kindergartens and local organisations across the municipality.
buildings.history: The library began in the first days after the liberation of Belgrade, when activists of the People's Front, the women's anti-fascist front and the pioneers walked the ruined streets with baskets, collecting books and quickly gathering about five thousand volumes. Many copies lacked their beginning or end, so a complete edition had to be found and the missing pages copied out — such volumes still turn up in the old collection. Work started on an amateur footing; training at the University Library under Milica Prodanović brought the first librarian, Smilja Atanacković. In 1950, on the proposal of Dragan Savković, the First District's commissioner for culture, the library took the name of Đorđe Jovanović. In 1960 the former Second District library, Jovan Popović, was merged into it, and in 1964 the central library moved into new premises.

buildings.description: The house of the merchant Nikola Predić, a partner of Captain Miša Anastasijević, was among the first private buildings to rise in Belgrade after the Turks sold off their estates and left the city. It stood on the new building line laid down by the plan for the town within the trench, and houses like it marked the beginning of the city core. Shops and warehouses occupied the ground floor, with the family living above.
buildings.history: The house went up soon after the Turkish withdrawal, when Belgrade was only beginning to acquire a regular street plan. It was designed wholly by the rules of academic architecture, its corner site stressed by a deep projecting bay. In 1906 the merchant Mijailo Pavlović bought it and turned it to rent, and at that point the facades were brought up to date with a restrained Secession ornament. That is the form in which the house has come down to us.

buildings.description: The French Institute in Serbia is the cultural and educational operator of the French Embassy and the successor of the French Cultural Centre. Its administration and language courses occupy premises in central Belgrade, while the media library sits on Knez Mihailova Street; the institute also has branches in Niš and Novi Sad. It runs exhibitions, language courses, lectures and debates, continuing a line that began with the French Club founded in Belgrade in 1920.
buildings.history: The first French cultural association appeared in Belgrade in 1920 as the Society of Friends of France, or French Club. War and occupation ended its work, yet the club's books stayed available in secret through a local library on Zmaj Jovina Street. In May 1945 a reading room opened on Knez Mihailova as the forerunner of the French Cultural Centre, which from its founding in 1951 occupied the Union building, completed in 1938 for the Union insurance company. In the first days of the 1999 NATO bombing the centre was partly looted, but it was later fully restored and reopened. In December 2001 President Jacques Chirac inaugurated the renovated centre, and on 1 January 2011 it was renamed the French Institute in Serbia.

buildings.description: The synagogue of Belgrade’s Ashkenazi congregation, built in 1924–26 to a design by Franja Urban with Milan Šlang taking part. It remains the only authentic working house of worship of the city’s Jewish community and one of the few surviving monuments of synagogue architecture.
buildings.history: The synagogue was built in 1924–26 to a design by the architect Franja Urban with Milan Šlang taking part; in 1929 Milutin Jovanović remodelled the interior. It served the Ashkenazi Jewish congregation until 1941, when the Nazi occupation of Belgrade stripped the building of its original purpose. After the war the synagogue recovered its function and now serves both Jewish congregations of the city. Besides the prayer hall with its gallery, the building held rooms for cultural and educational work, offices, a classroom and a committee hall, with a kosher kitchen and dining room in the basement.

buildings.description: The University of Arts in Belgrade is a public university that began in 1957, when four art schools were united as the Academy of Arts. In 1973 it became the city's second independent university, when the four academies turned into faculties of music, fine arts, applied arts and dramatic arts. It trains painters, musicians, actors and designers and remains one of the country's central institutions for artistic education.
buildings.history: Art education in Belgrade began on 31 March 1937, when a decree established the Academy of Music with a drama department and the Academy of Fine Arts. Preparations were under way for the first intake of students in autumn 1937; the applied-arts academy was founded on 26 November 1948, and the theatrical academy on 11 December 1948. On 10 June 1957 the parliament of the People's Republic of Serbia passed the law creating the Academy of Arts as a union of the four academies. On 21 May 1973 the academies became faculties and the Academy of Arts turned into the University of Arts.

buildings.description: The Faculty of Applied Arts grew out of the Academy of Applied Arts established in 1948. Its lineage reaches back to the evening craft course at Kirilo Kutlik's Serbian Drawing and Painting School in 1895 and to the Art and Craft School opened in 1905. Today it teaches ceramics, glass, textiles, scenography, graphics and design, continuing a line shaped by the teachers of the interwar School of Applied Art.
buildings.history: Evening craft courses at Kirilo Kutlik's school appeared in 1895, and in 1905 the Art and Craft School opened, led by the then well-known painter Rista Vukanović. The school operated until 1918 and from 1919 continued as the Royal Art School. In 1938 a secondary School of Applied Art opened, founded by its future teachers: sculptor Milan Nedeljković, architect Đorđe Krekić, painter Ivan Tabaković and sculptor Mihailo Tomić. In autumn 1948 the school was raised to an academy; the graphic artist Branko Šotra became its first rector, and teaching began with eight departments. In 1973 the academy became a faculty and the departments were replaced by chairs, from architecture and design to ceramics, glass, scenography, sculpture, graphics, costume, painting and textiles.

buildings.description: The French embassy in Belgrade stands between St. Michael's Cathedral and the Belgrade Fortress, above the Sava. It was designed in 1926 by the French architect Roger-Henri Expert with the Serbian architect Josif Najman as assistant, and was only the fourth purpose-built French embassy. A complete Art Deco work, from facades to furniture and lighting, it was inaugurated in December 1935 before Prince Paul and 800 guests.
buildings.history: The city sold part of an elementary school's yard for the legation despite protests from parents and the school board, and by June 1923 fences were already enclosing the French mission. The 1926 design came from Roger-Henri Expert, assisted by Josif Najman. Construction ran from 1929 to 1933, and the inauguration took place on the evening of 21 December 1935 with 800 guests, among them Milan Stojadinović and senior officials led by Prince Paul and Princess Olga. The building was a total Art Deco work, interior, furniture and lighting included, and in 1936 a high wall and the embassy park fence rose along the street.

buildings.description: The only authentic work by the Slovenian architect Josip Plečnik in Belgrade: he designed this church on the edge of the Vračar hills facing Zvezdara in the late 1920s. The bronze statue of the patron holding the infant Jesus is by Ivan Meštrović.
buildings.history: The church was built between 1929 and 1932 to Plečnik’s design: a rotunda with an eastern apse, a western porch and a cylindrical bell tower. Its main space, 25 metres across and 17.5 metres high, required three galleries, and a crypt was placed beneath the apse. In 1935 a bronze statue of Anthony of Padua by Ivan Meštrović was installed on the main altar. The monumental bell tower, 52 metres tall and 9 metres in diameter, followed only in 1962, from slightly altered Plečnik drawings and under the guidance of his pupil Janez Valentinčič.

buildings.description: A rare case of a church made inside an existing industrial building: the conversion was entrusted to the architect Momir Korunović, and the works were led by Anton Sara, then regarded as the best builder of domed churches in the Balkans.
buildings.history: The church appeared in 1933, when the industrial building standing here was rebuilt as a place of worship; Momir Korunović made the conversion design and Anton Sara carried out the works. It was conceived as a basilica with a choir, side galleries and a four-storey bell tower above the narthex, in the Byzantine spirit but with Romanesque features in the tower. In 1933 the Russian painter Ivan Dikij painted the altar wall, and in 1947 Živorad Nastasijević produced the first cycle of frescoes and the icons of the iconostasis. Between 1967 and 1973 the painter Milovan Arsić made the present frescoes and new icons, and in 1967–69 mosaics to his drawings were laid in the tympana above all three portals.

buildings.description: A building put up around 1846 for Prince Aleksandar Karađorđević on the site of the Great Market; from 1853 it was known as Belgrade’s second hotel, “Novo zdanje” or “Srpska kruna”. For almost a century afterwards it served the city municipality.
buildings.history: It was raised around 1846 for Prince Aleksandar Karađorđević on the site of the Great Market, which in the second half of the nineteenth century was the centre of the capital’s administrative and educational life. From 1853 the house is recorded as Belgrade’s second hotel, “Novo zdanje” or “Srpska kruna”: the most distinguished guests stayed there, and balls, theatre performances, concerts and painting exhibitions were held inside. The hotel traded until 1869, when the name “Srpska kruna” passed to a tavern at 56 Knez Mihailova Street. For almost a century afterwards the building served the needs of the Belgrade municipality, and the alterations and added floor of 1928 substantially changed its appearance.

buildings.description: The town house of Princess Ljubica and her sons Milan and Mihailo, which served both as a family home and as the prince's residence; it now belongs to the Belgrade City Museum. It was built in 1829–1830 under the direction of Hadži-Nikola Živković, the first builder of restored Serbia.
buildings.history: The konak was built in 1829–1830 on the site of the old, dilapidated palace, meant to reflect the growing power of Prince Miloš after he received the sultan's charter in 1830. Hadži-Nikola Živković of Voden, who became the first builder of restored Serbia, directed the works, and in 1836 a hammam was added. Under Prince Miloš the main state treasury was kept here, the regency held its sessions in the building, and Prince Mihailo lived in it until 1842. Later it housed the Lyceum until it moved to Captain Miša's building in 1863, then a grammar school, the courts and a school for deaf children; today it is part of the Belgrade City Museum.

buildings.description: The former Belgrade Stock Exchange of 1933–34, designed by Aleksandar Đorđević — a rare modernist excursion for an architect known for academic work. Since 1951 the building has housed the Ethnographic Museum, whose holdings exceed 100,000 objects.
buildings.history: The building went up in 1933–34 to a design by Aleksandar Đorđević for the Belgrade Stock Exchange; it was intended for business and residential use. Architecturally it belongs to mature modernism, with pronounced verticalism and foreign, mostly German, influences. The Ethnographic Museum, founded in 1901 when it separated from the National Museum, has occupied the house since 1951 and holds more than 100,000 objects, mainly of rural folk culture; the most recent reconstruction adapted the building to museum use.

buildings.description: The oldest surviving Belgrade building erected entirely in the European spirit and the city’s only example of classicism; since 1969 it has held the Pedagogical Museum. It went up around 1840 as the private residence of Cvetko Rajović, manager of the town of Belgrade.
buildings.history: Built around 1840 for Cvetko Rajović, administrator of the town and a prominent political figure, probably to a design by Franz Janke. The house later passed into public use: it held the English consulate, the gendarmerie and the military staff, and from 1867 until the Second World War the First Belgrade Realka. Kosta Glavinić, Milan Kapetanović and Nikola Nestorović were pupils here, while Stevan Todorović, Petar Ubavkić and Đorđe Krstić taught. At the beginning of the twentieth century, short of school space, the authorities added a two-storey wing with Secession façades. After the Second World War the building held a military school and later several schools, and since 1969 the Pedagogical Museum.

buildings.description: The Second Economics School traces its history to 25 May 1939, when the Ministry of Trade and Industry of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia founded the Second Trade Academy. Its first pupils were taught in the old building of the First Trade School, and since 1957 it has been housed on the border of Vračar and Voždovac. Today it trains economic technicians and financial administrators, and its library holds more than 14,000 volumes.
buildings.history: The academy opened in the 1939/40 school year in the premises of the First Trade School. From 1947/48, answering the postwar demand for economists, it became a three-year State Economic Technicum. Four-year schooling returned in 1951/52, and in 1957 the school moved into its own building. Between 1961 and 2005 new departments were added — accounting, commercial, tourism, finance and customs — followed by pilot classes for business and financial administrators. In 2008 its director, Dejan Nedić, wrote the school anthem.

buildings.description: The former residence of the Obrenović and Karađorđević dynasties and, since 1961, the seat of the Belgrade City Assembly. It was built in 1881–1884 to a design by Aleksandar Bugarski for King Milan I.
buildings.history: The palace was built in 1881–1884 as the left wing of a planned three-part complex: the centre was to replace the Old Konak, the right wing was meant for the heir to the throne, and the left for ceremonial receptions. Aleksandar Bugarski designed it following the ideas and instructions of King Milan himself; after the dynastic change of 1903 it became the official residence of the Karađorđević dynasty, where Peter I and Alexander I lived. In 1919 and 1920 the Assembly of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes sat in its halls, and after the Second World War and the 1947–1949 reconstruction by Dragiša Brašovan it housed the Presidium of the National Assembly, the government of FNR Yugoslavia and the Federal Executive Council. Since 1961 it has been the seat of the Belgrade City Assembly.

buildings.description: The Church of the Nativity of the Theotokos is the largest church in the old core of Zemun, consecrated in 1783. It was built with money from the town’s Orthodox residents, Serbs and Greeks, and its carved Baroque iconostasis came from the workshop of Aksentije of the Marković family.
buildings.history: The cornerstone of the new Orthodox church was laid in 1777; the Orthodox residents of Zemun, Serbs and Greeks, paid for the building, and the church was consecrated in 1783. It was conceived without a bell tower and kept traditional Serbian-Byzantine features like those of older churches in Vojvodina; the bell tower on the west was added at the turn of the nineteenth century, and in 1880 the church was thoroughly rebuilt. Beneath the bell tower lies a sunken ossuary, following rules still observed in the Greek Orthodox Church. The carved Baroque iconostasis came from Aksentije of the Marković family, with icons by Arsenije Teodorović; in 2000–2001 the church was restored, its wall paintings renewed and a new floor with underfloor heating installed.

buildings.description: The chapel of the Kontumac, the quarantine station of what was then the border town of Zemun, built in 1786 at the expense of the merchant and soap-maker Teodor Toša Apostolović. It is one of only two surviving structures of the Kontumac, founded in 1730.
buildings.history: The chapel was built in 1786 as the Orthodox church of the quarantine that Zemun, then a border town, had been granted back in 1730. The builder was the Zemun merchant and soap-maker Teodor Toša Apostolović; the western rooms, closed off from the nave, served travellers serving out their quarantine. The iconostasis was painted by the Zemun icon painters Dimitrije Bratoglić and Konstantin Lekić, and the church’s collection holds valuable paintings of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Only two buildings of the old Kontumac survive, and this chapel is one of them.

buildings.description: The Catholic chapel of St Roch was built in 1836, in the time of quarantine director Franz Minas. With the Orthodox chapel it is the only material trace of Zemun's Kontumac, the border quarantine and trading post.
buildings.history: The chapel was raised to the plans of the builder Josif Felber, on the site of an older Catholic quarantine chapel. Its quarantine role shows in the ground plan: besides the main entrance there were six more doors, three on each long façade. It now keeps a collection of nineteenth-century paintings, including works by Živko Petrović, Aleksandar Mašić, Dražanski and unknown authors.

buildings.description: The Church of St Nicholas in Zemun was built between 1745 and 1752 on the site of an older wooden Serbian church with a straw roof. It is the oldest Orthodox church in Zemun's old core and the oldest sacred building preserved anywhere in Belgrade.
buildings.history: The church replaced a thatched wooden Serbian church that had stood on the same spot. Inside are a richly carved iconostasis with icons by Dimitrije Bačević and wall paintings by the Zemun painter Živko Petrović. The guild banners of Zemun are singled out as evidence of the social standing of the town's craftsmen on the border. The original bell tower burned in 1867 and was rebuilt in 1870; buttresses were later added to the north and south walls for stability.

buildings.description: The Ministry of Justice building went up in 1883 to a design by Svetozar Ivačković. With the Old Palace rising next door at the same moment, it helped turn the Terazije line into the capital's administrative and representative centre.
buildings.history: It was built for the Ministry of Justice to Svetozar Ivačković's design. Construction coincided with the proclamation of the Kingdom of Serbia and with work on the Old Palace a few steps away, as the Terazije front was gradually remade into the capital's administrative and representative quarter. Planned as a single-storey building, it received a courtyard wing later, and one of its two symmetrical portals was walled up when the building was enlarged.

buildings.description: The house of the merchant Milan M. Stefanović, built in 1910–1912. For a time it held a branch of the Smederevo Bank, whose name the palace still carries; Milorad Ruvidić and Isail Fidanović were the architects.
buildings.history: Built for the merchant Milan Stefanović, the palace has kept its mixed residential and commercial use to this day. Here, for the first time in Serbian modern architecture, the wall was articulated spatially rather than decoratively, with the effect carried by varied loggias and balconies. It remains a visual accent on the lower stretch of Terazije and counts among the most representative Secession buildings in Serbia.

buildings.description: The endowment of Sima Andrejević Igumanov, a merchant of Prizren: income from this Terazije palace paid for the theological school he opened in Prizren in 1872. Raised in 1938, it is one of the key works of the Krstić brothers.
buildings.history: The palace was raised in 1938 to a design by Petar and Branko Krstić, and the inscription on its main façade names it the endowment of Igumanov of Prizren. Sima Igumanov (1804–1883), a merchant, opened a theological school in Prizren in 1872 and secured its upkeep by building the palace on Terazije and founding an endowment with a steady income. The roof originally carried a sculpture of Igumanov with orphans by the sculptor Lojze Dolinar.

buildings.description: The Anker Palace on Terazije was built in 1899, when the Vienna insurance company Anker put it up for its own needs. The design of the representative building was prepared by the Belgrade architect Milan Antonović (1850–1929) from a draft supplied by the company; he also designed its details and supervised the works. The palace joined the group of four buildings that shaped the face of Terazije at the turn of the century, and its decoration — distorted classicist elements and inverted capitals — became the architect's recognisable signature. For years it served as one of the hubs of the city's artistic life.
buildings.history: The Anker Palace was built in 1899, joining the row of buildings that gave Terazije its recognisable character at the turn of the twentieth century. The first house on the even side of the street had been the Krsmanović Palace of 1885, and over the following ten years it was joined by the Atina Palace, the Anker Palace and the Moskva Hotel. The building was put up for its own needs by the Vienna insurance company Anker, which is why it was also known as the Anker House. The project for the representative building was made by the Belgrade architect Milan Antonović (1850–1929) from a draft supplied by the company; he designed the details and supervised the works. His decoration became a kind of authorial signature: distorted classicist elements, inverted capitals and a two-part composition of risalits instead of the earlier three-part division, all in keeping with the so-called Vienna style. The palace also became a hub of the artistic life of Belgrade and Serbia, housing for years the seats of associations of artists, architects and musicians, among them the Music Youth of Belgrade and Serbia.

buildings.description: The Atena Palace was built in 1902 for the merchant Đorđe Vučo to a design by Dimitrije T. Leko. Its name comes from the Atena restaurant opened on the ground floor by Antonio de Franco, court chef to Petar I Karađorđević.
buildings.history: Leko designed three houses for Đorđe Vučo: the Atena on Terazije, Vučo's house on the Sava in Karađorđeva Street, and the family house in Deligradska near Slavija. The works were carried out by Janaćko Kostić, the best-known building contractor of the day. The ground-floor restaurant gave the palace its name, and the building belongs to the Terazije ensemble shaped around 1900.

buildings.description: The court church beside the princely konak in Topčider, built in 1832–1834, is held to be the highest achievement of church architecture under Prince Miloš Obrenović. The same builders who worked on Miloš's konak, Janja Mihailović and Nikola Đorđević, saw to its construction.
buildings.history: The church was built as the court chapel beside the konak. Its interior, above all the iconostasis, was entrusted to the Zemun painter Konstantin Lekić, the zograf Janja Moler and the painter Dimitrije Jakšić. The present iconostasis was installed in 1874, during the reign of Prince Milan Obrenović, and painted by Stevan Todorović and Nikola Marković.

buildings.description: The only surviving monument of Turkish sacred architecture in Belgrade. The mosque was raised between 1660 and 1688; the name Bajrakli, 'the banner one', stuck at the end of the eighteenth century, after the flag raised to signal the start of prayer to the other mosques.
buildings.history: Raised as an endowment, the mosque was first known as Čohadži Mosque, after one of its benefactors, the cloth merchant Hadži-Alija. Under Austrian rule from 1717 to 1739 it served as a Catholic church; with the return of the Turks it became a mosque again in 1741 and for a time bore the name of Hussein Bey, deputy to the Ottoman commander Ali Pasha. After the Turks left Belgrade it was restored, and since 1868 it has served as the only mosque of the city's remaining Muslim community.

buildings.description: A corner villa with a garden, built in 1901 for the painter couple Beta and Rista Vukanović: living rooms below, painting studios above. From 1902 to 1905 it housed their painting school, whose pupils included Nadežda Petrović, Kosta Miličević, Bora Stevanović and Dragomir Glišić.
buildings.history: The house was built to Milan Kapetanović's design as a corner villa with a garden. The painted decoration of the main façade, irises and peacock feathers by Beta Vukanović with three muses above the entrance, was lost when the building was altered and repartitioned in the 1930s. From 1902 to 1905 the Vukanovićs ran their painting school here, the last stage in the organisation of art teaching in the country before the state School of Arts and Crafts, later the Academy of Fine Arts, took over.

buildings.description: Dorćol Primary School, built in 1893 to Milan Kapetanović's design, was among the first schools in Belgrade raised entirely under the 1881 Rules on the Building of Schools and School Furniture, complete with a gym, a pool and an assembly hall.
buildings.history: The school was built in 1893, designed by Milan Kapetanović in the academic spirit of the nineteenth century. Its sixteen classrooms, gym, pool, cloakrooms and assembly hall were then unknown in Serbian primary schools, and the building became a model for later school construction in the country thanks to its European standard of programme and equipment.

buildings.description: The house where sculptor Dragomir Arambašić lived and worked was designed in 1906 by Branko Tanazević, one of the most committed advocates of the new Serbian style. Arambašić, a member of LADA and a co-founder of the Association of Fine Artists in Belgrade, is best known for the fountain "Awakening" by the Cvijeta Zuzorić Art Pavilion; today the building forms part of the "Leptirić" kindergarten.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1906 to a design by Branko Tanazević, then a lecturer at the architectural department of the Technical Faculty and, with Nikola Nestorović, the architect of the Technical Faculty building of the 1920s. Sculptor Dragomir Arambašić (1881–1945) lived and worked here; like Tanazević he studied in Munich, also in Dresden, and trained further in Rome and Paris. His best-known work is the fountain "Awakening", placed in 1936 in front of the main entrance of the Cvijeta Zuzorić Art Pavilion on Kalemegdan and still standing there. Today the house is used as part of the "Leptirić" kindergarten.

buildings.description: Rakovica Monastery, in the valley of the Rakovica river just outside Belgrade, was built in the 16th century on the site of an older place of worship, and owes its present appearance above all to the Obrenović family. The church of the Holy Archangels Michael and Gabriel holds the family tomb of Jevrem Obrenović, while Vasa Čarapić, a commander of the First Serbian Uprising, lies buried by its northern outer wall.
buildings.history: The Church of the Holy Archangels was raised in the 16th century on the site of an older place of worship, and the monastery was repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt. Its present appearance is owed above all to the Obrenović family — Prince Miloš and Tomanija, wife of his brother Jevrem, who financed and supervised the renovation of 1861–1865. The iconostasis was replaced at the beginning of the 20th century by the painter Rafailo Momčilović. Vasa Čarapić, a commander of the First Serbian Uprising, lies by the northern outer wall of the narthex, his tombstone designed by architect Kosta J. Jovanović on the order of King Petar I, and in 1888 a drinking fountain was built in front of the monastery gate to Jovan Ilkić's design.

buildings.description: Since 1926 this house on Svetozara Markovića Street has been the seat of the Archdiocese of Belgrade; before that it served the Austrian legation. A one-storey building of 1884 set in a well-kept garden, it ranked among the notable works of Belgrade architecture in the 1880s. Within its walls unfolded the events that led to the outbreak of the First World War.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1884 as the Austrian legation in Belgrade and has remained one of the city's notable addresses ever since. In 1926 the Archdiocese of Belgrade moved in, and together with the chapel of 1888, the garden and the parish office of the same year it became a single spatial and functional ensemble. The architecture follows the academism then in fashion, with neo-Renaissance detailing, and particular care was lavished on the northern facade facing the quiet, spacious garden. Here took place events of consequence for the modern history of Serbia, bound up with the circumstances in which the First World War began.

buildings.description: The Konstantinovic building at 3 Kralja Milana Street belongs to the Belgrade addresses where trade and housing were planned together from the outset: shops at street level, generous flats above. Bogdan Nestorovic, one of the most prominent architects of the interwar capital, raised it in 1926–1927. In its facade the academic discipline of the lower storey meets medieval Serbian motifs in the upper zones, and a fifth floor was added above the original four.
buildings.history: The house carries the name of Vitomir Konstantinovic and rose in 1926–1927. Bogdan Nestorovic prepared the design, and his work did much to shape the look of interwar Belgrade. The programme was that of a rentier building with two incomes, shops below and flats above for well-off tenants. Four storeys were built first, and the fifth came later. It belongs to the group of rental buildings that defined the city's appearance in those years.

buildings.description: The Vračar Savings Bank House on Kralja Milana Street was built in 1906 by architect Danilo Vladisavljević with engineer Miloš Savčić. It is one of Vladisavljević's notable works, conceived in the academic spirit that shaped Belgrade at the turn of the 20th century.
buildings.history: The Vračar Savings Bank House was built in 1906 to a design by architect Danilo Vladisavljević, with engineer Miloš Savčić taking part in the work. The institution's name stuck to the building, and the building itself became one of Vladisavljević's significant works. It follows the academic manner that dominated Europe and markedly influenced Belgrade's architecture in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

buildings.description: Krsmanović House on Terazije is remembered for two things: in 1918 the unification of the South Slavs into a single state was proclaimed here, and for a time the building served as the royal Court. It was built in 1885 to Jovan Ilkić's design for the merchant Marko O. Marković and was bought by the Krsmanović brothers in 1898.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1885 as a private residence for the merchant Marko O. Marković, designed by architect Jovan Ilkić in the academic manner of the 19th century. In 1898 the Krsmanović brothers bought the estate together with the house, and their name stayed with it. For a time the building served as the Court, and it was here that the unification of the South Slavs into a single state was proclaimed in 1918.

buildings.description: The studio of Milan Jovanović, the first and only building in Belgrade raised specifically for a photographer's work: it went up in 1903 for the court photographer to a design by Milan Antonović, an early champion of Art Nouveau in the city. Shops occupied the ground floor, the studio took the upper one. Its glazed front made it the earliest example in Belgrade of a facade without ornament.
buildings.history: By 1903 photography had been practised in Serbia for half a century, yet it had no home of its own — Milan Jovanović's studio was the first. The architect Milan Antonović, an early advocate of Art Nouveau, designed a commercial building with shops below, the studio above, a glazed roof and a run of timber-framed windows. Between the wars the glass front was replaced by a brick wall with a balcony and a wrought-iron railing. In 1911 the Koloseum cinema was built beside the studio; after the Second World War it was renamed Zvezda.

buildings.description: The Vuk Foundation House on Terazije has housed the Vuk Karadžić foundation since 1988; before that the Ministry of Education occupied it for nearly three-quarters of a century. It was built in 1870–71 for the judge Dimitrije Mita Golubović to a design by the architect Aleksandar Bugarski.
buildings.history: Almost at once the house became the seat of the Russian Imperial Consulate, then it sheltered the Serbian Institute for War Orphans, and from 1879 the Ministry of Education, which stayed until 1952. In 1912, as the ministry outgrew the premises, a wing was added towards the Sava slope and the main facade was rebuilt to Branko Tanazević’s design, with Dragutin Inkiostri in charge of the interiors, even though the two men were fierce opponents over what the national style should be. The last extension, the wing towards Kraljica Natalija Street, was carried out in 1924 to a design by Žarko Tatić, and in 1988 the house was handed to the Vuk Foundation.

buildings.description: Hotel Prag is the first art deco hotel building in Belgrade, raised on the corner of Kraljice Natalije in 1929 to a design by Djura Borosic. Two sisters commissioned it: Evgenija Milacevic, wife of the prominent lawyer Radomir Milacevic, and Natalija Maric. Its two wings follow the lines of two important streets, with the lift and an oval staircase tucked between them, and relief panels by the sculptor Svetomir Pocek still give the corner its character. The project travelled to exhibitions of modern architecture in Belgrade and Prague, and the hotel received mainly business guests from Serbia and Europe.
buildings.history: The hotel was built in 1929 and at first had four storeys. In 1936 it was extended and given another floor, again to Borosic's design, and a further round of work followed in 1977. The stepped corner front and the light relief sculpture gave the building its distinctive outline, and the project was shown at exhibitions of modern architecture in Belgrade and Prague. For guests from business circles in Serbia and Europe the hotel became an important centre of professional meetings and social life.

buildings.description: The building of the first Serbian observatory on Bulevar JNA was erected in 1891 to a design by the architect Dimitrije Leka. It was the outcome of half a century of development of the meteorological service in Serbia, and it appeared in the same years in which institutions of this kind were being founded in the more developed countries of Europe. It was designed specifically for meteorological and astronomical observation, which gave it the character of a free-standing pavilion, and its first director, Milan Nedeljković, equipped it with the most modern instruments. For a hundred and thirty years the building has not changed its purpose.
buildings.history: The meteorological observatory was built in 1891 to designs by the architect Dimitrije Leka, as the outcome of half a century of development of the meteorological service in Serbia. Its construction coincided with the emergence of institutions of this kind in the more developed countries of Europe. Through the efforts of Milan Nedeljković, its first director, the observatory was equipped with the most modern measuring instruments. Because it was intended for meteorological and astronomical observation, it received a distinctive architectural solution: freely placed in space, it was conceived as a pavilion-type building, its facades enlivened by horizontal bands in mortar and profiled cornices. For 130 years the building has not changed its purpose — the main meteorological station of Belgrade occupies the upper floor, the Climate Centre for Southeast Europe the ground floor, and the basement keeps old instruments and archival material. Every year, during the Night of Museums, that part of the building opens to the public as a kind of Museum of Meteorology.

buildings.description: Sokol House Matica on Deligradska Street was built between 1929 and 1935 to a design by Momir Korunović, a committed figure in the Sokol gymnastics movement. It was meant to be nothing less than a temple of Sokolstvo and the finest ornament of Vračar. King Aleksandar Karađorđević was its principal donor, and in 1934 the society renamed the building in his honour. The Great Hall carries Živorad Nastasijević's 1941 fresco "For the Honour of the Fatherland", showing the Serbian army crossing Albania.
buildings.history: Construction began in 1929, and the design changed as it went: the rich sculptural decoration first intended was never carried out. Matić, an architect, and Ristić, an engineer, supervised the final stages, while Nikola Krasnov supplied the main portal. In 1934, at a commemoration for King Alexander, the Sokol society resolved to rename the house after him. Sports grounds were laid out around the building, which for decades remained Belgrade's central sporting venue. In the Great Hall Živorad Nastasijević painted his fresco of the Serbian army crossing Albania in 1941; it was overpainted after the war and cleaned and restored in 1970–1971.

buildings.description: The Aero Club Building at the corner of Uzun Mirkova and Kralja Petra streets was built in 1934–1935 for the national aviation institution of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia to a design by Vojin Simeonović. It is one of Belgrade's most representative examples of Art Deco and a marked step towards the Europeanisation of the city's architecture.
buildings.history: The building was put up in 1934–1935 for the national aviation institution of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia to a design by Vojin Simeonović, one of Belgrade's leading architects. The stained glass on the theme of Daedalus and Icarus in the ceremonial hall was made by the painter Vasa Pomorišac. The part of the building facing Kralja Petra Street houses the legacy of the painter Petar Dobrović.

buildings.description: The corner house of the First Danube Steamship Company, where Kapetan Mišina meets Gospodar Jevremova, was built between 1924 and 1926 as the Vienna company's Belgrade representation and housing. The design came from Vienna, and the local engineer Stevan Tobolar adapted it to the terrain and to the needs of the branch. Its emphatically vertical corner made the building a landmark of the district and gave Belgrade one of its first examples of modernist expressionism.
buildings.history: Alexander Popp's preliminary drawings reached Belgrade from Vienna in November 1923, well before building began; the company had its head office in the Austrian capital. The task of developing them went to the construction firm of engineer Stevan Tobolar, which also carried out the works, fitting the scheme to the terrain and to the internal routine of a representation. The result was a mixed house of offices and flats, its corner pulling two wings apart and taking the role of the composition's centre. For Popp it was the first significant work of his career; for Belgrade it was evidence of the Viennese municipal housing tradition of 1919–1934.

buildings.description: The Pavlovic house at 39 Gospodar Jevremova was built in 1882 as a single-storey family home for Kosta Pavlovic, then head of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. It was more than a residence: its rooms hosted many figures from the political and cultural life of the capital. An academic design with a well-kept garden makes it a characteristic piece of Belgrade's urban architecture of the later nineteenth century, and in 1927 Aleksandar Sekulic's plans added a storey with an attic. Inside, the family built up over decades a collection of art, documents, decorations, furniture and books.
buildings.history: Kosta Pavlovic, a senior official of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, built himself a modest single-storey house in 1882. By the end of the nineteenth century houses of this kind, with their gardens, gave Belgrade its urban character, and the Pavlovic home remains a clear example of that townscape. In 1927 the building gained a storey and an attic to designs by Aleksandar Sekulic. Its drawing rooms were the setting for social occasions attended by many prominent figures in political and cultural life. The family also assembled a substantial collection of domestic and foreign art, documents, decorations, furniture and applied art, together with a large library.

buildings.description: The house where literary critic Jovan Skerlić lived from 1905 until his death in 1914 is a memorial address of Belgrade's culture at the beginning of the 20th century. Skerlić was a professor, editor of Srpski književni glasnik, a member of the Serbian Royal Academy and a member of parliament.
buildings.history: The house was built in the first decade of the 20th century as a family residence on the corner of two streets, of the kind bourgeois Belgrade built at the turn of the century. From 1905 until his death in 1914 Jovan Skerlić lived here with his family. This is where he worked as a critic, professor and editor of Srpski književni glasnik; his word was taken as a final verdict in literature, culture and politics alike. That fact gives the building its memorial character.

buildings.description: The sculptor Rade Stanković's house on Simina was built in 1912 as a courtyard dwelling, probably after a design by Nikola Nestorović. Its lower floor served as a studio and the upper one as living quarters, and in that studio Stanković worked from his arrival in Belgrade in 1936 until his death in 1996. The house still keeps the bulk of his oeuvre — sculpture that holds to classical tradition while taking in impressionist modelling and a Secessionist streak.
buildings.history: The house was put up in 1912 in the courtyard of a Simina street plot: a studio on the lower floor, living rooms above, a cubic volume with an asymmetric facade and almost no ornament. Its design is attributed to Nikola Nestorović. In 1936 the sculptor Rade Stanković moved in and stayed until his death in 1996, producing much of his work in the studio below. Trained in the circle of Ivan Meštrović, Frane Kršinić and Robert Frangeš, he taught generations of students at Belgrade's Academy of Applied Arts from its founding in 1948. His sculpture held to classical tradition while taking in impressionist modelling and Secessionist form, and the house keeps the largest part of that legacy — works that stand for Serbian sculpture of the twentieth century.

buildings.description: The house in Dositejeva Street ties together two strands of Belgrade's history: in 1878–1879 it sheltered the English Institute for Serbian Orphans, and later the composer Stevan Stojanović Mokranjac lived and worked in it. Jakov Damjanović, a building contractor, put it up in 1872 in the street that had just been laid out.
buildings.history: The house was built at the end of 1872 as the family home of Jakov Damjanović, a building contractor, in the just-regulated Dositejeva Street. From July 1878 to May 1879 it housed the English Institute for Serbian Orphans, founded after the Serbian-Turkish wars by the English physician Dr Henry Ziman, and a courtyard wing was added to the house for its needs. Stevan Stojanović Mokranjac (1856–1914) lived and worked here — a composer and choirmaster, teacher and collector of folk melodies, a representative of musical realism whose Rukoveti are considered his highest achievement.

buildings.description: The politician and statesman Nikola Pašić lived in this house on Francuska Street from 1893 until his death in 1926. Pašić had the modest 1872 house of the Džanga merchants thoroughly rebuilt in 1921 to a design by engineer Marijan Vujović.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1872 for the Džanga merchants as a modest family home. In 1893 it was bought by the politician and statesman Nikola Pašić, who lived here until his death in 1926. Its present appearance dates from 1921, when it was thoroughly rebuilt on the owner's ideas and to a design by engineer Marijan Vujović: a typical bourgeois house of the second half of the 19th century became a building in the spirit of interwar academic architecture, better suited to its owner's standing. In 1936 a marble memorial plaque was placed on the house in memory of Pašić — prime minister, leader of the Radical Party, president of the National Assembly and of the Ministerial Council, head of the Belgrade municipality and envoy to Russia.

buildings.description: The Leona Panajot House is a family house built in 1908 to a design by Petar Bajalović; as a striking work of the Secession it was shown at the Fourth Yugoslav Art Exhibition in Belgrade in 1912. It has since been recognised as a notable authorial work, important for the development of Belgrade architecture in the first half of the 20th century.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1908 to a design by architect Petar Bajalović. Only four years later it was shown at the Fourth Yugoslav Art Exhibition in Belgrade as an outstanding work of the Secession. Ever since, it has been counted among the works that shaped Belgrade architecture in the first half of the 20th century.

buildings.description: The only surviving family house in the oeuvre of Jelisaveta Načić, the first woman architect in Serbia. The home of the bookseller Marko Marković, on the Danube slope, remains an authentic example of middle-class city housing of the early twentieth century.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1904 to a design by Jelisaveta Načić; in 1936 minor alterations followed drawings by the engineer Jan Švejkar, leaving the original appearance almost untouched. It is the only surviving family house from the varied oeuvre of Serbia’s first woman architect. Its place on the Danube slope ties it to the long history of organised city life in this part of Belgrade.

buildings.description: The first building Andra Stevanović ever realised: a professor at the Technical Faculty of the Grand School, he would later sign some of Belgrade’s most important buildings. The house of Andra Đorđević rose in 1888 on the Danube slope, when prosperous families began moving into this quarter.
buildings.history: The house went up in 1888, at a moment when wealthy and respected Belgrade families were beginning to move into this part of the city, until then an exclusively Turkish quarter. Entry was through a street gate into the courtyard, and only from there into the house with its characteristic L-shaped plan. Andra Stevanović, professor at the Technical Faculty of the Grand School, designed it; this was the first of his projects to be built, and it opened a long career.

buildings.description: The house of the painter Đorđe Krstić, a leading figure of Serbian realism: he lived here, worked here and died here in 1907. The studio built specially for him survives as well, and it was there that his best-known canvases were painted.
buildings.history: The house was raised around 1890 in the academic style of the nineteenth century. Đorđe Krstić (1851–1907) held a state scholarship and spent ten years in Munich, where he finished the academy and painted his first canvases; later he travelled through Serbia and Italy, working on iconostases, historical compositions, icons and portraits. In 1888 he entered state service as a teacher of drawing. The house survives in its original form together with the studio, a rarity in Belgrade.

buildings.description: The oldest surviving building in Belgrade: the house of Elias Fleischman, a saddler, raised between 1724 and 1727 under the regulation plan of the Austrian administration. It is the only dwelling of the first half of the eighteenth century preserved in the city outside the fortress.
buildings.history: The saddler Elias Fleischman’s house was built between 1724 and 1727, during the Austrian occupation of Belgrade (1717–39), when the town was laid out afresh according to the regulation plan of Colonel Nikola Doxat de Morez. It stood as one of seven identical houses in a row, an early instance of planned development here. Today it is the only dwelling of the first half of the eighteenth century left in Belgrade’s urban fabric outside the fortress, and the oldest building in the city to have outlived every change in its architectural heritage.

buildings.description: The home of Ivan Ribar’s family, where his sons Ivo-Lola and the painter Jurica grew up — a memorial plaque in the hall records it. After the war Ribar gave the building to the Union of Youth, and it now serves as a day room for schoolchildren.
buildings.history: The house was built between 1920 and 1922 on the foundations of an older building; its first owner was Rudolf Pilc. In 1928 the one-storey family house, unremarkable in appearance, was bought by Dr Ivan Ribar, who lived and worked there with his family until the Second World War. After the war he gave the building to the Union of Youth, and it now provides a day room for schoolchildren.

buildings.description: One of the last bank palaces of interwar Belgrade: the Agrarian Bank building, put up in 1932–34 by Petar and Branko Krstić. Here the brothers struck a compromise between the academic and the modernist view of architecture, a device that did much to shape the city centre.
buildings.history: The building went up between 1932 and 1934 for the Agrarian Bank: bank palaces of the interwar years projected the political and economic strength of the state, and the Agrarian Bank received one of the last of them in Belgrade. The design by Petar and Branko Krstić joined academic tradition to a modernist handling of plan and volume, a deliberate compromise between the two schools. With this work the brothers left a visible mark on the architectural image of central Belgrade.

buildings.description: The former Bulevar hotel, where a first film was shown in 1899, only three years after the first film projection in Belgrade. From 1909 to 1911 the Belgrade Opera worked here under Žarko Savić, so the hotel became known as the Opera, and the cinema has borne the name Balkan since 1928.
buildings.history: The building was raised between 1867 and 1870 as the Bulevar hotel, and a wing was later added whose ground floor held a large hall. In 1899 the first film was shown in that hall, and from 1909 to 1911 the Belgrade Opera performed in the house. A permanent cinema opened in 1912 as the Grand Bioskop of the Gomon family at the Opera hotel, and for a time Brana Cvetković’s theatre played on the same stage. The name Balkan was adopted at the beginning of 1928.

buildings.description: The house of the Association of Purchasing Cooperatives of Civil Servants, built in 1928–29 to Dimitrije M. Lek’s competition entry, which took second prize. For over six decades its large hall served as Studio 10 of Radio Belgrade, where radio plays were recorded.
buildings.history: The house was built between mid-1928 and mid-1929 to Lek’s competition design and conceived as a monumental four-storey block of three wings arranged in a horseshoe. Offices, ceremonial public rooms and flats were combined under one roof. The sculptor Živojin Lukić executed the facade sculpture after Lek’s drawings, giving it the symbolism of fertility, happiness and prosperity associated with the institution’s work. The great hall later became a trademark of Radio Belgrade’s drama production.

buildings.description: The house of Jovan Smederevac at 27 Nusiceva is a rare case from 1901 of an engineer drawing up his own building. A narrow corner house crowned with a cupola, it holds the academic tradition and the first stirrings of Secession together: symmetrical facades with a firm horizontal division still speak the language of the nineteenth century, while the Secession ornament and the wrought-iron balcony railing speak the language of the new style. That ornament makes the house one of the earliest Belgrade examples of the new movement.
buildings.history: Jovan Smederevac, an engineer, built the house in 1901 to his own drawings. He took a corner plot, where the narrow front with its cupola could be seen from the street, and the double purpose of the building allowed living quarters and other rooms under one roof. The plan and the symmetry of the facades betray the academic school, yet the ornament on the free wall surfaces of the upper floor was new for Belgrade at the time. The balcony with a wrought-iron railing on the front added a characteristic element of the Secession vocabulary. Such details marked the moment when the Serbian capital began to try the new style.

buildings.description: The Pension Fund Palace, also known as the Beograd Palace, is the most important work of the Russian architect Grigory Ivanovich Samoilov and one of the ornaments of Terazije Square. The corner block of flats and offices was built in 1938–40.
buildings.history: The palace was built between 1938 and 1940 to a design by Grigory Ivanovich Samoilov, a Russian architect with many private villas, churches and industrial buildings to his name. Flats are grouped around a central rectangular core with a semicircular end, a plan dictated by the corner site. The design fuses academicism and modernism: Samoilov kept the academic frame yet used new materials, glass and metal, in the recessed ground floor.

buildings.description: The House of Trade Unions, built by Branko Petričić between 1947 and 1955, fixed for good the outline of one of the city’s principal squares. It hosted political and cultural gatherings, and in 1958 a concert organ by the Walcker firm was installed here.
buildings.history: The house was built between 1947 and 1955 to Branko Petričić’s design as a venue for major political and cultural gatherings. It consists of two wings: the main one, with a curved facade, abuts the side elevation of the Pension Fund Palace on one side and merges into the block on Dečanska Street on the other, while a passage under it leads into the Bezistan atrium. Traces of socialist realism and 1950s monumentalism remain in the interior, alongside the newer spirit of freely handled space. The Great and Small Halls were meant for cultural events, political meetings, film screenings and festivals, and that has remained their character.

buildings.description: The corner building of the engineer Miloš Savčić at Kralja Milana and Andrićev venac went up in 1925, in a season of commercial and social confidence in Belgrade. The drawings were signed by the client himself and by the architect Evgenije Gulin; offices occupied the ground floor and flats the upper storeys, as in most interwar buildings of dual purpose. The house still keeps to the academic tradition and, with its monumental neighbours, sustains the ceremonial character of the street.
buildings.history: The house at the corner of Kralja Milana and Andrićev venac was built in 1925 for the engineer Miloš Savčić, and the architect Evgenije Gulin signed the drawings alongside the client himself. Its arrival coincided with the economic and social rise of Belgrade between the wars. It belongs to the ordinary interwar type of dual-purpose building: offices and shops below, flats above. The treatment of the exterior still betrays an attachment to the earlier academic age, though the house already took its place in the row of monumental buildings that gave the street its formal character. That setting still defines its role in the city today.

buildings.description: The Belgrade home of the Journalists’ Association of Serbia, designed by Ernest Vajsman and completed in 1934. It ranks among the city’s most significant buildings conceived in the modern spirit, and it has long been a meeting place for journalists, publicists, writers and leading figures of Serbian cultural life.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1934 to a design by Ernest Vajsman as the seat of the Journalists’ Association of Serbia. Journalists, publicists and writers gathered there together with the most prominent figures in Serbian cultural life, and the building soon became one of the centres of the capital’s professional and cultural life.

buildings.description: The Petronijević Family House on Kneza Miloša Street is a speculative apartment and commercial building put up in 1922 for Dr Miloš Petronijević, who headed the foreign correspondence department of the National Bank. He was a grandson of Avram Petronijević and a son of Milan A. Petronijević, and the house was meant first of all for the family, with flats and shops let out for income. The architect Nikola Nestorović gave it an academic frame filled with the ornament of the Secession. Its ground floor lived off the street trade while the upper floors stayed residential, and in that pairing the building works as a piece of the old city's fabric.
buildings.history: Built in 1922 to Nestorović's design, the house follows the outline of its plot: a symmetrical, compound plan with two side light wells on each flank and one in the centre. Shops filled the ground floor, the mezzanine held two offices and two small flats, and each of the three upper storeys carried two large apartments, with a single flat and attic space under the mansard. Three-sided bays run up the main facade across three storeys, tied horizontally by semicircular balconies. The upper walls carry the floral vocabulary of the Secession in garlands and cartouches, and the ironwork of the balconies belongs to the same decorative language. The house also keeps the memory of three Serbian families — Petronijević, Piroćanac and Jurišić Šturm.

buildings.description: The building of the Officers' Cooperative on Masarykova Street was raised in 1908 to a design by three architects, Svetozar Jovanović, Danilo Vladisavljević and Vladimir Popović. It ranks among the most important works of the Belgrade Secession, and its dome — the work of the tinsmith Milan Ilić — is counted among the largest and finest in the city. The block was conceived as a free-standing building in which the working premises at the edges of the side wings are set apart from the public central section, left open to circulation.
buildings.history: The building was raised in 1908 to a design by the architects Svetozar Jovanović, Danilo Vladisavljević and Vladimir Popović in the spirit of the Secession. It was built of stone and brick in lime mortar, with a basement, a semi-basement, a ground floor and two upper floors. The separation of functions was carried through to the exterior: the side wings keep a traditional facade treatment with small openings, while the main facade was handled in a modern way, with windows running through several storeys. Secession models appear in the emphatic verticalism and in the ornament — female heads, floral sculpture, decorative consoles and wrought-iron grilles. The dome, made by the tinsmith Milan Ilić, is among the largest and finest in Belgrade, and the building is regarded as one of the most important Secession works in the city.

buildings.description: The Social Insurance Building on the corner of Nemanjina and Svetozara Markovića streets was raised in 1959–62 to a design by Aleksej Brkić. It is his most valued work and one of the buildings that marked a new stage in Serbian postwar architecture.
buildings.history: The building went up between 1959 and 1962 for the social insurance institution. Brkić combined a strictly functional layout with contrasting volumes and materials and with colour; among Serbian postwar buildings it remains the only one in which polychromy was given full rein. The block became the visual accent of the upper stretch of Nemanjina Street.

buildings.description: The corner house of the Veljković family, with a separate art pavilion in its yard built in 1931 expressly to display paintings and sculpture from the family’s valuable collection. The house itself dates from 1883.
buildings.history: The house was put up in 1883, and the courtyard residential building followed between 1878 and 1883. The Veljković family produced politicians, lawyers and officers who influenced the social, political and artistic life of Serbia. In 1931 a purpose-built art pavilion, designed by Vojislav Đokić and the engineer Aleksandar Gavrilović, was added to hold the family collection.

buildings.description: The Vukićević House on Bulevar oslobođenja was built in 1921 to a design by the architect Zarija Marković for the professor and politician Velimir Velja Vukićević, a notable figure in Serbian political life in the first decades of the twentieth century. Its post-academic composition, with restrained Secession motifs and a symmetrical plan centred on the staircase, makes it characteristic of Belgrade housing of its day. Its deeper value lies in continuity: three generations of the family lived and worked here, leaving a mark on Serbian art and culture in the second half of the twentieth century.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1921 to a design by the architect Zarija Marković for the professor and politician Velimir Velja Vukićević. It has a basement, a ground floor and two upper floors, with a symmetrical plan whose spatial organisation is concentrated on the central staircase. The composition is post-academic, with restrained Secession motifs in the decorative treatment of the facades. The house remained tied to a single family: three generations of Vukićevićs lived and worked in it. Velimir Velja Vukićević (1871–1930) held a significant place in politics in the first decades of the twentieth century, and his descendants left their mark on Serbian art and culture in the second half of the century.

buildings.description: The House of the Nikolić Brothers is one of the very few surviving Belgrade buildings in the Serbian-Byzantine style. Branko Tanazević, the leading advocate of the national style’s revival, built it in 1912–14 for Jovan and Maksim Nikolić.
buildings.history: The house was built between 1912 and 1914 for the brothers Jovan and Maksim Nikolić to a design by Branko Tanazević. Tanazević carried out here, consistently, his programme of reviving the national style, of which he was the chief advocate, and the house survives as one of the very few examples of that orientation in Belgrade.

buildings.description: The House of the Vračar Beautification Society was the first building in Belgrade to receive Secessionist elements. The society, founded in 1884 to look after the improvement of eastern and western Vračar, built its headquarters here in 1902 to a design by Milan Antonović.
buildings.history: The building was put up by the Vračar Beautification Society, founded in 1884, to a design by the architect Milan Antonović. From its completion in 1902 until the society was dissolved in 1941 the house served as its headquarters, the place from which the improvement of eastern and western Vračar was run.

buildings.description: The Turkish Embassy occupies a house next to the National Assembly building, a Belgrade address where diplomacy and literature share a roof. In the Habsburg era the building served as a palace, and the Serbian poet Jovan Jovanović Zmaj lived in it for a time, as a plaque on the facade recalls. Turkey bought the house in 1967, and it has housed the country’s top mission in Serbia ever since.
buildings.history: The first Ottoman ambassador to Serbia was Sermed efendi, who served from 1 January to 1 June 1881. During the Serbian monarchy the house was rented, and in 1967 Turkey purchased it outright. On 9 March 1983 the embassy was attacked by the Armenian organisation ASALA, and ambassador Galip Balkar was killed. The building has remained the seat of the Turkish mission ever since.

buildings.description: The Majestic Hotel on Obilićev venac is the most significant work of Milan S. Minić, who acted here as designer, contractor and owner at once. The hotel is made up of two purpose-built blocks that form a single functional whole.
buildings.history: The first block of the hotel went up in 1936; the second, set at a right angle to it, was added in 1940. Together they formed two wings of one hotel, conceived as a representative establishment with a basement, ground floor, gallery and six upper floors. Milan S. Minić, at once designer, contractor and owner, made the Majestic a synthesis of architecture, fine art and applied art.

buildings.description: The “Progres” building on Zmaj Jovina Street went up between 1993 and 1996 on the site of an old single-storey house damaged in the war and demolished in 1992. The six-storey office block, designed by Miodrag Mirković and Ljubiša Mangov after their winning entry in a 1990 competition, answered the historic surroundings of Knez Mihailova in the language of late postmodernism. Its ground floor holds the Progres Gallery, marked at the entrance by Olja Ivanjicki's bronze Mercury turning on a rotating pedestal.
buildings.history: The earlier house on the site had been damaged during the Second World War, when the whole wing towards Knez Mihailova was torn down; after the war it was repeatedly rebuilt and altered before its final demolition in 1992. The new block was designed through the 1990 competition and built between 1993 and 1996 on a tight corner plot. The architects sought a balance of old and new: one stretch of the Knez Mihailova facade ties in with the neighbouring house, another, convex stretch follows the corner of the French Cultural Centre, and a solid wall pierced by windows carries the eye from the glass corner to older buildings.
