Part of the block was later absorbed into the Millennium shopping centre, opening a route into the middle of the block, and Zmaj Jovina was landscaped after the works to Branislav Jovin's design. The Progres gallery opened in 1997 with an exhibition by Olja Ivanjicki, occupying the ground floor and the basement.

buildings.description: The Class Lottery Building, put up in 1899, was the first lottery building in Serbia and served economic ends: its revenues supported numerous artistic and educational events across the country. The design came from the architect Milan Kapetanović and the engineer Miloš Savčić.
buildings.history: The building was raised in 1899 for the Class Lottery, an institution of state standing whose revenues funded artistic and educational events in the country. At the time of construction it stood, together with Captain Miša’s Building and the National Theatre, among the most representative buildings on the stretch from Kalemegdan to today’s Republic Square. It remains a witness to the economic and urban rise of the capital at the turn of the twentieth century.

buildings.description: Kolarac People’s University is the endowment of Ilija Milosavljević Kolarac. Public lectures have been held here daily since the institution was founded, and its concert hall still has no acoustic rival in Belgrade.
buildings.history: Construction began in 1929 with a block in the courtyard of the existing single-storey house on land belonging to the endowment of Ilija Milosavljević Kolarac. In 1930 the great hall with its lecture rooms was completed; it was already one of Belgrade’s most important cultural centres, so in 1931 the decision was taken to build a new wing facing the street. Petar Bajalović was entrusted with the design, and the building was finished in 1932.

buildings.description: The merchant Stamenković’s apartment building, popularly known as “the house with green tiles”: built in 1907 to a design by Andra Stevanović and Nikola Nestorović, it is one of the high points of Secessionist architecture in Belgrade.
buildings.history: The house went up in 1907 and belongs to the group of residential buildings raised in Belgrade before the First World War, in which an academic conception was combined with Secessionist decoration. Because of the green ceramic tiles on its walls it is still popularly called the house with green tiles, and it is regarded as a high achievement of the style in the Serbian capital.

buildings.description: The Đura Jakšić House in Skadarlija is a cultural institution and one of the oldest buildings on the famous Belgrade street. It is the house where the Serbian poet and painter Đura Jakšić lived and died; he was the first of the celebrated Belgrade bohemians to settle in the quarter and was nicknamed "the first bohemian". Today literary evenings, concerts, theatre performances and exhibitions fill it almost every day, and the Stari Grad municipality runs the house.
buildings.history: In the early nineteenth century the area of today's Skadarlija was Ciganska mahala, a poor quarter beyond the town rampart where modest citizens settled. By the middle of the century it had about fifteen kafanas that drew artists, and the nearby National Theatre and Opera turned the area into a centre of bohemian life. In 1872 the city authorities renamed Ciganska mahala as Skadarska Street. In 1925 the newspaper Politika drew attention to the poet's house for fear it might vanish, and residents led by Čiča Ilija Stanojević placed a memorial plaque by sculptor Dušan Jovanović, unveiled on 6 December. In 1935 a memorial with Jakšić's likeness and a note that his life ended there was ceremonially unveiled, and in 1986 the house was renovated to create conditions for showing visual artists.

buildings.description: The first modern department store in Belgrade, built in 1907 to a design by the engineer Viktor Azriel and considered the most significant Serbian achievement of the Secession, both structurally and in form.
buildings.history: The store was built in 1907 and was the first commercial building in Belgrade in which several floors were opened to one another, so that the whole interior could be taken in from the galleries. Its author, the engineer Viktor Azriel, designed it in the Secessionist manner, which is why it is held to be the most significant Serbian work of that style.

buildings.description: The house of the merchant Crvenčanin stands in one of Belgrade’s oldest trading streets, where the ground floor and mezzanine were meant for shops from the start and the upper floors for living. It was designed by the architect Jovan Ilkić, and this is the first building in Belgrade to put a mezzanine above the ground floor.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1887 to a design by the architect Jovan Ilkić for the merchant Crvenčanin. Because the street was a trading one, the ground floor and mezzanine held shops while the floors above were given over to flats. The building is counted among Ilkić’s notable works and as an outstanding example of 19th-century academic architecture in Belgrade.

buildings.description: The house of the merchant Milorad Pavlović follows the logic of a trading street: shops at ground level, one grand apartment on each floor above. Two separate entrances lead into what is formally one house under a single roof, and the design is attributed to Jovan Ilkić.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1884 for the merchant Milorad Pavlović, and its design is attributed to the architect Jovan Ilkić. Two buildings with independent entrances share one roof and a single treatment of the façades. Because the street was a trading one, the ground floor held shops and each upper floor a single representative flat. The house belongs to the small group of grand bourgeois houses built in Belgrade at the end of the 19th century.

buildings.description: A house designed for painters: four leading Yugoslav artists — Stojan Aralica, Ivan Tabaković, Milenko Šerban and Peđa Milosavljević — moved into its studios, and since 1961 its ground floor has housed the gallery now known as the Salon of the Museum of Contemporary Art. The architect was Miroslav Jovanović.
buildings.history: The house went up between 1956 and 1960 to a design by Miroslav Jovanović, one of the leading Serbian architects of the second half of the century. Its programme combined flats with painters’ studios and a space meant for showing contemporary art. Four established Yugoslav artists moved in once it was finished, and in 1961 the Modern Gallery opened on the ground floor — the present Salon of the Museum of Contemporary Art, which has been exhibiting major Yugoslav and international artists for more than fifty years.

buildings.description: A family house of the late 18th century, one of Belgrade’s earliest examples of a newer way of building and a witness to the shift from Balkan to Central European architecture. Its position marks the old town plan, and it survives as a rare trace of the former Varoš Gate.
buildings.history: The house was built at the end of the 18th century as a family home. It was raised in timber-frame construction, in the manner of Pannonian town houses that mixed baroque and classicist elements. Later repairs substantially altered the wooden porch on the courtyard side. The building documents the period when Belgrade moved from Balkan to Central European patterns of building and living.

buildings.description: A respected merchant’s house with a paper shop on its lower floors: Milan Antonović gave it early Secession touches then new to Belgrade, and the decorative painter Dragutin Inkiostri decorated the entrance hall. Two floors were added later without essentially changing the original look.
buildings.history: The building went up in 1904 to a design by the well-known Belgrade architect Milan Antonović as a combined shop and dwelling: paper was traded in the basement and ground floor, with flats above. The entrance hall was painted by the decorative artist Dragutin Inkiostri. In 1926–27 the architect Samuel Sumbul added two floors, which did not substantially alter the original appearance.

buildings.description: A corner apartment house by Nikola Nestorović, built in 1912 as a single flat arranged around a central hall. It later held the Danube horsemen’s club “Knez Mihailo”, popularly called the Jockey Club, and after the Second World War became home to the Institute of Criminological and Sociological Research.
buildings.history: The building was raised in 1912 to a design by the architect Nikola Nestorović as a corner house with one large flat developing around a central hall. Its use changed over time, and it was extended and repartitioned accordingly. For a while it housed the “Knez Mihailo” Danube horsemen’s club, popularly known as the Jockey Club, when a large hall for festivities was added. After the Second World War the Institute of Criminological and Sociological Research moved in.

buildings.description: The Faculty of Philosophy is the oldest faculty of the University of Belgrade, tracing its origins to the Belgrade Higher School of 1838. Its building stands at the corner of Čika-Ljubina and Knez Mihailova, in the middle of the city's main pedestrian zone. Ten departments teach philosophy, history, archaeology, psychology and more, and Roman baths survive on the plateau in front of the house.
buildings.history: The faculty was among those that formed the University of Belgrade at its founding in 1905. In 1947 the natural sciences and mathematics split away into a separate faculty, followed in 1960 by philology. Today more than 250 teaching staff work with several thousand students, from undergraduate to doctoral level. Roman baths and a buried archaeological site, described in the 1970s, lie on the plateau in front of the building.

buildings.description: Hotel Balkan occupies the corner of Terazije and Prizrenska, where Belgrade's commercial life has been concentrated since the nineteenth century. A tavern had stood on the site since 1835, and around 1860 the first, single-storey hotel rose here to a design by the engineer Andrija Vuković. In 1935 the old building was demolished and the present hotel was built in its place.
buildings.history: The hotel was designed around 1860 by the engineer Andrija Vuković, and a beer hall called Balkan operated inside it. In 1896 it was bought by Samuilo and Golub Janić, and in 1918 it passed to Golub's widow, Bosiljka Janić. In 1928 she established a foundation and bequeathed the hotel to the Serbian Royal Academy, so that its income would fund primary schools with flats for teachers in southern Serbia. Back in 1904 the hotelier Popara had thoroughly renovated the house and reopened it on 30 May with coloured sunshades and Munich Salvator beer. The building was adapted several times and extended towards Prizrenska Street in 1928.

buildings.description: The Ljubomir Miladinović building is known simply as “The Garage”, because its ground floor was designed as parking. Momčilo Belobrk’s scheme is counted among the purest examples of Belgrade functionalism.
buildings.history: The building was completed in 1938 to a design by the architect Momčilo Belobrk. Its ground floor, given over to garages, earned it the name “The Garage”. The scheme is regarded as a high point in Belobrk’s own work and in Serbian modern architecture more broadly, noted for its modern handling and consistent functionalism.

buildings.description: Moderna Garage on Majke Jevrosime was the first modern car park in Belgrade and, for that matter, in the Western Balkans, built in 1929 to a design by the Russian engineer and architect Valerij Vladimirovich Stashevsky. Inside it is a single hall under one roof; outside, an academic block with post-Secession touches and sculpture above the monumental entrance. It served not only as parking but as a workshop where cars were maintained and repaired, and it soon became a hub of Belgrade's motoring sport.
buildings.history: The garage went up in 1929 to a design by Valerij Stashevsky, a Russian engineer and architect who lived and worked in Belgrade until the Second World War. It was built to European standards but dressed in academic forms with post-Secession detail: sculpture over the monumental doorway, doubled windows giving the side wings a vertical pull. The interior was left as one hall, so that cars could be parked, serviced and repaired under the same roof. Before the war it operated as a public garage; afterwards it housed the city taxi service and later the fleet of Radio Television Belgrade. Since 1994 it has been the Museum of Automobiles, showing more than fifty veteran and rare cars collected by Bratislav Petković.

buildings.description: The Belgrade home of the Beočin Cement Factory pension fund went up in 1934 to a design by Dragiša Brašovan. It belonged to the fund, yet it came out as a manifesto: the corner pushed forward in balconies, window strips running in rhythm, and an open roof terrace were read as a statement about modernity. Later commentators treated the building as a model for the residential blocks through which the city absorbed modernism.
buildings.history: In 1934 the pension fund of the Beočin cement works obtained a residential building in Belgrade, designed by Dragiša Brašovan, by then an established name. The architect sank the ground and top floors inward and pushed the corner out in balconies, so that the block reads first of all as a silhouette. A roof terrace with columns and a band closed the composition, and for decades it served as a test case for judging whether a piece of architecture still felt contemporary. Round attic windows and a flagpole on the roof reinforced the building's formality. With its balanced relation of parts to whole and its attention to detail, the house became a model for the residential quarters Belgrade built in the modernist spirit.

buildings.description: Atelje 212 is one of Belgrade's most visited theatres, born in 1956 in the offices of the Borba newspaper, where a hall of 212 seats gave the company its name. It was here that Waiting for Godot had its first open public performance in post-war Eastern Europe, and later came Hair and Jesus Christ Superstar. Since the 1960s the company has worked in a building on Svetogorska Street designed by Bojan Stupica, with a revolving stage and a roof that opens in summer.
buildings.history: The theatre was founded on 12 November 1956 in the Borba building, and its opening production was Goethe's Faust, directed by Mira Trailović. From the start the company favoured avant-garde writers such as Sartre, Ionesco, Jarry and Genet, with Radoš Novaković and Bojan Stupica as its first managers. After a few years as a tenant it moved into its own house on Svetogorska Street, designed by Stupica, whose stage could rotate and whose roof was retractable in summer. In 1967 Trailović launched BITEF, the international festival of new theatre tendencies that grew out of the company's artistic profile. Hair played here in 1969, before many major world stages, and Jesus Christ Superstar followed in 1972; a statue of Zoran Radmilović in his King Ibia costume stands by the main entrance.

buildings.description: The studio of Uroš Predić, one of Serbia’s leading painters of academic realism, where he worked for 44 years, from 1909 until his death in 1953. The house itself was built in 1908 to a design by Nikola Nestorović for the painter’s brother, Josif Predić.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1908 to Nestorović’s design as the family home of Josif Predić, the painter’s brother. Uroš Predić (1857–1953) moved in in 1909 and spent 44 years in the studio until his death. His most valuable paintings, which did much to shape Serbian painting in the first decade of the 20th century, were made here.

buildings.description: The purpose-built home of the National Library of Serbia, the country's oldest institution, founded in 1832 and repeatedly stripped of its collections by war. Ivo Kurtović designed it, and it opened on 6 April 1973 — the date the library had long observed in memory of its destruction in 1941.
buildings.history: The library began in 1832 in Gligorije Vozarović's bookshop, and that November Prince Miloš ordered that one copy of every book printed in the country be deposited with it — the origin of legal deposit in Serbia. In the First World War the collections were carried off as war booty, and the building on Kosančićev venac, bought in 1920 from Milan Vapa's cardboard factory, burned on 6 April 1941 in the German bombing of Belgrade, when some 500,000 volumes and 1,424 Cyrillic manuscripts and charters were lost. The new building in Vračar went up between 1966, when the cornerstone was laid, and 1972; Ivo Kurtović was the architect and the move began in May 1972. Willy Brandt, the first foreign statesman to visit the new building, brought books as a gift when it opened on 6 April 1973.

buildings.description: The first purpose-built home of the University Children’s Clinic, founded in 1924 together with the Belgrade Medical Faculty. Milan Zloković’s building of 1936–40 is regarded as a model of consistent modernist practice and one of the high points of the movement in Serbian architecture.
buildings.history: The clinic was founded in 1924, immediately after the Medical Faculty in Belgrade was established, and for years it had no building of its own. The new house was built to Milan Zloković’s design between 1936 and 1940; only after moving in and installing medical equipment could the institution fully develop its work. The commission came at the height of Zloković’s maturity, the period in which he brought Serbian architecture into modern European currents.

buildings.description: The headquarters of the National Bank of Serbia on Slavija Square, completed and inaugurated in 2006 to a design by the architect Grujo Golijanin. The bank it serves traces its line back to 1884, when the Privileged National Bank of the Kingdom of Serbia was founded.
buildings.history: The work was long: construction began in the early 1990s for the National Bank of Yugoslavia, stopped because of the country’s financial and political troubles, restarted only in the 2000s and the building was inaugurated in 2006. A law that came into force on 19 July 2003 gave the bank its present name, the National Bank of Serbia. The institution itself is older than the house: in 1941–44 it operated from its London representation, and in September 1946 it was nationalised.

buildings.description: The house of Josif Šojat in Kralja Milutina Street is a rare Belgrade example of Art Deco: Milan Zloković combined motifs of the Italian Renaissance with relief and painted decoration on the facade. It is one of his earliest works and one of the most important in his whole opus.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1926–27 to a design by Milan Zloković, an architect of the modernist generation. In this early work he used an eclectic method, shaping a modernised structure with stylistic elements of Renaissance palaces of central and northern Italy and relief accents inspired by the Baroque and Mannerism. Relief and painted decoration with figure compositions completed the facades, and the result — a rare example of Art Deco — helped establish the style in Belgrade and Serbia between the two world wars.

buildings.description: The State Chemical Laboratory opened in 1882 through the efforts of Ferdinand Šams, although the need for such an institution had been recognised back in 1859. Its longest-serving head was the chemist Marko Leko, who ran it from 1894 to 1920.
buildings.history: The building went up in 1882 as a single-storey house in the academic manner, sized to the state's means and the needs of the profession. A first floor was added in 1926–27, following the architecture already in place. The laboratory was meant to be a place where all the chemists of Serbia would gather; over time it became important for the country's cultural history as much as for its science, and Marko Leko, professor and rector of the Great School, directed it from 1894 to 1920.

buildings.description: The house of the Krstić brothers is where the architects Petar and Branko Krstić were born — the pair behind the award-winning Yugoslav Pavilion at the 1925 Philadelphia exhibition and the award-winning design for the Church of Saint Sava. Decorative details point to Jovan Ilkić.
buildings.history: The house was built at the end of the nineteenth century as a representative residential building, and the Krstić family moved in soon afterwards; Petar and Branko were born there. Their careers began with an award for the Yugoslav Pavilion at the Philadelphia exhibition of 1925, followed by one for the design of the Church of Saint Sava in 1927. They belonged to the Group of Architects of the Modern Movement, and their joint work includes dozens of buildings, among them the Agrarian Bank palace, the Church of Saint Mark and Igumanova palata. The house is one of the few small residential buildings preserved between Terazije and Slavija Square.

buildings.description: The house of the mathematician Bogdan Gavrilović — a modest civic home where the professor, rector of Belgrade University and later president of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts lived for more than half a century. His personal papers and belongings are still kept there.
buildings.history: The house was raised at the turn of the twentieth century, in 1898–99, as a family home. Dr Bogdan Gavrilović (1863–1947), a distinguished mathematician and humanist, lived and worked in it and for more than fifty years took an active part in the cultural, educational and scientific life of the country. His personal legacy survives in the house, which is also a solid example of Belgrade academic architecture at the close of the nineteenth century.

buildings.description: The house of Dr Stanoje Stanojević was built between 1897 and 1899 and, in its functional and spatial layout, represents a representative form of bourgeois housing. From 1904 to 1937 it was the home and workplace of the historian Stanoje Stanojević (1874–1937), professor at Belgrade University, member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences, editor of the first modern Serbian encyclopedia and one of the founders of Politika. The house keeps the memory of a scholar who helped establish Byzantine studies in Serbia and wrote Byzantium and the Serbs and The History of the Serbian People.
buildings.history: The house was built between 1897 and 1899 and in its functional and spatial layout represents a representative form of bourgeois housing. From 1904 to 1937 it was the home and workplace of Dr Stanoje Stanojević (1874–1937), historian, member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences, long-standing professor at Belgrade University, editor of the first modern Serbian encyclopedia and one of the founders of Politika. He studied history in Vienna under Konstantin Jireček and Vatroslav Jagić and took his doctorate there in 1896. A follower of Ilarion Ruvarac and his critical historical school, he belonged to the first generation of European-trained historians, of wide culture and interests and extensive knowledge, whose main orientation was the medieval history of Serbia and the Serbian lands. He was one of the founders of Byzantine studies among the Serbs, and his bibliography runs to more than six hundred items. His most important works are Byzantium and the Serbs and The History of the Serbian People, and he was a corresponding member of the academies of sciences in Bucharest, Prague and Munich.

buildings.description: The Trade Academy, built in 1926 to a design by Jezdimir Denić on the site of the older Trade School. The academy itself, an idea nursed since the middle of the nineteenth century, occupied the house for only three years. Today it belongs to a school of legal and office professions, and in Serbian architecture it is regarded as the purest secular use of the Serbian-Byzantine style on a public building.
buildings.history: A Trade School had stood on the site before; in 1926 Jezdimir Denić designed the present building for the Trade Academy. The idea of founding such an academy had been discussed since the mid-nineteenth century and was only realized at the beginning of the twentieth. The academy stayed in the new house for three years; today the building trains lawyers and office clerks. Architecturally it belongs to the academicized branch of the Serbian-Byzantine style, and specialists regard it as the clearest case of that style applied to a secular public building.

buildings.description: From 1912 the house in Takovska Street was home and workplace to Filip Filipović, one of the most prominent revolutionaries of pre-war Serbia and a founder of the Socialist Workers' Party of Yugoslavia. It belongs to the type of paired houses once common on the outskirts of Belgrade. Its worth lies not in its architecture but in the memory of a man who gave his life to the workers' movement and to the Party.
buildings.history: The house was put up at the end of the nineteenth or the beginning of the twentieth century, when Belgrade's outskirts were filling with paired houses. Filip Filipović moved in in 1912 and made it both home and workplace, giving his time to revolutionary work and to party theory. He was among the founders of the Socialist Workers' Party of Yugoslavia and led it for many years. That chapter of his life is what gives the building its meaning; without it, the house would be entirely ordinary.

buildings.description: Colonel Elezović's house on Njegoševa went up in 1927 to a design by Aleksandar Deroko. It was built to be let, yet Deroko gave it the air of a representative residence, weaving Serbian-Byzantine motifs into the vocabulary of late Secession and setting a relief arabesque by the sculptor Živojin Lukić above the loggia arches. When academism and modernism set the tone in Belgrade, the house stood out as a mature example of the national style applied to a city dwelling.
buildings.history: In 1927 a house designed by Aleksandar Deroko rose on Njegoševa, built to be rented out. Deroko treated the medieval inheritance freely rather than as quotation, folding Serbian-Byzantine motifs into late Secession handling and placing a carved arabesque by Živojin Lukić above the loggia arches. The shallow reliefs across the facade were his own reading of medieval themes. Coming when academism and modernism were competing for Belgrade's housing, the building offered a fresher expression and strong light-and-shadow contrasts, and it counts among the mature achievements of Serbian residential architecture with national colouring.

buildings.description: The family house of Đorđe Genčić, a politician who mattered in Serbia's last decades of the nineteenth century, was built in 1927–1929 to a design by Dragiša Brašovan. Here the architect began the slow modernisation of academic form: a cubic volume, an entrance shaped as a triumphal arch, every facade treated alike. Since 1952 it has housed the Nikola Tesla Museum and its charge, the inventor's scientific and personal legacy.
buildings.history: The house was built for the Genčić family between 1927 and 1929, while Belgrade was expanding fast. Brašovan was then working his way out of academic historicism, and the house shows it: masses held in balance, ornament kept down, yet the classical grammar still audible. After the Second World War the building took on a new purpose, and in 1952 the Nikola Tesla Museum was installed in it. Ever since, the house has held the inventor's manuscripts, instruments and private papers.

buildings.description: The Škarka Villa on Deligradska was built in 1926–27 for Richard Škarka, a Czech engineer who directed the Belgrade branch of the Prague Credit Bank. Dragiša Brašovan, one of the leading figures of Serbian architecture between the wars, designed it during his pre-modernist phase. The result is a representative city villa in which romantic play with historical styles is held together by a clear, almost modern sense of the whole.
buildings.history: The villa was built in 1926–27 for Richard Škarka, the Czech engineer who ran the Belgrade branch of the Prague Credit Bank. Dragiša Brašovan, already counted among the leading architects of the country, worked here in a pre-modernist key: he took the language of academic eclecticism with a romantic accent and broke its ornament into clearly bounded groups. He drew on Romanesque, Venetian Gothic and Baroque sources, repeating the broken arch and baroque volutes on the entrance gate. The interior matched the exterior, and the ceiling of the circular ground-floor hall still carries a wall painting by an unknown hand. Brašovan gave the same care to the courtyard facades that many contemporaries neglected, so that the whole building holds together. With the Genčić house, the villa is counted among the finest of his city villas.

buildings.description: The Home for Orphaned Children was built by the Society for the Education and Protection of Children, founded in 1879: the building in Svetozara Markovića Street was raised with voluntary donations from Belgrade citizens, and from 1887 to 1918 it took in war orphans and abandoned children.
buildings.history: The building was put up between 1887 and 1892 to a design by the Viennese architect Anton Haderer, in the spirit of nineteenth-century academicism. The Society for the Education and Protection of Children, founded in 1879, built it from voluntary contributions of Belgrade citizens as the Home for Orphaned Children. From 1887 to 1918 the house sheltered, schooled and brought up war orphans and abandoned children from the territory of the Serbian and later the Yugoslav state. As an educational institution it was unusually highly regarded in its day and played a major part in the care and socialisation of children without parents.

buildings.description: The house the architect Jovan Ilkić built for his own family in 1896 — a free-standing mansion with a side carriage passage into the courtyard, living rooms on the upper floor and a working study in the basement.
buildings.history: Ilkić built the house in 1896 as a family home on the street line, with a separate side passage for carriages into the courtyard. Living rooms took the upper floor, while the basement held service rooms and chambers used as a study and office; the mansard in the corner risalit was residential as well. In 1925 the house was extended: an annex with a basement and ground floor, designed by Ilkić's son, the architect Pavle Ilkić, was added to the south-west facade, and a curving balustraded staircase in the Baroque manner linked it to the older part.

buildings.description: Hotel Nacional, opened in 1869 as the Narodna Gostionica on the site of an older inn. It belongs to the so-called Kalemegdan hotels, which sprang up on the seam between the town and the fortress right after 1867. For a full century the house kept a public, hospitality role — a rare continuity in Belgrade.
buildings.history: The hotel opened in 1869 under the sign of the Narodna Gostionica, on a site already occupied by an inn. It went up just as Serbian towns were liberated in 1867 and hotels began to line the border between the town and the fortress. The street facades were handled in the academic manner, with neo-Renaissance detail. A century of continuous public use followed, something few Belgrade buildings can claim.

buildings.description: Branislav Kojić built this house for himself in 1926, and that decision turned the building into a statement. A founder of the Group of Architects of the Modern Direction, he spent years testing how the motifs of village building could be joined to modern form, and his own house became the outstanding example of that folklorism in interwar Belgrade. Stylised bay windows borrowed from rural houses give the wall its soft, undulating line and place the building among the first experiments in expressionism in local residential architecture.
buildings.history: Kojić belonged to the circle of architects who were looking for a new language for Belgrade between the wars, and he designed his own house as an experiment rather than a commission. The idea grew out of his research: recognisable devices of folk building — bay windows, a steep roof, a soft wall line — were to be joined with the elements of modern architecture. The house of 1926 became the fullest statement of that programme in residential building. A projecting roof that follows the roundness of the volume and a supple, undulating wall gave it the softness the author was after.

buildings.description: An outbuilding of the Princess Ljubica's Residence, raised around 1836 and later handed to the art school. It stood in the area of the former Town Gate, the heart of political and social life in the Principality of Serbia. Over the years it served as a prince's home, as ministries, as a gymnasium and as an arts-and-crafts school that grew into the Academy of Fine Arts.
buildings.history: The outbuilding of Princess Ljubica's Residence was put up around 1836 in the timber-frame technique usual in Belgrade in the first half of the nineteenth century. Prince Mihailo Obrenović lived there until 1842. The rooms then housed the offices of the ministers of the interior, education and justice, followed by the First Belgrade Gymnasium and later the arts-and-crafts school. That school grew into the Academy of Fine Arts, and today the building holds the Faculty of Applied Arts.

buildings.description: The “?” Kafana on Kralja Petra Street is the oldest tavern in Belgrade. Naum Ičko, a bazaar headman, built it in 1823 for Prince Miloš Obrenović, who then gave the house to Toma Kostić in reward for his service in the Second Serbian Uprising. A tavern kept the lower floor from 1826, and the house went on changing hands and signs. Its odd name dates from 1892, when a priest's complaint forced the owner to take down the sign overnight and a large question mark was hung in its place — where it has stayed ever since.
buildings.history: The house was set on the street line, with a garden and courtyard filling the depth of the plot; a wooden doksat looked out over the yard and its well, the roof was laid in tile, and the whole structure rested on a timber frame. In 1826 Toma, Naum Ičko's son-in-law, opened a tavern on the lower floor under the name “Ećim-Tomina”. That name lasted until 1878, when a new tenant, Bogosav Marjanović from Užice, renamed it “Kod pastira”. A few years later the house passed to Ivan Pavlović, a dealer in church goods, who in 1892 opened a shop and tavern called “Kod Saborne crkve”. The parish priest Novica Lazarević threatened him with court, the sign came down overnight, and the question mark hung in its place won the city's affection.

buildings.description: Dimitrije Krsmanović, a member of a prominent merchant family, had this house raised in 1898–1899 as a representative family residence a short walk from the Cathedral Church and the Belgrade Fortress. The design came from Milorad Ruvidić, who had finished his studies in Germany in 1893 and brought the currents of German architecture back with him. The plot met the street at an unusually sharp angle, and the architect turned that constraint into the building's signature: a narrow central front, treated as the formal face of the house toward the cathedral quarter and Kosančićev venac.
buildings.history: The house was commissioned in 1898–1899 by Dimitrije Krsmanović of the respected Krsmanović trading family, and it was meant as a family residence rather than a rental property. The site was chosen with care: the Cathedral Church and the Belgrade Fortress stood nearby, placing the house in the oldest and most prestigious part of the city. Milorad Ruvidić, who had completed his training in Germany in 1893, handled the design and applied what he had learned there, treating the academic vocabulary with a freedom that was new for Belgrade. The awkward sharp corner then set the whole composition — a narrow central front carrying the bay window, the balcony and the pyramidal dome took on the representational role, while the two side walls were kept calm. Contemporaries valued the result as much for its place in the cathedral quarter and Kosančićev venac as for its architecture.

buildings.description: The home of Mika Alas — the mathematician Mihailo Petrović Alas, who spent almost his whole life here and wrote not only on mathematics but also on fishing. The house was built in 1910 to a design by Petar Bajalović.
buildings.history: The plans were drawn by the architect Petar Bajalović and the house was completed in 1910. Mihailo Petrović Alas (1868–1943) is one of the great names of Serbian science: professor at Belgrade University, academician, theorist and researcher, author of numerous scientific papers, travel writing and studies of fishing. It was through his efforts that an advanced research-based method entered the Serbian school system, and in this house on Kosančićev venac he spent almost his entire life and working career.

buildings.description: The Museum of the Serbian Orthodox Church occupies the Patriarchate in Belgrade and holds 40,000 objects of church history, from early Christian crosses and Byzantine seals to icons, books and vestments. Only some 800 of them are on view: the building was not designed as a museum, and the rest stays in the depot.
buildings.history: Church antiquities were being gathered long before the museum opened: in 1856 Metropolitan Petar urged the clergy of the principality to collect “Serbian painted works”, and in 1858 the icons thus assembled formed a gallery at the Belgrade Metropolitanate. In 1937 the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and the Serbian Orthodox Church agreed on a fifty-year lease of Princess Ljubica’s Residence to house the museum, but the opening planned for October 1940 was prevented by the war. In 1946 the new authorities cancelled the lease and the surviving objects were moved to the Patriarchate; the museum received visitors from 14 June 1954, when Patriarch Vikentije II opened it.

buildings.description: The building of the Social Accounting Service of Yugoslavia in Pop Lukina Street is one of the most consistently applied examples of structural architecture in Belgrade. It was put up in 1969 to a design by the architect Petar Vulović as the home of that service. Six storeys and a mezzanine stand on the ground-floor columns, which carry a facade screen of identical white concrete window frames reading as a regular honeycomb. Standing where Kosančićev venac begins and where the city is entered from New Belgrade, it works as a gate between the new town and the old.
buildings.history: The building went up in 1969 to Petar Vulović's design and was conceived from the start for an institution. Vulović worked from the geometry of the international movement, and the result is counted among the most consistently applied examples of a structural architectural concept. The facade is assembled from identical rectangular window frames cast in white concrete, with parapet panels of natural stone set into them. Slanted parapets and the emphasised crossings of the grid's horizontals and verticals give the plane its movement. The mezzanine above the ground floor adds to the impression of monumentality, and the block itself marks the entrance to Kosančićev venac and the gateway into the old city.

buildings.description: The rental building of the contractor Josif Šojat in Brankova Street is typical of Belgrade's housing shortage: Petar and Branko Krstić built it in 1935 as a block of flats with shops at ground level, and it is one of the key works of interwar functionalism.
buildings.history: The building went up in 1935 to a design by the architects Petar and Branko Krstić as a rental house — in the years of the housing shortage such buildings let out to tenants made up the largest share of new construction. It has a basement, a ground floor with shops, four upper floors and a set-back attic storey. The facade is shaped as a simple, clearly legible form based on the rhythmic alternation of solid and open wall surfaces. Today the house counts as one of the most important works of interwar functionalism and one of the significant achievements of the Krstić brothers, in which the modernist idea of architecture without ornament came fully into its own.

buildings.description: The house of the engineer Miladin Pećinar, who designed it himself in 1928 and lived in it until the end of his life. Pećinar was a pioneer of dam engineering, an academician and a professor at the Faculty of Civil Engineering.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1928 to a design by the engineer Miladin Pećinar himself, in the manner of academicism. Pećinar (Ljubinić, 1893 – Belgrade, 1973) went to school in Užice, studied at the civil engineering faculties in Belgrade and Rome, fought in the wars of 1912–1918 and completed his interrupted studies in hydraulic engineering in Belgrade in 1921. He worked in the General Directorate of Waters, the independent Hydraulic Bureau and the Hydrometeorological Service, and from 1949 taught at the Faculty of Civil Engineering. As a designer, professor and consultant he is regarded as a pioneer of dam construction in the country.

buildings.description: The Ministry of Public Administration and Local Self-Government is the Serbian government body responsible for how the state administration, ministries, special organisations, agencies and public services are organised and run, and for local self-government. Its remit also covers the protection of human rights and national minorities. It works in Belgrade and is divided into five sectors, with a secretariat and the minister's office.
buildings.history: The portfolios of public administration and local self-government were repeatedly merged with other departments and separated again. Between 2012 and 2014, under Ivica Dačić's government, the two areas were split: state administration went to the Ministry of Justice, local self-government to the Ministry of Regional Development. From 2002 the post passed through a long line of ministers, among them Rodoljub Šabić, Zoran Lončar, Milan Marković, Kori Udovički, Ana Brnabić, Branko Ružić, Marija Obradović and Aleksandar Martinović. Jelena Kovačević held the office in 2024–2025, and Snežana Paunović took over in 2025.

buildings.description: The Italian Institute of Culture is Italy's own institution for cultural work in Serbia, founded in 1940 to keep the Italian language and culture present in Belgrade. Since 2006 it has occupied the former Albanian embassy building on Kneza Miloša Street, in the city centre. It runs language and culture courses, Italian certification and a lending library, and appears regularly at BITEF, BEMUS, BELEF, FEST and the Belgrade Book Fair.
buildings.history: The institute was founded in 1940, but the war and the post-war years cut its presence in Belgrade for a long period. It resumed work in 1965 in premises on Obilićev venac, in the city centre. In 1972 it moved to Njegoševa Street 47, a house built in 1920, where it used the first and second floors. From January 2006 it sat at Krunska 9, and on 1 July 2006 it moved into the former Albanian embassy on Kneza Miloša Street 56. Its remit was extended to Montenegro in 2016 and to North Macedonia in March 2022.

buildings.description: Croatia's diplomatic mission to Serbia has occupied the Archdiocese Palace on Kneza Miloša Street in Belgrade since the embassy opened. The two countries opened relations only in 1996, once they had recognised each other and the war in Croatia had ended with the Erdut Agreement, after failed soundings in 1992 and 1993. The building made news in February 2008, when it was attacked along with the neighbouring American and German embassies after Kosovo's declaration of independence.
buildings.history: Ideas about formal ties and a Belgrade embassy were floated in 1992 already, when Franjo Tuđman met Dobrica Ćosić. In 1993 Tuđman and Slobodan Milošević met again, but the talks stalled because Serbia would not recognise Croatia's borders. Relations were finally established on 9 September 1996, after mutual recognition and the Erdut Agreement, and the chancery settled in the Archdiocese Palace at 62 Kneza Miloša Street. In February 2008 the embassy was vandalised along with the neighbouring US and German missions after Kosovo declared independence. A fire in the embassy's residential building in Senjak in February 2022 was put out by 21 firefighters and ruled accidental, and in November 2023 Belgrade declared the embassy's first secretary, Hrvoje Šnajder, persona non grata.

buildings.description: One of the most original works of Art Nouveau in Belgrade: the house of the priest Mihailo Popović, designed by Stojan Titelbah. It was built by the client’s brothers, Gorča and Milić Popović, later well-known Belgrade builders.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1905 for the priest Mihailo Popović; the work was carried out by his brothers Gorča and Milić Popović, later well-known Belgrade builders, to a design by Stojan Titelbah. It was only slightly altered after the First World War, but after the Second it ceased to be a dwelling: passing into municipal ownership, it was given over to business use. Reworking of the interior and of the facade destroyed its chief value, the decorative ornament.

buildings.description: The corner house on Glavna Street where Jova Karamata’s printing house operated in the late nineteenth century, printing significant works of the national literature. It belonged to the well-known Zemun family Stefanović-Vilovski and for a time housed the Evropa hotel.
buildings.history: The house was raised at the turn of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, with trade on the ground floor and dwellings above. At the end of the nineteenth century it held Jova Karamata’s printing house, where significant works of the national literature were printed, and for a time the Evropa hotel. As a corner building it fixes a stretch of the street network laid out in the eighteenth century.

buildings.description: The town house of the wealthy and influential Zemun family Spirta, one of the first tall family houses in the old core of Zemun. Since 1971 it has held the permanent exhibition of the Zemun Homeland Museum.
buildings.history: The house was built around 1840 for the wealthy and influential Zemun family Spirta, and its architecture set it apart from other Zemun houses, a sign of the owners’ particular standing and taste. For a time it housed the Garni hotel, and since 1971 it has held the permanent display of the Zemun Homeland Museum, covering the town’s past from its beginnings to 1945.

buildings.description: The house of the builder Karl Knol on Bulevar despota Stefana is an unusual case of a client who also ran the site: the architect Vladimir Simic drew the plans, and Knol himself carried out the works between 1911 and 1913. One of Belgrade's leading builders at the start of the twentieth century, he made his own family house a meeting of a traditional plan and a Secession facade, with floral and geometric ornament, polychromy and wrought iron. From this address he went to the First World War and died a Serbian soldier in 1915; his descendants have lived in the house ever since.
buildings.history: Karl Knol, born in 1880, was among the leading Belgrade builders at the start of the twentieth century. Between 1904 and 1912 he worked on a large number of buildings of very different kinds, from private family houses and representative palaces to modern factory plants, and made his name above all with Secession designs. His own house on the former Knez Mileta Street was built in 1911–1913 to Vladimir Simic's design, with Knol himself running the works. He lived here until the First World War, in which he died as a Serbian soldier in 1915. The family stayed: descendants of Karl Knol, among them his grandson, Professor Slobodan Vitanovic, have lived in the house continuously. Secession is present both outside and inside, in the polychromy and the wrought iron.

buildings.description: The house of Vojvoda Petar Bojović (1853–1945), one of the most distinguished commanders of the Serbian army, who lived and worked here from 1928 until his death. Bojović commanded the First Army and in December 1915 took over the Supreme Command staff from Vojvoda Putnik.
buildings.history: Vojvoda Petar Bojović lived and worked in this house from 1928 until his death in 1945. He had passed through the Military Academy and general-staff training and held a series of commands, at one point heading the Main General Staff; he fought in the wars of 1876–78, 1885–86 and 1912–13, and gave his greatest contribution in the war of 1914–18. In December 1915 he succeeded Vojvoda Putnik at the head of the Supreme Command staff, led the reorganisation of the army on Corfu and the 1916 operations that took Kajmakčalan and Bitola, and from June 1918 commanded the First Army again in the breakthrough of the Salonika front.

buildings.description: The house and studio of the sculptor Đorđe Jovanović, one of the founders of the Art School in Belgrade and the author of the Monument to the Kosovo Heroes in Kruševac and of the Vuk Karadžić monument. The villa with its garden was built in 1926 to a design by Dragutin Šidjanski and the engineer Stojan Veljković.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1926 as a villa with a garden, serving as the sculptor’s home and studio; the design was made by the architect Dragutin Šidjanski and the engineer Stojan Veljković. Jovanović trained in Belgrade, Vienna, Munich and Paris and, together with Petar Ubavkić, became one of the leading names of Serbian sculpture at the turn of the twentieth century. He was a founder of the Art School from which the Art Academy later grew and devoted much energy to teaching; his main works include the Monument to the Kosovo Heroes in Kruševac, the Prince Miloš in Požarevac, and the Vuk Karadžić and Vojvoda Vuk monuments in Belgrade, as well as a series of monuments at the New Cemetery.

buildings.description: The Evangelical Church on Drinčićeva Street is a unique case in Belgrade: a sacred building whose architecture and purpose were conceived together in an unusual way. It was raised in 1940, giving the city's German Protestant community its first purpose-designed and purpose-built church. The concept came from Otto Bartning, one of the founders of the Bauhaus movement and a well-known church builder in Germany, while the working drawings were developed by the architect Đorđe V. Staševski. Since 1989 the building has housed the avant-garde Bitef Theatre, so the nave now serves the stage rather than a congregation.
buildings.history: Otto Bartning supplied the idea; by 1940 he was already known for his churches in Germany and was counted among the founders of the Bauhaus, and the architect Đorđe V. Staševski turned that concept into working drawings. The German Protestant community of Belgrade thus obtained the first building in the city designed and erected specifically as a church, and its plan followed the rite: a central volume for worship, side wings for priests' flats and auxiliary rooms. Outside, the wall was left almost bare and enlivened by rough hand-made brick, while the tall bell tower, closed by a pyramidal dome, carried the vertical emphasis. The church lost its sacred function already during the Second World War. After 1945 it served a succession of institutions, and from 1989 it has been home to the Bitef Theatre, one of the city's leading avant-garde stages.

buildings.description: The House of Nevena Zaborski on Dalmatinska Street is a modest family house with a single flat, built in 1931 to a design by Milan Zloković. The living room sits at ground level, the bedrooms above, but the section was treated as three-dimensional planning in the manner of the Raumplan, with each room given the height it needed. Outside, a symmetrical street wall, two shallow Ionic pilasters and a relief set on the house's axis introduce an Art Deco note. The building marks an early step in Zloković's career and in the opening of Belgrade's architectural scene to modern ideas.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1931 for Nevena Zaborski, with Milan Zloković responsible for the design. It provided a single flat of the kind the architect returned to repeatedly in his Belgrade houses: living room at ground level, bedrooms upstairs. What set it apart was the section. Zloković calculated the height each room actually needed and then assembled the house from those volumes, an approach derived from the Raumplan and applied here with geometric discipline. The street front he treated as a smooth plane pierced by openings, animated by two Ionic pilasters and a relief at the top. Completed at a moment when Belgrade was beginning to absorb modern ideas, the house stands near the start of Zloković's career and of the city's modernism.

buildings.description: The Plastika art foundry on Carigradska Street is among the oldest in Serbia and still casts by a process that has survived almost unchanged. The building itself began as a soap factory before the First World War, was converted into a car workshop with a small foundry, and after the Second World War passed to the Association of Fine Artists of Serbia, which opened a sculpture workshop there. Plastika introduced lost-wax casting to the country and remained the only place where it was practised. Sreten Stojanović, Loje Dolinar, Franjo Kršinić, Olga Jančić and Vida Jocić all had work cast here, along with many of the country's public monuments.
buildings.history: Construction began shortly before the First World War, and the single-storey soap factory seems to have followed patterns taken from German technical manuals. After the war the process changed: the building became a car workshop, and a small foundry with casting furnaces was added for it. The conversion was designed by Milan Antonović, among the most prominent Serbian architects of the day. After the Second World War the Association of Fine Artists of Serbia moved in — the furnaces and crane tracks were already there, so the workshop carried on as an art foundry. In 1953 the architect N. Ristić, working for the Plan bureau, drew up the adaptation, and from these rooms came the sculpture of the country's leading artists.

buildings.description: The house where the academician Milutin Milanković (1879–1958), author of the astronomical theory of ice ages, lived and worked; a lunar crater and an asteroid carry his name. The villa was built in 1927 for the professor in the newly laid out Professors’ Colony to a design by Svetozar Jovanović, Petar Krstić and Mihailo Radovanović.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1927 for Milutin Milanković, a university professor, on one of the type designs for the newly formed Professors’ Colony, drawn up by Svetozar Jovanović, Petar Krstić and Mihailo Radovanović. Here the scientist lived and worked: he published more than a hundred papers, was the first in the Balkans to lecture on Einstein’s theory of relativity, and formulated the astronomical theory of ice ages that brought him world fame. Milanković was elected to the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts and was a corresponding member of the Yugoslav Academy and of the German Academy of Naturalists in Halle.

buildings.description: The steam bath of the Krsmanović brothers, formed between 1901 and the 1920s around the remains of the old “Little Hamam”, thought to date from the eighteenth century. At its centre survive the round hamam pool and a smaller polygonal cold-water pool.
buildings.history: The complex took shape between 1901 and the 1920s around the remains of the earlier “Little Hamam”, which is thought to go back to the eighteenth century. The bath building follows academic architecture, and at its centre the round hamam pool and a smaller polygonal cold-water pool have survived.

buildings.description: The architect Milan Zloković’s own house, built in 1927, was the first project in which he could realise his progressive ideas and it anticipates the modernist movement in Serbian interwar architecture. The house keeps a rich legacy of his work.
buildings.history: Zloković designed and built his own family house in Kotež-Neimar in 1927, the first occasion on which he could carry out his progressive ideas. Instead of the usual academic emphasis on the corner, the dramatic corner of the house is produced by the intersection of two three-dimensional systems, while the free plan and the ornament-free cubic structure bring it close to the modernist understanding of architecture. In 1928 he became one of the founders of the Group of Architects of Modern Direction, which did much to bring new ideas into the then conservative Serbian milieu.

buildings.description: The office and residential block of Petar Janković, put up between 1933 and 1936 to a design by Jan Dubovi, one of the founders of Belgrade's group of modern-minded architects. It brings offices and flats together in a single block with particular success, and does so in the spirit of pure modernism at a moment when the movement was only beginning in the city. Preserved in its authentic form, the building is still studied as an example of that first modernist wave.
buildings.history: The block went up over three years, between 1933 and 1936. Jan Dubovi, one of the founders of the group of modern-minded architects, combined offices and flats in a single volume — a combination he resolved with particular success. Pure modernism was then only dawning in Belgrade, both as an architectural idea and as an artistic direction. Because the building survives in its authentic form, it is valued both as evidence of how Belgrade's architecture developed and as a mature work by a prominent author.

buildings.description: The Fiat car service building, put up in 1939–42 to a design by Milan Zloković, one of the founders of the Group of Architects of Modern Direction. It is one of the key examples of Belgrade modern architecture and a rarity at a time when monumentalism was gathering strength before the Second World War.
buildings.history: The building went up between 1939 and 1942 to Zloković’s design, with the finishing work on the last wings carried out after the Second World War. It combined different functions: a sales showroom on the ground floor of the main wing with flats above, a garage in the middle wing and workshops in the lowest wing facing Rudnička Street. Among Zloković’s works the source places it immediately after the University Children’s Clinic and the Šterić and Prentić family villas, and it is counted among the outstanding examples of Belgrade modernism.

buildings.description: Villa Prendić on Osmana Đikića Street was built in 1932/33 for Jovan and Dragojla Prendić to a design by Milan Zloković, one of the leading Serbian modernists. The house stands free with its front turned to a park, and it was made for two purposes at once: a family home and a doctor's practice. Zloković separated them by level, putting the waiting room and the consulting room in a separate cube at street level and lifting the living quarters a metre above. Stepped masses and an outside stair to the practice wing give the villa the movement through which Belgrade's architecture came close to European models.
buildings.history: The villa was built in 1932/33 for Jovan and Dragojla Prendić, who commissioned Milan Zloković. Its plan had to reconcile living and working: the waiting room and the practice itself were placed in a separate cube at street level, while the living space was raised a metre above the practice. Zloković then split the home into a representative public zone of hall, salon and dining room on the high ground floor, a service zone of kitchen, stores and toilet behind the practice and in the basement, and a private zone of bedrooms, bathroom and wardrobe on the upper floor. He carried the same principle into the masses, pulling the stair outside and stepping the volumes against one another. The result is one of the houses through which Belgrade's architecture came close to European models of modernism.

buildings.description: The New Palace, built between 1911 and 1922 for King Petar I Karađorđević to a design by Stojan Titelbah, his most important work. King Alexander moved in in 1922, and today the building houses the Presidency of the Republic of Serbia.
buildings.history: The palace was built between 1911 and 1922 for King Petar I; work was interrupted by the Balkan wars and the First World War and finished under King Alexander, who moved in in 1922. In 1918 the building, damaged in the bombing, was repaired, completed and extended under the supervision of the architect Momir Korunović, and the next two years were given to interior decoration and furnishing. Until 1934, when King Alexander was assassinated in Marseille, the New Palace served as the official royal residence; it was then adapted for the Museum of Prince Paul. A second reconstruction followed in 1952 to a design by Milan Minić: the palace was extended towards the Old Palace and given new facades, a new entrance and a ceremonial hall.

buildings.description: The National Assembly, built over three decades, from 1907 to 1936, to a design by Jovan Ilkić and finished under the eye of his son Pavle. The palace exists because a new constitution turned Serbia into a two-chamber state, which made the earlier scheme for a single house obsolete. The interiors were the work of Nikola Krasnov, and in 1939 Toma Rosandić's bronze groups “Igrail se konji vrani” were set before the main entrance.
buildings.history: The first scheme for a parliament was drawn in the early 1890s, when Konstantin Jovanović produced a monumental design for a single-chamber house. A new constitution at the start of the twentieth century gave Serbia two chambers, and that scheme was dropped. A competition followed in 1902; Jovan Ilkić won first prize with a proposal that leaned heavily on Jovanović's abandoned drawing. Work began in 1907 and stopped in 1914 with the outbreak of the First World War. The building was finished only in 1936, after Ilkić's death, under his son Pavle, who introduced changes of his own. In 1939 two bronze groups by Toma Rosandić were placed before the main entrance.

buildings.description: The National Theatre was put up at the initiative of Prince Mihailo Obrenović, and Aleksandar Bugarski modelled his design on the European theatre houses of the period, above all La Scala in Milan. Josif Bukavac gave the building its Secessionist dress between 1911 and 1922, and the reconstruction of 1986–1989 brought that appearance back.
buildings.history: The building went up in 1868–1869 to a design by Aleksandar Bugarski, on the initiative of Prince Mihailo Obrenović. It was altered in 1885 and again in 1903, and between 1911 and 1922 Josif Bukavac reworked Bugarski’s classicist scheme, giving the whole a Secessionist character. Bombing in 1941 left the theatre badly damaged, and the repairs of 1941–1942 greatly simplified its exterior and interior decoration. The reconstruction of 1986–1989 restored the architectural state of 1922, renewed the interior and added a rear wing towards Braće Jugovića Street after plans by Slobodan Drinjaković and Ljubomir Zdravković.

buildings.description: The Popović house was built in 1928 to a design by the civil engineer Dragoljub A. Popović for the family of Vojvoda Vuk Vojin Popović and his brother Gligorije, a member of the Belgrade city administration. The vojvoda himself was a celebrated Serbian commander of the Balkan Wars and the First World War.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1928 for the family of Vojvoda Vuk Vojin Popović and his brother Gligorije, a member of the Belgrade city administration, and its design was by the civil engineer Dragoljub A. Popović. It was set on the regulation line of the former Podrinjska Street. Beyond its architectural qualities the house carries historical weight, for the vojvoda was a celebrated commander in the Balkan Wars and the First World War, at Čelopek, Kumanovo, Bregalnica, Prilep and Bitola.

buildings.description: The Baptist Church in Belgrade is a congregation in Zvezdara whose story goes back to 1930, when the first service was held in its original meeting house in Aleksandrova Street. That building was pulled down on 31 January 1973 during the reconstruction of Bulevar kralja Aleksandra, and the congregation had to go through a long court case. In December 1976 it bought a house at 33 Slobodanke Danke Savić Street, where the first service was held at Pentecost 1977 and where the church still meets.
buildings.history: The first service in the congregation's meeting house at 264 Aleksandrova Street was held in 1930. The building was demolished on 31 January 1973 during the reconstruction of what was then Bulevar kralja Aleksandra, without any expropriation decision being issued to the church at the time. A decision on the expropriation of its property came only in 1980, after a long court case. Meanwhile, in December 1976, the congregation bought a house at 33 Slobodanke Danke Savić Street, and the first service there was held at Pentecost in 1977.

buildings.description: Momir Korunović built this house for himself in 1924, to his own design, as a single-storey family house with an attic. Korunović (1883–1969) was the most prominent figure of the “national direction” in Serbian architecture of the first half of the 20th century.
buildings.history: The house went up in 1924 to the architect’s own design: a single-storey family house with an attic, modelled on Central European family houses with a garden. Korunović kept a study there with technical instruments and a library, and the building still preserved the complete technical documentation, drawings and plans of the houses and buildings he designed and put up. Alongside his design work he studied and helped protect old architectural monuments.

buildings.description: The family villa was built in 1932 to a design by the architect Milutin Borisavljević; four years later Ignjat Flašar bought it and had the same architect add a floor with a terrace. The house has been known by his name ever since.
buildings.history: The villa was built in 1932 as a family house of rectangular plan with a single upper floor and a fully symmetrical arrangement of rooms, designed by Milutin Borisavljević. In 1936 Ignjat Flašar bought it from its owners and a further floor with a terrace was added, again to a design by Borisavljević. The new floor covered only half of the roof, the other half being left as an open terrace.

buildings.description: The Kosta Manojlović Music School in Zemun is one of Serbia's largest music schools, grown out of a department of the Stanković school opened on 1 September 1939 so that Zemun children would not have to travel to Belgrade for lessons. It took the name of the composer, musicologist and first rector of Belgrade's Music Academy in 1954. The present building opened in 1971, and in 1979 the school added a secondary level.
buildings.history: The school began as a department of Belgrade's Stanković Music School on 1 September 1939, teaching on the first floor of a private three-room flat at 23 Svetosavska Street under Ljudevit Kiš. Its first year had 42 pupils — 29 pianists, ten violinists, a cellist and two solo singers. It became a regular six-year school in 1949 and was renamed after Kosta Manojlović in 1954. In 1957 it moved into rooms at the House of Culture, and when that building was pulled down in 1970 the school received a new building, opening there on 6 February 1971. It gained secondary status in 1979, and in 1981 the music department for visually impaired pupils at the Veljko Ramadanović school was merged into it.

buildings.description: The Serbian Orthodox Church Community House in Zemun, completed in 1909, brought two institutions under one roof: the community's own premises with a ceremonial hall and an elementary school. Its plans were drawn by Kosta Atanacković-Stanišić, a gifted Zemun architect who died young, and the building remains one of the few by which his name survives. The site carried its own history — a confessional school of the eighteenth century and the old Kod Kneza Miloša inn had stood there before — so the new house continued a long schooling tradition in the quarter. Standing at the head of the block between Bežanijska, Svetosavska and Rajačićeva streets, it still commands that corner of old Zemun.
buildings.history: The community house and school went up in 1909 to plans by Kosta Atanacković-Stanišić, a Zemun architect of recognized talent who died young and left few built works behind him. The brief was unusually mixed: the building had to hold the church community's premises and an elementary school, and it also provided shops and flats, so each part received its own layout. Most of the block follows a single-tract plan, while the ceremonial hall was pushed out to the corner of Bežanijska and Svetosavska and marked by a cut corner and a richly worked crowning cornice. In style the house belongs to Neo-Romanticism, with a restless, articulated facade handled on a monumental scale. When it was finished it ranked among the largest buildings in the old core of Zemun, and it still documents the city's long tradition of elementary schooling.

buildings.description: Branislav Nušić put up this Belgrade house in 1937, shortly before his death, to a design by the civil engineer Zoran Tomić. The furniture of his study and salon, his personal belongings, photographs and documents are kept in the Museum of the City of Belgrade, intended for display in the house as a memorial museum.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1937 to a design by the engineer Zoran Tomić, a typical Belgrade dwelling that Nušić raised near the end of his life. Branislav Nušić (Smederevo 1864 – Belgrade 1938) was educated in Belgrade and Graz, served in the diplomatic corps, directed a theatre, headed the arts department of the Ministry of Education and was a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts. His legacy — the furniture of his study and salon, personal objects, photographs and documents — passed to the Museum of the City of Belgrade, to be shown in the house as part of a memorial museum.

buildings.description: The architect Đorđe Stanić designed this house specifically to hold an illegal printing press. The uneven site was used to build a hidden room reached through a wardrobe on the first floor.
buildings.history: The building was put up just before the Second World War, damaged in the air raid of 6 April 1941 and finished only in October 1941. From 1 August 1941 to 31 August 1943 the illegal printing press of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia worked here; three national heroes — Branko Đonović, Slobodan Jović and Milo Bošković — were largely responsible for keeping it running, and the enemy never managed to find it. In 1950 the building was turned into a memorial museum and marked with a plaque, and the museum stayed open until August 2000.

buildings.description: The house of Vladislav Ribnikar, where on 4 July 1941 the members of the Politburo of the Yugoslav Communist Party’s Central Committee resolved to raise an uprising against the occupiers. From 1950 to 2003 it held the Museum of 4 July, named after that day.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1934 for Vladislav Ribnikar; before the war a shelter was dug in the yard and the building was fitted out for underground work, hiding fugitives and, for a time, printing the bulletin of the Supreme Headquarters. Upstairs was the room where Josip Broz Tito stayed, and among those who lived here were Edvard Kardelj, Vladimir Dedijer and Ivo Lola Ribar. In 1943, after the owners left for the partisans, the house was confiscated and German officers moved in; once the country was liberated, Ribnikar gave the emptied building to the Communist Party to make a museum. In 2003 the museum closed and the house went back to the Ribnikar family, which decided to open there a museum of the Politika newspaper and the Serbian press.

buildings.description: The villa on Topčider Hill went up in 1933 to a design by Milan Zloković, one of the key figures of Serbian modernism. It was built to his own taste and needs by the industrialist Dragoljub Šterić, who took part in developing the defence industry of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.
buildings.history: The house was raised in 1933 as a free-standing two-storey residence of G-shaped plan, composed of cubic volumes and conceived in the spirit of functionalist architecture. Its cubic massing shows the influence of Adolf Loos, while the harmony of interior and exterior, the branching plan and the stepping of planes in depth point to the International Style. Function and form are joined and fitted into the natural setting, which places the building very high by the criteria of aesthetic functionalism.

buildings.description: The villa was built in 1931 to a design by Petar and Branko Krstić for Dušan Tomić, a professor at the Technical Faculty. It is one of the brothers’ finest works and one of the earliest Serbian houses whose façades carry no ornament at all.
buildings.history: The villa was built in 1931 to a design by Petar and Branko Krstić for Dušan Tomić, a professor at the Technical Faculty and a great lover of architecture who founded the Award for the Most Beautiful Façade, the pre-war equivalent of the grand architecture prize. The Krstić brothers reached one of their finest achievements here, and the modern cubic structure was fitted with skill into the existing setting of Topčider Hill. The spatial organisation follows the demands of functionalism.

buildings.description: The villa of Olga Mos went up in 1938 on Topčider Hill, while the area was being intensively developed, to a design by Svetomir Lazić, a modernist from the group known for its interior-architecture studio. It ranks among Lazić’s most successful works.
buildings.history: The house was put up in 1938. Its ground floor held a formal reception room, a living room and a study, while a central hall rising through both storeys linked the levels. The study was shaped with a projection that became the most striking element of the street façade, and horizontal window bands and large panes in metal frames brought light into the rooms — the characteristic motifs of modern architecture.

buildings.description: An early example of the modernist turn in the work of the brothers Petar and Branko Krstić: the Villa of Stevka Milićević holds a special place both in their oeuvre and in Belgrade architecture between the two world wars. It stands on a large plot with a tended garden, in one of the oldest streets of the Dedinje residential district.
buildings.history: The villa was built in 1929–1930 to a design by Petar and Branko Krstić, in the spirit of early modernism with academic reminiscences. Its layout follows the usual interwar Belgrade type of a single-storey family villa, though with a free, non-standard plan: reception and private rooms on the ground floor, service quarters in the basement. For the Krstić brothers it is one of the earliest works to show elements of a modernist orientation, and within the wider context of interwar Belgrade architecture a valuable example of the move towards a modern expression.

buildings.description: The Legacy of Milica Zorić and Rodoljub Čolaković is a gallery of Belgrade's Museum of Contemporary Art, opened to the public in December 1980 in the house on Dedinje where the couple had lived since 1946. Milica Zorić, who took up tapestry in 1957, left some two hundred works in that medium, and with her husband, the revolutionary and writer Rodoljub Čolaković, she gave the collection to Belgrade and Bijeljina. Pieces from the legacy are now kept in the gallery itself, in the Museum of Contemporary Art, the Museum of Applied Arts and the Semberija Museum in Bijeljina.
buildings.history: Milica Zorić (1909–1989) and Rodoljub Čolaković married in prison between the two world wars; he spent the Second World War in hiding while she was interned from 1941 to 1944. From 1946 they lived in Belgrade at Drajzerov prolaz 2, today's Rodoljuba Čolakovića Street, which became their legacy from 1975. Pavle Beljanski, a close friend of the couple, set an example of giving that helped prompt their decision to donate. Milica came to tapestry in 1957, already well into her years, and produced around two hundred works that earned her a singular place in Yugoslav modernism. The gallery opened to the public in December 1980 and is run by the Museum of Contemporary Art, which shares the holdings with the Museum of Applied Arts and the Semberija Museum in Bijeljina.

buildings.description: A small villa on Cara Iraklija Street, built at the end of the nineteenth century, earned its place in history through its occupant rather than its architecture. From 1940 until his death in 1960 it was home and study to Aleksandar Belić, one of the leading linguists of Serbian scholarship and a scholar of world standing. His library stood here, and many works on the science of language were written within these walls.
buildings.history: The house belongs to the type of small summer villas of very modest architectural merit, and on its own it is no landmark of Belgrade building. Its importance was defined by Aleksandar Belić (1876–1960), who was born and died in Belgrade: he studied there, in Odesa and in Moscow, taught from 1899 at the Great School and later at Belgrade University, and trained generations of linguists. From 1906 he was a full member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences, which elected him its president in 1937. In that post, and at the head of the Institute for the Serbo-Croatian Language, the Kolarac People's University and the journals Južnoslovenski filolog and Naš jezik, Belić did much to win Serbian scholarship recognition abroad. From 1940 until the end of his life he lived in this house, where his library was kept.

buildings.description: The residence of the first metropolitans: Milentije Pavlović and Petar Jovanović were based here, and in July 1835 the first constitution of the Orthodox Church in the Principality of Serbia was drawn up inside these walls. Since the 1860s the konak has served as the flat of the Topčider church priest.
buildings.history: The konak was built between 1830 and 1832 as a large Šumadija house in the tradition of local secular building. It housed the seat of the first metropolitans, Milentije Pavlović and Petar Jovanović; in July 1835 the first constitution of the Orthodox Church in the Principality of Serbia was drawn up here, and the National Assembly in Kragujevac adopted it on 31 January 1836. From the 1860s to the present day the building has served as the residence of the Topčider church priest.

buildings.description: One of the first residential buildings Dragiša Brašovan conceived in a modernist spirit: the villa of the merchant Dušan Lazić in Dedinje. In its architectural composition it belongs among the luxury villas raised in this quarter between the two world wars and represents a distinct Belgrade idiom of the type.
buildings.history: The villa was built in 1932 to a design by Dragiša Brašovan. The architect divided the house into three conventional parts — service, reception and private — yet subordinated them to his own modern idiom; for him it is one of the first residentially conceived modernist works.
