According to the heritage service, the building later housed the residence of Zaire.

buildings.description: A work by Dušan Babić, one of the leading Serbian architects of the 1930s: the Villa Reich ranks among the most striking examples of Belgrade modern architecture. Its decorative treatment of the facades aligns it with Art Deco, a movement that persisted across Europe until the outbreak of the Second World War.
buildings.history: The villa was raised in 1931 to a design by Dušan Babić, in the current of the modern architectural thinking of the day. The project became one of the architect’s most accomplished works and secured his standing among the leading Serbian architects of the 1930s.

buildings.description: A house built for the Belgrade actress Marica Popović — Marija Pavlović — who spent three decades on the stage of the National Theatre. The architect was Grigorije Samojlov, one of the most significant Russian builders working in Serbia in the 1920s and 1930s.
buildings.history: The villa went up in 1939 as a family home for the actress, designed by Grigorije Samojlov. Marica Popović is remembered in the theatre and partly in film for her dramatic, character and comic roles, played over three decades at the National Theatre, whose permanent member she was from 1927 until her retirement in 1960. The house is counted among Samojlov’s most important and original residential works on Senjak and Dedinje.

buildings.description: The Toma Rosandić Museum is Belgrade's first memorial museum, opened in 1963 in the house the sculptor built for himself and where he lived and worked. Rosandić (1878–1958) worked in Split, Rome, Florence and Vienna, and in 1927 he raised his own house with a studio on Senjak, keeping home and craft under one roof. By will he left the city that house, a large body of his work, objects of applied art, personal papers, correspondence and sculpting tools, so that a private studio became a public collection.
buildings.history: Rosandić's tie to Belgrade began before the First World War, when he moved in and settled in the house that held the kafana “?”. He spent the war in emigration and, on his return, received the Božić house from the Belgrade municipality to live in. In 1927 he built himself a home with a studio on Senjak and worked there until he left for his native Split in 1955. He taught at the Art School, founded the Art Academy and served as its first rector, and from 1946 was a full member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences. He left the city the house and studio together with a large body of works, applied-art objects, personal papers, correspondence and sculpting tools, and in 1963 the house opened as Belgrade's first memorial museum.

buildings.description: Vavedenje Monastery on Savski Venac grew out of a single bequest: in 1937 the Belgrade benefactor Persida R. Milenković paid for a church and a residence, and the two buildings still make up the complex. The church is the work of Petar Popović, an early advocate of a Serbian national style in modern Serbian architecture. Its plan of an inscribed cross, crowned by a central dome and four smaller ones between the arms, quotes the Serbian medieval tradition of the fourteenth century. Set among ordinary city blocks, the monastery shows how a sacred building could be grafted onto a modern capital.
buildings.history: The monastery was founded in 1937, when Persida R. Milenković financed a church and a residence as her endowment to Belgrade. Petar Popović, who believed a modern Serbian architecture should grow from national tradition, was given the commission. He chose a five-dome scheme — one dome over the crossing, four smaller ones between the arms of an inscribed cross — modelled on fourteenth-century Serbian churches. Inside, a stone altar screen was built, and the walls were painted in al seco by the academic painter Dušan Mihailović between 1973 and 1985. The church went up among city streets and apartment blocks — a deliberate attempt to keep a sacred building in step with the city around it.

buildings.description: The home of the actor and director Dragoljub Gošić, a notable figure in Serbian theatre during its first five decades. In 1933 the house was altered and the mansard became a full storey, probably to a design by the Czech architect Jan Dubový, one of the founders of Serbian modernism.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1927–1928 to a design by Vojislav Kostić as a single-storey building; in 1933 the ground floor was reworked and the mansard turned into a full storey, probably by Jan Dubový. The property belonged to Dragoljub Gošić, a man of the theatre whose fame was tied to the Belgrade stage: after the First World War he appeared before audiences almost three thousand times, and critics singled out his hadži Toma in Koštana and Ignac Glembaj in Miroslav Krleža’s The Glembays. As a director he staged nineteen plays, mostly from the national repertoire, and closed his theatrical career teaching at the Drama Studio of the National Theatre in Belgrade.

buildings.description: The first and only museum in South-East Europe devoted exclusively to the cultures and arts of Africa, it grew out of the collection of Veda Zagorac and the diplomat Zdravko Pečar, given to Belgrade. It opened on 23 May 1977 in Moša Pijade's former studio in Senjak.
buildings.history: The Pečars' collection had been part of the Ethnographic Museum's holdings since 1974, and the city assembly then handed the former studio of Moša Pijade, Zora Petrović and Boško Karanović to the new institution. Building to Slobodan Ilić's design started in June 1975 and was finished in September 1976; the museum received its first visitors on 23 May 1977, an opening that counted among the events marking forty-five years of Tito's leadership of the Communist Party. In 1989 a dome designed by Slobodan Milićević was raised over the central part of the display, closing the roof lanterns. The founders stayed away from the opening: Pečar was then Yugoslavia's ambassador to Ghana.

buildings.description: A double villa by the brothers Petar and Branko Krstić: two mirror-symmetric halves physically joined by a covered colonnade and repeating each other completely — in plan, in architecture and in the layout of the garden. It is described as an outstanding example of modern thinking about the form of the double house.
buildings.history: The villa was built in 1931 to a design by Petar and Branko Krstić in the modernist manner. The architects made the two volumes identical, down to the organisation of the flats: the central room on the ground floor opens wide towards the salon and the main staircase, while the private rooms sit upstairs. For the Krstić brothers, among Belgrade’s leading architects of the 1930s, the double house became one of their key works.

buildings.description: The Popovic-Predic house on Pushkinova Street in Senjak was built in 1937 as a country retreat for quiet work, and became the home where three scholarly brothers did their writing. Bogdan, Dimitrije and Pavle Popovic asked the architect Mihailo Radovanovic for a design modelled on the summer houses of the turn of the century. The modest building stands at the corner of a large plot, on its highest point, looking out to Topcider and Banovo brdo. Later the dramatist Milan Predic, nephew of the painter Uros Predic, also lived here.
buildings.history: The Popovic brothers decided to build outside the city in order to have a quiet place for work; Senjak was then the summer retreat of Belgrade families. The design of 1937 came from Mihailo Radovanovic, who took the summer houses of the turn of the century as his model. The house was set at the corner of the plot, on its highest ground, where the view opens over Topcider and Banovo brdo. It was deliberately kept small and unassuming so as not to disturb the landscape around it. Bogdan Popovic, critic and aesthetician, the diplomat Dimitrije Popovic and the literary historian Pavle Popovic all lived and worked here, and their legacy is kept in the house. The dramatist Milan Predic, director of the National Theatre, spent many years here, and after his death documents, personal belongings and paintings remained.

buildings.description: Isidora Sekulić spent the last twenty years of her life in this house on Topčidersko brdo. She left her library and the contents of her study to the University Library in Belgrade.
buildings.history: The house was built between the two world wars as a typical family home with a garden on Topčidersko brdo. Isidora Sekulić (1877–1958) lived here for the last twenty years of her life; little in the interior now recalls them, apart from the library and the contents of her study, which the writer left to the University Library. Her range shows through her pedagogical, translating and literary work: she ranks among the most important essayists of Serbian literature, and her writing reaches into philosophy, aesthetics and literary criticism.

buildings.description: A town villa of a high residential standard in the Old Core of Zemun, built in 1911 to the plans of Franja Jenč. The house remains part of the historic fabric from the years when Zemun was enjoying economic, social and cultural growth.
buildings.history: The house was raised in 1911 as a representative residence to the plans of Franja Jenč. A one-family villa with generous plans and a complex brief spread over two levels, it belonged among town villas of a high standard, shaped in the spirit of the Secession. It remains a house of a unique architectural concept within the Old Core of Zemun and a witness to how representative housing developed at the start of the last century.

buildings.description: Headquarters of the Water Community of south-eastern Srem, raised in 1908 as the first building on ground won by clearing Zemun’s outer defensive ditches. The community, known today as Galovica, still occupies the house.
buildings.history: The house was put up in 1908 for the Cooperative for the Drainage of South-Eastern Srem — the water community that still works here under the name Galovica. The building work was carried out by the builders Franja Jenč and Josip Katinčić. In 1928 the attic was rebuilt and adapted with the original architectural features kept and the mixed residential and office use preserved. For Zemun’s old core the house is telling: it opened the built-up area on the expanded town ground and belongs to the rise of hydraulic engineering in south-eastern Srem at the beginning of the last century.

buildings.description: Zemun’s customs house of 1781: the salt warehouses beside it made the pair a backbone of trade in a town that sat on the border of two empires.
buildings.history: The customs house was raised in 1781 where an older building from the days of the customs-and-salt office had stood. It was built of brick in lime mortar, with vaults in the basement and ground floor and an architrave on the upper floor; the plan has two ranges of rooms with a corridor towards the courtyard. In Zemun’s old core it ranked among the largest buildings, and together with the salt warehouses it shows what sustained a town on the border of two empires.

buildings.description: One of the finest examples of a well-off Zemun household around 1800: with the neighbouring houses of the block it forms a single setting in the old core.
buildings.history: The house was built around 1800 for two purposes at once, dwelling and trade. It has two ranges of rooms, a basement under part of the building and a high roof. The gate of its main carriage entrance is counted among the best preserved period gates in Zemun’s old core, and with the neighbouring houses of the block it forms a single setting.

buildings.description: Three generations of the Pantelić family cast bells and built tower clocks here, growing a small locksmith’s workshop of 1854 into a bell foundry and clock factory.
buildings.history: The business began in 1854 as a small locksmith’s shop run by Đorđe Pantelić and over time specialised in casting bells and making clocks for church towers and important town buildings, the workshops growing alongside both programmes. The present look and layout date from 1926, when the old workshop was rebuilt to plans by the Zemun builder Josif Marks and given new façades. The forge, the locksmith’s shop, the old and the new foundry, the store and the offices survive with their equipment and tools. Of the decoration only the metal bell is left; the corner clock, the founding year and the owner’s name are gone, and the building itself is dilapidated.

buildings.description: A corner house with shops below and flats above, standing on Glavna Street in the old core of Zemun, went up in 1823. Trade occupied the ground floor and families the floor above, while the shallow, restrained treatment of the main facade belongs to the Empire manner and places the building among the most harmonious civic houses of the old town. A projecting corner bay marks its position at a crossing, and on the Dubrovačka side a sundial survives as a rarity worth a detour of its own.
buildings.history: The house went up in 1823 and was extended towards Dubrovačka Street in 1908. Brick walls, vaulted and trabeated ceilings between the floors and a two-tract plan belong to the building practice of the day, and the interior was split between trade below and dwellings above. The main facade carries a shallow Empire treatment, restrained enough that the house is counted among the most harmonious civic buildings of old Zemun. Its corner bay holds the crossing, and the sundial on the Dubrovačka side has long been regarded as a curiosity of particular value.

buildings.description: The Zemun Gymnasium is a pair of schoolhouses by the town park: the Great Realka, raised in 1879 to plans by the Zagreb architect Nikola Kolar on the site of the former quarantine, and the 1916 building that closed the block. The Royal District of Zemun paid for the second house, and the board that received the projects refused a modern design, demanding instead that it rhyme with the older building in a Renaissance key, which gave the old core of Zemun one of its first unmistakably modern school buildings. Mansard roofs and broad windows carried unfamiliar elements into that streetscape, and the two houses together record two centuries of schooling in Zemun.
buildings.history: The Great Realka went up in 1879, right after the plot passed from military into magistracy hands: the Zagreb architect Nikola Kolar drew the plans, and the house was set on the ground of the former quarantine. It came out imposing and monumental in the Neo-Renaissance manner, with a marked centre to the main front, and was laid out in a single range, corridors facing the yard and classrooms facing the park. In 1912 plans were drawn for an extension of the gymnasium and of the Commercial Academy attached to it, signed with the initials V. R. The aim was to close the building block, and this was done in 1916 with a second wing paid for by the Royal District of Zemun; the board that reviewed the designs rejected a modern scheme and asked for a Renaissance echo of the older house, so the new building took a post-Secession form with restrained ornament. Mansard roofs and large windows, together with the repeated single-range plan, tied it to the earlier school, though its programme was markedly more modern.

buildings.description: The house where Petar Ičko lived in 1802–1803 — a merchant and rebel diplomat whose work fed into the preparations for the First Serbian Uprising. A tavern called Kraljević Marko kept the ground floor.
buildings.history: The house went up in 1793 with two purposes: a tavern called Kraljević Marko traded on the ground floor while the floor above, fitted into a tall mansard roof, served as living space. In 1802–1803 Petar Ičko stayed here — a trade consul and go-between for merchants in Zemun, Thessaloniki and elsewhere, who had moved from Belgrade to the border town once the dahijas took over. His contacts fed into the preparations for the 1804 uprising. The house was altered repeatedly and fully reconstructed in the 1980s.

buildings.description: The Gallery of the Natural History Museum occupies one of Belgrade's oldest buildings, a former guardhouse by the Stambol Gate on Kalemegdan. A Turkish plan already marks it as a karaula, the post that watched over the main approach to the fortress. Restored in the early 1990s and opened in 1994, it now holds the museum's natural history displays and also hosts lectures and workshops.
buildings.history: Research dates the building to 1825–1835, and its classicist appearance still reflects its first purpose. From 1957 to 1973 it housed the Museum of Forestry and Hunting, which later became a separate unit of the Natural History Museum. After renovation in 1992–1994 the gallery opened on 19 December 1994 with an exhibition drawn from the museum's collections, timed to its centenary. Some sixty natural history exhibitions have been held here since, alongside lectures, promotions and seminars. Local tradition also links the house with vizier Mustafa Pasha and with an assembly of Karadjordje's insurgent leaders.

buildings.description: Belgrade Planetarium sits inside an old Turkish hamam in Belgrade Fortress's Lower Town; until 1967 the building was simply known as the Turkish bath. A circular structure was inserted into the historic interior, and the dome above it serves as the projector's screen. The venue is run by the Astronomical Society Ruđer Bošković and is one of only two planetariums in Serbia.
buildings.history: The hamam was built between 1860 and 1867, as the Ottomans were leaving the fortress, and during the First World War it served as a military bath. The 1944 explosion at the nearby Eastern Gate almost destroyed it; reconstruction began in 1962 and was completed in 1964, though the building then stood unused. The first plan was a lapidarium for stone monuments, epitaphs and statues, but it was abandoned in favour of a planetarium. The Zeiss ZKP-2 projector was bought at the 1966 Belgrade technology fair with Tito's backing, the equipment was installed in 1967–1968, and the planetarium opened unofficially in 1969 and officially in 1970. Its hall seats 80 people under an eight-metre dome, and in 2019, for its fiftieth anniversary, it received a new projector and a partly renewed roof.

buildings.description: The corner house where Dimitrije Davidović was born in 1789: Prince Miloš’s secretary, founder of Srpske novine and the man behind the 1835 Sretenje constitution.
buildings.history: The house was built at the end of the eighteenth century as a one-storey dwelling of two ranges of rooms around an inner courtyard, and was extended in stages until the end of the second half of the nineteenth century, gaining longer fronts on both streets while a single treatment of the façades tied the phases together. Later the residential ground floor was turned into shops, which changed much of the original appearance. Its weight for Zemun is historical as well: Dimitrije Davidović was born here — Prince Miloš’s secretary, writer and journalist, diplomat and minister of education in restored Serbia, founder of Srpske novine and author of the 1835 Sretenje constitution.

buildings.description: A house where the Austrian commander-in-chief had his headquarters in 1788–89 and Emperor Joseph II stayed twice, and where the Main Serbian National Committee sat in 1848–49; the Karamata family has owned it since 1779.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1764 for the Zemun merchant Kuzman Jovanović and bought in 1779 by Dimitrije Karamata, a newcomer from Katranica in Macedonia; it has stayed with the family ever since. In 1827 the middle section gained its upper floor and the whole house was rebuilt, which produced the single façade whose gate carries that year. During the Austro-Turkish war of 1788–89 the Austrian commander-in-chief had his headquarters here and Emperor Joseph II stayed twice; in 1848–49 the Main Serbian National Committee and Patriarch Josif Rajačić moved in. Period furniture, applied art and family portraits of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries survive inside, and conservation work followed in 1967.

buildings.description: The corner house of the town physician Sava Nedeljković, built in 1905: its rich secession ornament makes it one of the most representative buildings of Zemun’s Gornja varoš suburb.
buildings.history: The corner house with a high ground floor and an L-shaped plan was built in 1905 for the town physician Sava Nedeljković. Its façade, with an even rhythm of windows, carries rich sculptural ornament in the secession manner, and the source counts it among the most representative houses of Zemun’s Gornja varoš suburb.

buildings.description: The Hariš chapel, built by the Zemun merchant Grigorije Hariš under the will of his wife Marija, née Petrović. Svetozar Ivačković designed it, and its iconostasis was the last work of the painter Pavle Simić.
buildings.history: The chapel was built around 1874–1875 and dedicated to the Great Martyr Demetrius, patron of the Petrović family. Grigorije Hariš, a Zemun merchant, commissioned it to carry out the wish of his late wife Marija, née Petrović; Svetozar Ivačković designed it, Josif Marks built it, Pavle Simić painted the iconostasis, Jovan Kistner carved it and Samuel Kolmajer gilded it. The chapel belongs to the history of two well-known Zemun families and counts as a notable work by Ivačković, one of the leading Serbian architects of the turn of the twentieth century.

buildings.description: Home of the engineer Pavle Horvat, who drew up Zemun’s new regulatory plan in 1911. Its secession ornament is carried through consistently within the traditional frame of a town house, which places it among the town’s cultural-historical values.
buildings.history: The town house was built in 1910 in the secession manner and belonged to the engineer Pavle Horvat, who produced a new regulatory plan for Zemun in 1911. Its secession decoration is applied consistently to the traditional scheme of a Zemun house, which is why it is counted among the properties of cultural-historical value. It stands in the border area of the protected spatial whole Old Core of Zemun and continues its architectural line.

buildings.description: The former Žarkovo municipal building, taken over by the elementary school in 1880 and still used for teaching: one of the few surviving 19th-century village schools in the wider Belgrade area.
buildings.history: The building was put up in the mid-19th century as the administrative seat of the Žarkovo municipality; in 1880 the elementary school moved in and has kept the same purpose ever since. It is a rare surviving example of a 19th-century village school and documents how rural schooling developed and under what conditions primary teaching was carried out in the wider Belgrade area. Its plainly cubic, type-built architecture reflects the modest means of a society that had only recently consolidated.

buildings.description: The Church of Saints Cyril and Methodius in Čukarica is a Catholic church built in 1929 for believers who had moved to Belgrade's outskirts after the First World War and worked in the area. The design came from the Zemun architect Blaž Katušić, and the church went up within months: Archbishop Rafael Rodić consecrated it that November. A statue of the two saints brought from Celje, blessed back in 1851, stands in the main altar, and the door carries the words 'That they may all be one'.
buildings.history: At the start of the twentieth century Belgrade's outskirts needed a Catholic church for the believers who had settled there after the First World War and worked locally. The apostolic nuncio Ermenegildo Pellegrinetti and Archbishop Rafael Rodić asked Vincentian missionaries from Slovenia to take a parish on the edge of the city, offering them Čukarica or Karaburma, and on 5 July 1929 Leonim Schmid and his confrere Alojz Plantarič chose Čukarica. The Lazarists bought a house on Požeška Street and opened a chapel there, where the first Mass was said on 5 August 1929, then bought land beside it and began the church. The cornerstone was blessed on 18 August 1929 by Alojzije Wagner, parish priest of Christ the King, and the church was finished and consecrated that November by Archbishop Rodić.

buildings.description: The country's first national mint: the building went up in 1927–1929 to a design by Josif Najman on the initiative of the National Bank of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and still serves as the Institute for the Production of Banknotes and Coins.
buildings.history: The mint was built in 1927–1929 as a purpose-designed facility built on the initiative of the National Bank of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and counts among the first modern industrial buildings in Belgrade; it later grew into a complex. After 1956 a single-storey administrative wing by Milutin Jovanović was added west of the production hall, matched in style to the main building and linked to it by a corridor. As the first national mint, it remained the only institution of its kind in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.

buildings.description: The Church of Saint George stands at the edge of the hill above the Sava, beside old Čukarica, and has been a landmark for this Belgrade suburb since the 1930s. It was built between 1928 and 1932 to a design by the Russian architect Androsov, in the neo-Byzantine manner common for interwar churches in the city. Its iconostasis, on which craftsmen worked for more than twenty years, is one of its most distinctive features.
buildings.history: The church was built between 1928 and 1932 to a design by the Russian architect Androsov, on a trefoil plan of the inscribed-cross type. The builders took medieval Serbian churches of the Morava school as their model, and the whole is treated in the neo-Byzantine manner of the period. The iconostasis was a long project: it was begun in 1930 and finished only in May 1952, carved in the Macedonian tradition by Nestor Aleksijev of Skopje and painted by an unknown Russian artist. An icon of Saint George hangs above the main entrance on the west side. A choir attached to the church could already look back on more than eight decades when it was written about in 2018.

buildings.description: The Milutin Bojić Library is the central library of Belgrade's Palilula municipality, named after the poet who wrote Plava grobnica. It was founded in 1957 as the district's public library, and over time it grew into a network of branches across the municipality, from Hadžipopovac to Borča and Ovča. In 2014 an original manuscript of Plava grobnica was found in one of its safes; after restoration at the National Library of Serbia it became the most valuable item in the library's local-history collection.
buildings.history: The library opened on 16 October 1957, when the People's Committee of Palilula set it up as the municipality's central library under the name Milutin Bojić. In 1988 its staff voted at a referendum against joining the Belgrade City Library, so the institution stayed independent, with the City of Belgrade as its founder. It now runs a main department and more than ten branches across the municipality, from Hadžipopovac and Stara Karaburma to Dunavski venac, Kotež, Borča, Ovča and Padinska Skela. A local-history department at the main building collects material about the poet and about Palilula. In 2014 the manuscript of Plava grobnica came to light during a clear-out of one of the library's safes and was restored by experts from the National Library of Serbia. In 2017, a century after the poet's death, the National Library hosted Olga Ječmenica's exhibition 100 Years of Plava grobnica, and the library created a department for book collections and legacies.

buildings.description: The White Bear kafana is the oldest surviving building in Zemun and the only example of Balkan architecture in its old core. It is thought to date from the end of the 17th century, and it is remembered as the house where Prince Eugene of Savoy stayed during the siege of Belgrade in 1717. When the Turks were driven out of Zemun the whole čaršija and almost all Turkish houses burned, yet this plain building from before Austrian rule came through. A kafana occupied the ground floor, while the upper floor has always been lived in.
buildings.history: The house was built in a timber-framed bondruk system on sloping ground at the foot of the loess terrace and the Ćukovac settlement. In the oldest plans of Zemun it appears as a square of five by five fathoms, roughly 9.5 by 9.5 metres, under the name Zartaken. Its ground floor opens to the street, while the upper floor is reached through a walled courtyard and was formed around an open porch whose plan originally followed the Cyrillic letter P, with wooden posts and a fence of profiled slats facing the street. Beneath it a brick lagum survives, two branches of ten and fourteen metres, the longer eastern one with a ventilation opening that comes out on the edge of Ćukovac. The double use of kafana below and dwelling above has lasted to this day and, with the lagum and the porch, makes the house a rare survival of its kind.

buildings.description: The church of Zemun's Evangelical congregation, raised in 1926–1930 at the corner of Prilaz and Tošin bunar. It is attributed to the circle of Hugo Ehrlich and Viktor Kovačić and counts as a rare, consistently modernist sacred building in Zemun.
buildings.history: The church was built between 1926 and 1930 on the corner of Prilaz and Tošin bunar. Its authorship is not documented and the design is most often attributed to the school of architects Hugo Ehrlich and Viktor Kovačić. Above the dome a lantern originally carried a cross as the symbol of Christ's Passion, and the building remains a testimony to the life of an Evangelical congregation in interwar Zemun.

buildings.description: The Church of Saint Joseph the Worker serves the youngest Catholic parish in Belgrade, in Stara Karaburma. The parish was established in 1972 and the present church opened on 1 May 1991; from the outset it was entrusted to the Salesians. The dedication was no accident: most local residents belonged to the working class, and the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker falls on 1 May.
buildings.history: The plot in Stara Karaburma had already been bought and prepared in 1942, but the war, the nationalisation of the land and the loss of the collected building material put an end to the plan, and a supermarket was later built on the site. Gabrijel Bukatko, who had taken charge of the Belgrade Archdiocese in 1964, set out to realise his predecessor's wish, asking the Salesians, whom he knew well, to establish a parish here; because most residents were workers, Saint Joseph the Worker, whose feast falls on 1 May, became its patron. A small house on Sime Šolaja Street was bought and turned into the first public chapel, where the first Mass was said on 22 June 1965 under the care of Slovenian Sisters of Mercy. On 7 September 1967 a new chapel opened in Pribojska Street, blessed by Bukatko, and the Salesian Herman Habič became the first parish priest. Neither Habič nor his successor Antun Horvat managed to build the church in the face of opposition from the local community, and only the hall of the future church went up before 1986. In 1989 the new parish priest, the Slovenian Salesian Ciril Zajec, began building over that hall; the church opened on 1 May 1991, blessed by Archbishop Franc Perko, and the bell tower was added a few years later.

buildings.description: The parish church of Bežanija, dedicated to St George the Great Martyr. Its present furnishing dates from the 1938 overhaul, when the Russian painter Andrei Bitsenko made the new iconostasis and wall decoration, while the royal doors and throne icons of the old one went to the village of Kupinovo.
buildings.history: The church was built in 1827 as a single-nave building with a semicircular apse and a tall three-storey bell tower over the narthex. A major repair followed in 1938, when a new iconostasis and wall paintings were made by the Russian painter Andrei Bitsenko. The most important part of the earlier iconostasis of the old Bežanija church — the royal doors, the throne icons and other pieces — was moved to the village of Kupinovo after that repair, though several icons that belonged to it are still kept in the Bežanija church.

buildings.description: Villa Mozer is a free-standing two-storey house of 1929–1930, built by Milan Zloković inside the production complex of Bruno Mozer's winery. Its rooms are stacked vertically: a basement, a ground floor with hall, dining room, terrace and pool, an upper floor with four rooms and two terraces, and a top level with laundry and attic. The cubic volumes, the clean geometry and the close relation between interior and garden carry the lesson of Adolf Loos and the international style. After the war the villa was nationalised and turned into offices for the Navip firm, and a concrete sculpture in the shape of a wine bottle still stands in the garden.
buildings.history: The villa went up in 1929–1930 as a residential two-storey house within the complex of Bruno Mozer's winery. Zloković assembled it from cubic forms and held interior and exterior together, stepping the plans in depth, and the handling of the cube shows the influence of Adolf Loos. Traditional materials — brick in lime mortar, concrete and timber — are combined with modernistically designed interior elements. After the Second World War the house was nationalised and adapted as the administrative building of the Navip enterprise: open terraces above the first and second floors were built over so that the house was levelled with the roof plane, with smaller changes inside and in the facade openings to suit offices. The last reconstruction of the upper storey stayed within the modern concept, and the building today shows no structural damage.

buildings.description: The Church of the Ascension in Žarkovo is a parish church in Belgrade's Čukarica municipality, whose feast, Spasovdan, is also the slava of Žarkovo and of the city. It was built between 1936 and 1938 to a design by Viktor Lukomsky, one of the best-known architects of interwar Serbia, who also designed the Serbian Patriarchate and the Church of Saint Sava. In May 1938 Patriarch Gavrilo Dožić consecrated the church, and two years later it received its first iconostasis.
buildings.history: The initiative to build the church arose in 1929, and in 1930 a church committee for its construction was formed. Work began in 1936 with the blessing of Patriarch Varnava, and on 7 September of that year Bishop Sava Trlajić consecrated the foundations. The building was finished in 1938 and consecrated on 2 (15) May by Patriarch Gavrilo Dožić. In 1940 the church received its first iconostasis, carved by Blagoje Milojević, with icons by Aleksandar Trojicki and bells cast by Živo Burić. In 1941 the Germans turned the churchyard into a military base and took the parish priest and several people attached to the church to a camp. Painting of the interior began in 1966, the structure was renovated in 1997–1998, and in 2012 restoration of the frescoes started with the blessing of Patriarch Irinej.

buildings.description: Zemun Health Centre is a medical institution serving the Belgrade municipality of Zemun with routine care. Its catchment area reaches beyond the municipality into neighbouring Surčin, covering 442 km² and more than 200,000 people. Its departments range from paediatrics, school medicine and gynaecology to dentistry, radiology, physical medicine and psychiatry — almost the full set of outpatient services.
buildings.history: Zemun Health Centre was conceived to provide routine care to the residents of Zemun, and its catchment area later stretched into neighbouring Surčin as well — 442 km² and more than 200,000 people. Over time it developed a broad range of services, from paediatrics, school medicine and gynaecology to adult health care, occupational medicine, home care, dentistry, radiology and medical biology. Pharmacology, internal medicine, ophthalmology, otorhinolaryngology, physical medicine and rehabilitation, social medicine and psychiatry complete the structure. At the end of 2010 the centre employed 684 people on a permanent basis, including 123 dentists and 5 pharmacists, while non-medical staff numbered 94.

buildings.description: The Serbian school in Gornja Varoš, Zemun, founded in 1872 and extended in 1912 to a design by Milan J. Jeremić and Josef Marx. Standing beside the Svetotrojičina church as part of its complex, it testifies to the growth of schooling in Zemun.
buildings.history: The school building here dates from 1872; in 1912 it was extended to a design by Milan J. Jeremić and Josef Marx. Standing by the Svetotrojičina church and forming part of its complex, the school reads as a chapter in the history of schooling in Zemun.

buildings.description: A home for orphans from Srem, opened in 1919 in a building put up by Franja Katinčić and financed by Queen Maria's Fund for the raising and maintenance of orphaned children — a testimony to the Court's care for abandoned children.
buildings.history: The building was erected in 1919 to a design by the builder Franja Katinčić. It housed the Children's Home of Queen Maria, also known as the Home for Srem Orphans, financed from Queen Maria's Fund for the raising and maintenance of orphans. It belongs to Zemun's historic building stock from the years of the town's economic, social and cultural rise.

buildings.description: The property of the painter Dragomir Glišić: a family house and a purpose-built studio with its authentic interior, kept together with 96 oils, 30 drawings, painters' tools, a library and personal belongings.
buildings.history: The Glišić family house was built in the 1890s, and the studio, purpose-built and functionally shaped for painting, was added in the 1930s. The bequest is arranged so that the painter's development can be followed chronologically and thematically — portraits, landscapes, large figure compositions and still lifes. His war painting from the Balkan Wars and the First World War is absent from the collection and is kept, with other documents of the period, in the Military Museum in Belgrade.

buildings.description: The Officers' Home on Kralja Milana Street was raised in 1895 to a design by Jovan Ilkić and Milorad Ruvidić, in a quarter that had held barracks and a riding hall throughout the nineteenth century. It existed for the recreation of the officer corps, and between the wars its halls carried balls and exhibitions. In 1969–1971 it was rebuilt for the Student Cultural Centre, and the old officers' club became a stage for the city's young.
buildings.history: The Home opened in 1895, when Serbia had recently become a kingdom and its army was acquiring the institutions of a modern state. The site was no accident: this was the military quarter, with the old Miloš barracks, the riding hall and the barracks of the 7th Regiment close by. Officers came here to rest, and in the interwar decades the hall filled for balls and exhibitions. Between 1969 and 1971 the building was remade for the Student Cultural Centre: the corner entrance was walled up and a new one opened from Resavska Street. Outwardly it kept its main lines, and the corner tower still gives the block its fortress-like air.

buildings.description: Belgrade Youth Centre is a cultural centre devoted primarily to young people, with a programme that ranges across contemporary art, music, theatre and film. It opened in 1964 under the culture secretariat of the Belgrade Assembly and still receives its funding from the city. Around a thousand events a year bring in more than 180,000 young visitors.
buildings.history: The centre was founded in 1964 and has kept the Belgrade Assembly as its financier ever since. Its work is organised through five units covering music, visual arts and multimedia, education and interactive communication, publishing, and a laboratory of initiatives. The Belgrade Jazz Festival and the Belgrade Author Rock Festival are among the events associated with the house. In 2013–2015 the director was the actor Marko Stojanović, followed by Nenad Dragović. Apart from the main building near Republic Square, the centre also runs the Magacin in Kraljevića Marka Street, a converted warehouse of more than 5,000 square metres.

buildings.description: St Nicholas in Višnjica is a small single-nave church raised in 1842, with a semicircular apse to the east and matching bays to the north and south. It belongs to the reign of Prince Miloš, a moment when Baroque models in Serbian church building gave way to the medieval inheritance. A blind arcade runs the length of the walls, and the west front is dominated by a decorated portal whose niche holds a mosaic of the patron saint. Northwest of the church stands a two-storey brick bell tower, buttressed at the corners.
buildings.history: The church was built in 1842, one of the modest single-nave churches raised in Serbia during the reign of Prince Miloš. Stone walls were plastered and covered with a barrel vault, and the interior kept as one space — sanctuary and nave, with the side bays opening off it. On the outside the builder ran a band of blind arcades along the walls, a signal that Serbian medieval forms were returning to church design after the Baroque period. The west portal took a niche with a mosaic of St Nicholas, the patron. The iconostasis is a much later addition; the brick bell tower with its buttresses was raised to the northwest.

buildings.description: The house built in 1824 for Dr Vita Romita, one of the first physicians of restored Serbia. Since 1861 it has served as a medical institution; today it houses the Psychiatric Clinic.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1824 for Dr Vita Romita; its rough stone walls and the small ground-floor windows earned it the popular name Doctor's Tower. Combining features of a tower, a konak and a palace, it ranks among the first larger buildings raised in Serbia after the Second Serbian Uprising, while the height and size of its rooms point to Central European models. In 1861 it was given over to health care, and that purpose has lasted: the Psychiatric Clinic is still housed there.

buildings.description: The Military Archives, the archive service of Serbia's Ministry of Defence, is one of the country's national and cultural institutions and stands outside its archival system. Its history goes back to 5 February 1876, when a decree of Prince Milan Obrenović created the First Military Archive, and its holdings run to some 40 million records, from the Serbian-Ottoman wars to the Second World War. Because the material is military in provenance, a researcher must know the unit and formation involved before a document can be traced.
buildings.history: The idea came from Lieutenant Jovan Dragašević, who taught military history and geography at the Artillery School and in 1865 proposed to the war minister Milivoj Petrović Blaznavac that Serbia begin collecting war records. Eleven years later a decree of Prince Milan Obrenović dated 5 February 1876 created the first military archive in Serbia and ordered the third department of the Main General Staff to gather data, write war history, keep the archive and run the staff library. Wars destroyed much valuable material, and until 1935 the department worked to fill the gaps by arranging the holdings and collecting memoirs, producing inventories of the operational records. A royal decree dated 6 March 1940 restructured the History Department and renamed it the Military History Institute, but a year later, after the April War and the capitulation, it ceased to work. In March 1945 a history department with an archival section was set up inside the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, and between 1949 and 2006 it operated under the name Military History Institute, and the archives formed one of its units. In 1999 NATO bombing severely damaged the archives and destroyed much of the microfilming equipment and the conservation laboratory, although most documents were rescued by the staff, and independent legal status followed in 2006.

buildings.description: The Seismological Institute in Tašmajdan Park took shape over three decades, from the foundation stone of 10 September 1908 to the last works of 1939. Its first stage was a plain single-storey brick pavilion of 1909, designed by Momir Korunović and built by Stevan Hibner's Belgrade firm. Additions in 1912, 1926 and 1939 gradually gave the utilitarian box a romantic air. The result is Korunović's earliest realised work and the oldest public building on Tašmajdan.
buildings.history: The foundation stone was laid on 10 September 1908, on a site in Tašmajdan Park. Within a year Stevan Hibner's Belgrade building firm had finished the pavilion designed by Momir Korunović: square in plan, built entirely of brick, its facade left plain and without ornament. Work resumed in 1912 to plans by Đura Bajalović, and two further campaigns, in 1926 and 1939, followed. Each addition softened the original austerity — arched window heads appeared, and a regular rhythm of dentils ran above the cornice, giving the building its romantic character. For Korunović it was the first realised commission of a career that would make him one of the defining Serbian architects of the twentieth century.

buildings.description: The Church of Saint Tryphon at the Topčider Cemetery is a small tomb church built in 1905 at the behest of Nikola Spasić, one of Serbia's great benefactors. Its founder left a bequest that the liturgy be served there only twice a year: on the family's slava, the feast of Saint Tryphon, and on the day of his death. Spasić himself died on Corfu in 1916, and his body was brought to the church only in 1923, after the First World War.
buildings.history: The church was begun in 1905 as a memorial chapel at Nikola Spasić's grave, and from the outset it was intended for that burial place alone. The bequest limited services to two days a year — the family's slava and the day of the founder's death. After the retreat across Albania Spasić fell gravely ill in Greece, and his last wish was that his body be brought to this church once the war was over; he died on Corfu in 1916, and the bequest was fulfilled in 1923. From 1988, when the protoierej-stavrofor Dejan Dejanović became rector, the liturgy was served on all feasts of Serbian, Russian and Greek saints, whether or not they are marked in red in the calendar. Around him a brotherhood of more than two thousand believers gathered.

buildings.description: The village school built for Bežanija in 1891: by 1896 it already taught 136 girls and boys. It is the oldest surviving building of the second half of the 19th century on the territory of the Novi Beograd municipality.
buildings.history: The school was built in 1891 as a type design for elementary teaching; archival records show that by 1896 it already had 136 girls and boys. After the school moved to a new building in 1959 the house changed use, which brought minor alterations to the internal layout and the shape of the windows. It remains the oldest surviving building of the second half of the 19th century in the Novi Beograd municipality.

buildings.description: The Church of Saint Athanasius the Great is a young parish church in the Zemun neighbourhood of Plavi Horizonti in Belgrade. Patriarch Irinej consecrated the land for it on 3 May 2012 and the foundations four months later. The building work culminated on 3 March 2019, when the patriarch consecrated the finished church; in October 2023 a monument to people from Peć who died in the war in Kosovo and Metohija was erected in its yard.
buildings.history: Patriarch Irinej consecrated the land for the church on 3 May 2012, and on 30 August of the same year he consecrated the foundations. The construction was crowned by the consecration of the church on 3 March 2019, performed by the patriarch. In October 2023 a monument to people from Peć who died in the war in Kosovo and Metohija was erected in the churchyard.

buildings.description: Built in 1780–1785 on the site of an older eighteenth-century church, the church of the Holy Archangels Michael and Gabriel still defines the centre of this Zemun suburb and is the oldest architectural monument in Batajnica.
buildings.history: The church was built between 1780 and 1785 on the site of an eighteenth-century predecessor. It keeps a collection of church art from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries: twenty-eight icons by the Zemun painter Živko Petrović, applied-art pieces, rare books and archival documents. The building is listed among Serbia's protected cultural monuments.

buildings.description: The Church of St Nicholas in Dobanovci is dedicated to the translation of the relics of St Nicholas and has stood since 1803 on the site of eighteenth-century churches. The old confessional school founded beside it was the earliest educational institution in the area.
buildings.history: The church was built in 1803 on the site of earlier eighteenth-century churches. Georgije Dević, a noted Vojvodina woodcarver, made the iconostasis and its carved woodwork in 1836, and Petar Čortanović painted the icons in 1841–1842. A confessional school was founded at the church and built at the same time; the parish also keeps rare icons, old printed books and registers of births, marriages and deaths from the eighteenth to the twentieth century.

buildings.description: The Catholic church of the Holy Trinity in Surčin was built in 1896 and belonged to the old Zemun parish until 1930. A single altar held the image of the Trinity, with two smaller altars beside it dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and the Sacred Heart of Mary, while a tower carrying three bells rose above the roof. Renovated in 2006–2007, it still serves as Surčin's parish church.
buildings.history: The church was built of brick and covered with tiles, and three bells were hung in its tower. Inside stood a single altar with the image of the Trinity and two smaller ones dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and the Sacred Heart of Mary. Until 1930 the church belonged to the old Zemun parish, after which it passed to the parish of Surčin. In 2006–2007 the building was thoroughly renovated.

buildings.description: Known as the Serbian School, the village school in Batajnica was built by Knez Nikola Vulko between 1875 and 1880. It is one of the few surviving Belgrade buildings from the second half of the nineteenth century and today houses the Boško Palkovljević Pinki primary school.
buildings.history: The building went up between 1875 and 1880 for the village school; Knez Nikola Vulko was its builder. It is one of the few Belgrade buildings preserved from the second half of the nineteenth century and documents the continuity of schooling in south-eastern Srem. In July 2018 it was declared a cultural monument; today the Boško Palkovljević Pinki school is housed in it, while some classes moved to the newer block built beside it in the 1960s.

buildings.description: The only surviving structure of Belgrade’s first airport: the hangar-workshop built to the design and under the supervision of Milutin Milanković. Here he used a concrete shell for the first time in the country, a notable structural innovation of its day.
buildings.history: Belgrade’s airport was built between 1926 and 1932 in two phases on empty ground at Dojno polje near Bežanijska kosa. The second phase, begun in 1929, brought two grass runways, a modern terminal, an officers’ club and a technical section with a hangar-workshop for aircraft repair and overhaul. Milutin Milanković designed and supervised the hangar, and it is the only building of the complex still standing.

buildings.description: Serbia’s first factory purpose-built for industrial paper production, erected by the industrialist Milan Vapa to a design by the architect Karl Hanisch. For three decades it remained the only paper factory of its kind in the country.
buildings.history: The factory was built between 1921 and 1924, with the engineer Vladimir Bilinski supervising the construction. Besides paper production and storage, the building held the owner’s office, a kitchen and dining room, and a workers’ clinic with rest rooms. Foreign experts compared the plant to paper factories in the developed countries of Europe.

buildings.description: The Church of the Ascension in Jakovo, in the Surčin municipality, was raised between 1807 and 1810 on the site of an older eighteenth-century church. The mason Josef Vertich and the carpenter Johann Mayer gave it a classicist shell touched by baroque and empire detail. Inside, Petar Jakšić's iconostasis carries icons and wall paintings made by the Zemun artist Živko Petrović between 1855 and 1862.
buildings.history: A village church from the eighteenth century stood on this spot until the new one replaced it. Work ran from 1807 to 1810 under Josef Vertich, assisted by Johann Mayer. In the middle of the nineteenth century Petar Jakšić carved the iconostasis, a rare example of Serbian classicism preserved almost in full. Živko Petrović painted the icons and the wall compositions between 1855 and 1862. The church still keeps a rich collection of movable pieces — kissing icons, furniture, seventeenth- and eighteenth-century books and parish registers.

buildings.description: On the corner of Studentski trg and Višnjićeva Street stood the tekke of hadži-sheikh Muhamed, a lodge of the powerful Kadiri dervish order. Beside its main building a turbe was raised in 1783–1784 over the grave of Sheikh Mustafa, who had for a time headed the lodge: a hexagonal stone mausoleum beneath a round dome, its walls inscribed with verses from the Quran. During the Serbian uprising of 1804–1813 the tekke briefly housed the Governing Council, the highest executive authority of the newly created state, and in 1811 Dositej Obradović died within its walls.
buildings.history: The lodge of hadži-sheikh Muhamed occupied a corner plot facing what is now Studentski trg, and its dervishes belonged to the Kadiri order. The main building had a rectangular plan; seen from the square it seemed to rise only one storey, while the falling ground behind made the courtyard side a full floor higher. Beside it, in 1783–1784, a turbe was built over the grave of Sheikh Mustafa, at one time the head of the lodge, and the date can still be read on the plaque above the door. The mausoleum was laid in stone: a hexagonal body carries a hexagonal drum and a round dome, the portal frame and cornices are moulded, and the chamber is inscribed with passages from the Quran around a covered sarcophagus. In the uprising years of 1804–1813 the Governing Council sat in the lodge, and Dositej Obradović died there in 1811.

buildings.description: The Manjež on Kralja Milana Street was begun around 1860 for the royal cavalry squadron, and at first it was little more than a stable. A few decades later the National Theatre moved temporarily into the neglected building, turning the old riding hall into a stage. After the fire of 1927 the Russian architect Nikola Krasnov added a storey and joined old and new into one whole, and in 1929 the theatre reopened. Today it is the Yugoslav Drama Theatre — a house that burned twice and was each time rebuilt out of its architects' legacy.
buildings.history: The riding hall went up around 1860, while Serbia was still a principality; it served the royal cavalry squadron and stood along what is now Kralja Milana Street. A few decades later its original purpose faded: the National Theatre moved temporarily into the run-down stable, and plays were staged there until 1927, when the building burned. Nikola Krasnov added an upper storey and a vestibule on the south side, the sculptor Vojislav Ratimirović Šikoparija peopled the facade with figures, and the renewed theatre opened in 1929. Two years on it was converted for the National Assembly, and after the Second World War, in 1947, it was adapted for the stage once more to a design by Momčilo N. Belobrk — the birth of the Yugoslav Drama Theatre in its modernist guise. The fire of 1997 destroyed the house, and the rebuilding by Zoran Radojičić and Dejan Miljković set glass and metal against Krasnov's preserved facade and Belobrk's entrance portico.

buildings.description: The Fifth Belgrade Gymnasium grew out of the First Women's Real Gymnasium, opened in 1905 as the first school of its rank in Serbia meant for girls. Its staff included Nadežda Petrović, Desanka Maksimović and Vene Bogoslavov, and its alumni number statesmen, actors, musicians and writers. The school holds a distinctive place in the history of women's education and emancipation in Serbia.
buildings.history: A higher women's school had existed in Belgrade since 1863, but it ranked below the gymnasiums, and a full secondary school for girls appeared only at the start of the twentieth century. The founding followed a long public argument about a woman's place: critics called a separate girls' gymnasium unnecessary. Until then a girl could enter a boys' gymnasium only with special permission from the education authorities, and her studies could be cut short at any moment. On 5 September 1905 the newspaper Politika printed a sharp attack on 'modern Belgrade misses' on its front page. Despite the controversy, the school established itself among the city's most prestigious.

buildings.description: The Snaga i svetlost thermal power plant occupies the right bank of the Danube in Belgrade, a complex raised between 1930 and 1932 to drawings supplied by the Swiss Society for Electrification and Transport of Basel. With it, a low-voltage alternating-current distribution network came into use in the city for the first time, and through the interwar years the station contributed substantially to Belgrade's electricity supply. Boiler house, machine hall and switchboard room were only part of the scheme: a pumping station, filtration basins and a portal crane running on rails beside a 140-metre channel to the river completed it. Cubist volumes, exposed steel and glass, and an architecture that puts function first place the plant firmly in the Bauhaus orbit.
buildings.history: Construction ran from 1930 to 1932 on the Danube's right bank, following a design prepared by the Swiss Society for Electrification and Transport in Basel. The brief was never just a power station: a pumping house with its pipework and filtration basins stood at the end of the channel, and a lattice portal crane travelled the rails beside it, driven by its own two electric motors. Inside, the boiler house, the machine hall and the control room each answered a separate need. When the plant came on stream, Belgrade obtained a low-voltage alternating-current supply and could begin applying new technology to transport and telecommunications. Electricity altered daily habits and, in time, redrew the social profile of the city's population.

buildings.description: Dimitrije Leko designed this house on the Sava for the Vučo family, and every building the family commissioned in Belgrade came from his drawing board. Shops filled the ground floor, flats the upper storeys, and the Art Nouveau facade faces the Belgrade Cooperative building across the way.
buildings.history: Built in 1908 for Đorđe Vučo, the house combined shops at street level with flats above. It belongs to the former Mali pijac on the Sava and answers the Belgrade Cooperative building opposite. Leko designed every house for the Vučo family, a relationship unique in Belgrade architecture.

buildings.description: Archibald Reiss, a Swiss chemist and forensic expert, came to Serbia in 1914 to investigate the crimes of the Austro-Hungarian army and never left, dying in Belgrade in 1929. In 1921 a grateful country gave him a plot in Topčider, where he built a house to the design of the builder Lazar Lacković and named it Villa Dobro Polje after the Macedonian field of a decisive 1918 battle. He wanted it to resemble a Serbian village house, and gave its interior over to his own idea of the Serbian countryside and its people.
buildings.history: Reiss arrived in Serbia in 1914 at the invitation of the government, a neutral expert sent to establish what the Austro-Hungarian army had done in Mačva. Once war came he worked as an investigator for the royal government and army, gathering evidence of crimes committed in Serbia and bringing it before the world, and he also served as a volunteer, crossing Albania with the Serbian army. After 1918 he did not go home; he settled in Belgrade. The plot in Topčider, given to him in 1921, carried the name Dobro Polje in memory of one of the decisive battles on the Salonika front in 1918. He lived there until his death in 1929.

buildings.description: The Craftsmen's House on Hilendarska Street was conceived as a single address for all of Belgrade's craft institutions. Money began to be collected back in 1914, but war postponed the work, and only in 1931 was the design entrusted to Bogdan Nestorović, a firm advocate of modernism without ornament. The building opened on 1 May 1933 with halls for the guilds, a hotel and a cinema; since 1947 it has housed Radio Belgrade.
buildings.history: The idea of a house of their own grew out of the example set by other corporate homes: every craft institution founded so far was to be gathered under one roof. In 1914 the various craft funds raised the money and began building to a design of 1912 by the architect Danilo Vladisavljević, but war and poor conditions halted the work. The scheme was revived in 1931, when the planning passed to Bogdan Nestorović, a prominent champion of modernist architecture stripped of decoration. The corner building with two wings along Hilendarska and Svetogorska streets gained a central two-stage tower, and above the main entrance a sculpture of the Blacksmith by the stone carver N. Lukaček was set in place. The house was finished on 1 May 1933 and, besides rooms for the unions, offered a hotel and a cinema; since 1947 it has been the home of Radio Belgrade.

buildings.description: The Church of St Nicholas in Ostružnica was built in 1831–1833 at the expense of Knez Miloš. It stands on the hill at the crossroads in the centre of the village where Karađorđe convened the First National Assembly during the First Serbian Uprising.
buildings.history: Construction ran from 1831 to 1833, paid for by Knez Miloš, the church's ktitor. The churchyard also held the old wooden šindralija church from the end of the eighteenth century. The church became the centre of village life, where people gathered to agree and organise the struggle to free Serbia from the Turks. At the start of the twentieth century the bell tower was built at the expense of the wealthy merchant Kosta Janić and his wife Sofija.

buildings.description: Founded in 1911, the Stanković Music School was, with the Mokranjac school, the only source of musical talent in Serbia until the Music Academy opened. Almost everyone who shaped Belgrade’s musical life studied or taught within its walls.
buildings.history: The school opened in 1911 as a music-pedagogical institution in a residential house from the 1890s. Petar Bajalović extended and rebuilt it between 1913 and 1914. Until the Second World War the school, together with Mokranjac, trained composers, performers, musicologists and teachers, and concert life, opera and the philharmonic grew out of its work.

buildings.description: The Memorial Museum of Nadežda and Rastko Petrović occupies the family house of the Belgrade painter Ljubica Luković, sister of Nadežda and Rastko Petrović, built between 1928 and 1935 as a typical house of the Professors' Colony. The rich legacy of the Petrović family — from Nadežda's paintings to Rastko's letters and personal belongings — was gathered by Ljubica Luković and given to the National Museum in Belgrade. That collection now forms the museum's display: paintings and sketches by Nadežda Petrović, family correspondence, travel films and gramophone records.
buildings.history: The house was built between 1928 and 1935 as a typical house of the Professors' Colony, and it belonged to the Belgrade painter Ljubica Luković, sister of Nadežda and Rastko Petrović. It holds the rich legacy of the Petrović family, tied to the life and work of Mita Petrović (1852–1911), a writer and scientific worker, the painter Nadežda Petrović (1873–1915) and the writer Rastko Petrović (1898–1949). Ljubica Luković gathered that collection and presented it to the National Museum in Belgrade, and it now forms the display of the museum housed here. It includes paintings and sketches by Nadežda Petrović, private correspondence between family members, artworks and objects that belonged to Rastko Petrović, travel films and gramophone records. Together they make it possible to see the life and work of people without whom the recent cultural past of Serbia is hard to imagine.

buildings.description: The Serbian Orthodox church of the Apostle Matthew stands in Novi Surčin and was founded in 2018, the first church raised in Surčin in more than two hundred years. It took three years to build: work started in 2015 and the cornerstone, brought from Čelinac, was laid in March 2016. Bishop Vasilije of Srem consecrated the temple and served the first hierarchical liturgy there.
buildings.history: Construction began in 2015, and on 6 March 2016 the foundations were consecrated by Bishop Vasilije Vadić of Srem together with Stefan Šuša, president of the Surčin municipality. The cornerstone came from Čelinac, and stones from Hilandar and the Krka monastery were lowered into the foundations with the names of those present carved on them. Building took three years, and in 2018 the church was founded within the Eparchy of Srem. After the consecration the first hierarchical liturgy was served, with priests from several parishes concelebrating with the bishop.

buildings.description: The church of Saint Stephen the First Martyr in Veliko Selo was raised in 1834 from the material of the demolished monastery of Saint Stephen in Slanci, which earned it the popular name of monastery church. It served two villages at once, Veliko Selo and Slanci, and received the monastery's unfinished iconostasis, begun in 1812. Frescoes cover only the altar, and a school built beside it in 1936 was among the first five village schools in Serbia.
buildings.history: The new church rose in 1834, built with material taken from the dismantled monastery of Saint Stephen in Slanci. The monastery's unfinished iconostasis, begun in 1812, was carried over into the new building. The church was meant for the people of both Veliko Selo and Slanci. Only the altar received frescoes, and the church is dedicated to the summer feast of Saint Stephen, the translation of his relics on 15 August, while his main feast falls on 9 January. In 1936 a school was built beside the church, among the first five village schools in Serbia.

buildings.description: The church of Saint Mary Magdalene in Beli Potok was raised in 1883 with contributions and labour from the villagers themselves. It was dedicated to Mary Magdalene because that feast served as the village's slava during the nineteenth century. Metropolitan Mihailo of Belgrade consecrated it in 1885, and the churchyard later received monuments to the Serbian warriors of 1912–1918 and to Vasa Čarapić.
buildings.history: The village built the church itself: money came as contributions from the inhabitants, who also supplied the labour. The dedication to Mary Magdalene followed the fact that her feast was the village slava through the nineteenth century. Construction was completed in 1883, and two years later, in 1885, Metropolitan Mihailo of Belgrade consecrated the building. Later the churchyard received a monument to Serbian warriors of 1912–1918 and one to Vasa Čarapić.

buildings.description: Janić Kafana is an old mehana from the first half of the nineteenth century in the centre of Ostružnica, long owned by the Janić family. It was the main gathering place for villagers and travellers, a kind of public tribune where the affairs of the village were debated.
buildings.history: The house was built in the first half of the nineteenth century and stood half-ruined until 1971, when its then owner reconstructed it under conservation conditions issued by the Belgrade Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, largely working himself and with his own money. The work returned the mehana to its original state, and in 1972 it was declared a cultural monument. Today it is adapted to modern life and keeps the continuity of Ostružnica's centre.

buildings.description: Built in the first half of the nineteenth century as a kafana, this building in the centre of Ostružnica took on a commercial role at the beginning of the twentieth century and is known as Janić's Shops. It is a surviving example of the so-called newer Moravian house.
buildings.history: The building was raised in the first half of the nineteenth century as a kafana, with two dining halls at the front, a kitchen and storerooms at the back, and the owner's two rooms in the eastern wing, cut off by a corridor. At the beginning of the twentieth century it took on a commercial role and underwent minor adaptations. It is protected as a cultural monument and remains one of the characteristic examples of the newer Moravian house.

buildings.description: The Mitrović House on Avala is the oldest surviving building of its kind in Serbia: a mountain lodge raised in 1926 to replace the first huts of the Serbian Mountaineering Society. It takes its name from Dr Dušan Špirta Mitrović, a physician and volunteer on the Salonika front who pressed for the lodge to be built and popularised mountain excursions. Its form draws on romanticised academism with echoes of vernacular building.
buildings.history: Mountain tourism in Serbia grew out of the first scientific expeditions in biology, geology and mineralogy. When the Serbian Mountaineering Society was founded in 1901 with the geology professor Jovan Žujović as its first president, the movement acquired a broad public following. Its beginnings are tied to Avala: a first lodge appeared here in 1902, a second in 1910, and in 1926 the Mitrović House. That one remains today the oldest surviving structure of its purpose in the country. It is named after Dr Dušan Špirta Mitrović, a physician and volunteer on the Salonika front, who deserves credit both for the building itself and for the growing popularity of mountain travel.

buildings.description: Built in 1908 as the passenger station of the steamship line, to plans by the Viennese architect Remel, the Old Captaincy faces the Danube in Zemun. Since 1985 it has housed the Stara kapetanija art gallery, the seat of Zemun’s association of fine and applied artists.
buildings.history: The building served the steamship passenger station, combining the agency’s and the transport functions. In time the arcades of the left wing facing the Danube were walled up. No older buildings of the 18th- and 19th-century river administration survived, so the Captaincy remains the key witness to Zemun’s role in Danube shipping. For the last three decades it has been one of the seats of Belgrade’s cultural and artistic life.

buildings.description: Hotel Avala was raised in 1931 to a design by the Russian architect Viktor Lukomsky, on the plateau before the paths and flights of steps that climb gently to the summit of Avala and the Monument to the Unknown Hero. A tall two-storey block with the entrance and lower, broadly spread annexes step down the hillside, their romantic, lively massing pairing a Renaissance handling of forms with subdued Serbian-Byzantine ornament. Arcaded porches and openings carry the national note, yet the flat roof in place of a hipped one and the insistent rectangular windows give the building a far more modern look; on the terrace stairway stand two large sphinxes of artificial stone by the Russian sculptor Vladimir Zagorodnyuk.
buildings.history: The hotel was built in 1931 on the plateau at the foot of the climb to the summit of Avala, where the paths and flights of steps begin their rise towards the Monument to the Unknown Hero. Lukomsky composed it of a tall two-storey block with the entrance and low, widely spread annexes stepping down the slope. In the detailing he married Renaissance plasticity to restrained Serbian-Byzantine motifs — cornices, columns, capitals and archivolts — while arcaded porches and openings carried the national note. At the same time he gave up the hipped roof for a flat one and insisted on regular rectangular windows, which lent the house its modern character. On the north side, along the railing of the terrace stair, he set two large sphinxes of artificial stone made by the sculptor Vladimir Zagorodnyuk, and the hotel is counted among the leading works of his opus.

buildings.description: Memorial complex on Avala conceived by the sculptor Ivan Meštrović as a public mausoleum, in which landscape, architecture and sculpture all serve a single purpose — honouring everyone who fell for freedom. The site had already been marked in 1922, when peasants from the surrounding villages raised a stone cross over an unknown soldier’s grave.
buildings.history: In 1922 peasants from the surrounding villages put up a modest stone cross on Avala, over the grave of an unknown soldier. The present monument was built between 1934 and 1938 to a design by the sculptor Ivan Meštrović, and its architectural concept took in the whole complex on the site of the medieval town of Žrnov. The mausoleum is built of black Jablanica granite; long approach walks lead to the two entrances of the tomb, where granite caryatids — women in the folk dress of the Yugoslav peoples — stand four to each side.

buildings.description: The Zemun church of the Holy Trinity, built to the plans of Josef Felber between 1839 and 1842. Its iconostasis was carved by Gavrilo Ninković, while the icons and the wall paintings came from the Zemun painter Živko Petrović.
buildings.history: The church went up between 1839 and 1842 to Felber’s plans. Its gilded wood-carved iconostasis, baroque in spirit with classicist detail, was made by the carver Gavrilo Ninković and the painter Živko Petrović, who also painted the walls. The classicist iron railing around the churchyard survives as one of the site’s particular values.

buildings.description: The Catholic church of Saint Peter in Belgrade's Stari Grad belongs to the Jesuit community that returned to the city in 1930 after a long absence. The 1933 building rose in the courtyard of a house erected in 1845 for Jovan Stejić, physician to the royal family, and was designed by the Zagreb architect Juraj Denzler. A year later the icon of the Madonna of Belgrade was brought back from Petrovaradin, and it remains an object of special veneration.
buildings.history: Jesuits tried to settle in Belgrade while it was still under Ottoman rule: in 1612 Father Bartol Kašić opened a humanist school for thirty-two pupils there, the first of its kind in the Balkans. After Eugene of Savoy took the city in 1717 the order returned, and in 1718 a larger group formed a community in Dorćol and received from Petrovaradin a baroque image of the Madonna and Child. Their gymnasium had seventy-seven pupils in 1735, yet when Belgrade passed back to the Turks in 1739 the Jesuits left, carrying only that icon away. Suppressed between 1773 and 1814, they came back only in 1930, and at New Year 1931 began work in the newly founded parish of Saint Peter. In 1933 the church was built in the courtyard of the purchased house to Juraj Denzler's design, and in 1934 the Madonna of Belgrade returned from Petrovaradin.

buildings.description: The Faculty of Organizational Sciences (FON) is one of the University of Belgrade's leading schools, founded in 1971, with roots reaching back to the late 1960s. Its first classes met in the halls of the '21. maj' engine factory in Rakovica, and since 1981 it has worked in Voždovac. It now ranks as the region's leading centre for information systems, management and quality management.
buildings.history: The final decision to establish the faculty was taken on 28 April 1969, and in November 1970 the University Council voted to bring it into the University of Belgrade. It opened formally on 4 November 1971, with teaching beginning in the '21. maj' engine works in the Rakovica industrial basin. Studies were organised in three streams — organisational-cybernetic, organisational-personnel and organisational-production — and postgraduate programmes followed two years later. Intensive research began in 1975 and a faculty sports society was founded in 1977. In 1981 the school moved to a new site in Voždovac, and in 2009 it was accredited with fourteen study programmes. In January 2018 the Serbian government and the faculty signed a contract for a new building of 7,619 square metres.

buildings.description: The Temple of the Holy Apostles Bartholomew and Barnabas is a Serbian Orthodox parish church in Belgrade's Rakovica district. Its story began in 1935, when the neighbourhood, growing into an industrial zone after the First World War, sought a church of its own, since Rakovica had until then belonged to the parish of the Monastery of Saint Archangel Michael. The building was made possible by the bequest of Jelena Radojkić, who gave 319,000 dinars to commemorate her husband Nikola, a former treasurer of the Ministry of Education, and their daughter Bisenija. The new church was meant to be the centre of an enlarged parish that took in both Rakovica and Košutnjak.
buildings.history: Rakovica was growing into an industrial zone after the First World War, and in 1935 its people began to think of a church of their own. A year later the church administration of the Kneževac parish resolved to build it there, at the centre of the enlarged parish, and sent a delegation to Patriarch Varnava in Sremski Karlovci for his blessing. Residents of Košutnjak meanwhile proposed a site on Kanarevo Hill, and the patriarch sent engineer Zađin and architect Milovanović to start on that scheme. The people of Rakovica insisted on their own neighbourhood, so the patriarch blessed the purchase of monastery land, the first plan was set aside, and a new design was prepared by engineer Radovanović with professor Zađin. Patriarch Varnava suggested to the widowed Jelena Radojkić that she build the church in Rakovica, and she agreed to put her husband's bequest into it.

buildings.description: The Church of the Holy Venerable Martyrs Deacon Avakum and Abbot Paisije is an Orthodox church in Belgrade dedicated to Saint Deacon Avakum and Saint Abbot Paisije. It was built in the Serbian-Byzantine style to a design by the architect Ljubica Bošnjak. Its foundations were consecrated on 15 November 2009, and the wall paintings, made under the supervision of the painter Dragomir Marunić, were finished in 2020.
buildings.history: The church was dedicated to Saint Deacon Avakum and Saint Abbot Paisije and built in the Serbian-Byzantine style to a design by the architect Ljubica Bošnjak. Its foundations were consecrated on 15 November 2009. The interior paintings were made under the supervision of the painter Dragomir Marunić and completed in 2020, more than a decade after the foundation ceremony.
