buildings.description: Dositej's Lyceum at 21 Gospodar Jevremova is one of the oldest surviving houses in Belgrade. It is thought to have been put up by a wealthy Turkish family late in the eighteenth century, most probably between 1739 and 1789. Between 1808 and 1813 it housed the Great School, the first institution of higher learning in Serbia, and that is why this modest house entered the country's history. It belongs to the Balkan type: a plain rectangular plan, a ground floor given over to work and trade, and an upper floor where family rooms were kept apart from those used for receiving guests.
buildings.history: The house is dated to the late eighteenth century, most probably to the years between 1739 and 1789. Its arrangement followed Balkan practice: shop, hearth and service rooms below, living rooms above, set apart from the rooms used for receiving guests. The roof was covered with tiles and a broad overhang, as was usual in oriental building. From 1808 to 1813 the Great School, the first institution of higher learning in Serbia, occupied the house. After the collapse of the First Serbian Uprising the building often changed owners and purposes, which altered its interior arrangement but left its architectural qualities intact. In 1948 conservation and restoration work returned it to its original appearance, and the Museum of Vuk and Dositej moved in afterwards.

buildings.description: The Temple of Saint Prince Lazar the Great Martyr is a Serbian Orthodox church in Zemun Polje, in Belgrade's Zemun municipality. Built in 1991 to a design by the architect Branko Pešić, it was the first church beyond the Sava in the Belgrade-Karlovci archbishopric to be raised since 1842. The building follows the Lazarica, the church of Saint First Martyr Stefan in Kruševac, and its motifs come from Hilandar, Gračanica and the Peć Patriarchate. The land was a gift of the Zemun Polje Institute for Maize.
buildings.history: The church in Zemun Polje was built in 1991 through the efforts of the Zemun protopriest-stavrophor Jovan Košević. The design was prepared by Branko Pešić, a Yugoslav and Serbian architect who also worked on the Temple of Saint Sava in Vračar. He modelled it on the Lazarica, the church of Saint First Martyr Stefan in Kruševac, choosing motifs from Hilandar, Gračanica and the Peć Patriarchate. The iconostasis and the frescoes on the walls and vault were made by Mateja Milić. The new church was the first beyond the Sava in the Belgrade-Karlovci archbishopric since 1842.

buildings.description: The Church of Saint Luke in Krnjača is a Serbian Orthodox parish church in Belgrade's Palilula municipality. Its story goes back to Patriarch German, who pressed for a church in the neighbourhood, and in the 1960s an ordinary house was adapted for worship and dedicated to the Apostle and Evangelist Luke. The present church was begun after the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia ended, its foundations were consecrated by Patriarch Pavle in 2001, and the design came from the architect and professor Predrag Ristić.
buildings.history: Patriarch German pressed for a church in Krnjača, and in the 1960s one of the houses there was adapted for worship. The new church began to rise after the NATO bombing of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ended. In 2001 Patriarch Pavle consecrated its foundations. The design was the work of the architect and professor Predrag Ristić. The churchyard was later laid out with a car park, a drinking fountain and a children's playground, while a candle workshop, a souvenir shop, an office and a small parish hall stood nearby.

buildings.description: The mill was raised in 1902 for the First Joint-Stock Breadmaking Association, the first mill in Serbia to be built by a joint-stock company. Its machinery was modern enough to rival mills in far more developed countries, and in 1912–1913 it became the first mill in Serbia to run on electric power. Between the wars it ranked among the largest and most important mills in Yugoslavia by capacity and output.
buildings.history: The association was founded in 1901 and the mill itself went up a year later, the first in Serbia to belong to a joint-stock company rather than a single owner. Steam engines drove the machinery, and dynamos supplied current on the spot; in 1912–1913 the mill switched to electric drive and was again the first in the country to do so. Through the interwar years it worked at full capacity and stood among Yugoslavia's leading mills. Its form follows production rather than display, which is what makes it a characteristic piece of industrial architecture.

buildings.description: Home of the Saint Sava Society, founded in 1886 to spread enlightenment and national feeling among the people; the 1890 building by Jovan Ilkić housed the society’s administration and its institutions.
buildings.history: The Saint Sava Society, founded in 1886, put up its own home in 1890 to Ilkić’s design, for its administration and institutions. The coats of arms of the Serbian lands in the lunettes above the first-floor windows were carved by Jovan Hajnrih Noken from drawings by the painter Đoka Jovanović. A third floor went up in 1923 to a design by Petar Bajalović, with some changes to the upper part of the main facade. In volume and architecture the house was reckoned the largest and finest building in the Danube quarter of Belgrade.

buildings.description: The Faculty of Geography of the University of Belgrade trains geographers, spatial planners, demographers, environmental specialists and tourismologists. It grew out of the Geographical Institute founded by Jovan Cvijić in 1893 and became a faculty in its own right in 1994, when it split from the Faculty of Natural Sciences and Mathematics. It has no building of its own: teaching is spread between Studentski Trg, Crveni Krst and, since 2011, the former Desanka Maksimović primary school in Zemun.
buildings.history: Geography was first taught in Serbia at the lyceum in Kragujevac from 1853, a date that still appears on the faculty's logo. In 1893 Jovan Cvijić set up the Geographical Institute, and university-level teaching ran first at the Faculty of Philosophy and then at the Faculty of Natural Sciences and Mathematics. Between 1990 and 1994 the body existed as the Geographical Faculty within that larger faculty before gaining independence. In 2011 it received the building of the former Desanka Maksimović primary school in Zemun and a teaching base in the village of Blaževo below Kopaonik. The Serbian government has announced a purpose-built home in a complex to be shared with two other faculties that lack space.

buildings.description: Church raised in 1939 to honour the liberators of the First World War, with the names of its donors Milan and Radmila Vukićević recorded in the inscription above the entrance. The architect Grigorije Samojlov designed it, and the iconostasis and carved furniture follow his own drawings.
buildings.history: The church was built in 1939 to a design by Grigorije Samojlov. Its ktitors, Milan and Radmila Vukićević, have their names set in the inscription above the entrance, together with the dedication to the liberators of the First World War. The carved iconostasis and the church furniture were made to the architect’s own drawings. The throne icons were painted by Dragomir Glišić, who also produced the wall paintings of 1985–1987.

buildings.description: The Museum of Pedagogy in Belgrade is one of Serbia's oldest museum institutions, founded on 24 November 1896 by the Society of Teachers of Serbia. It grew out of an idea of the teacher Dimitrije Putniković, who during a study stay in Prague saw the power of visual teaching and wanted Belgrade to have a reference collection of teaching aids for schools. Since 1969 the museum has occupied the Realka building near Kalemegdan, where it displays the permanent exhibition Ten Centuries of Serbian School.
buildings.history: The idea took shape during Dimitrije Putniković's study stay in Prague in 1894/95, where he examined how Czech schools were organised and saw what teaching aids could do. On his return he proposed a School Museum in Belgrade as a reference institution for the continuing education of teachers. On 24 November 1896 the Main Board of the Teachers' Association adopted the museum as its own institution and elected a board headed by Putniković. The first exhibition opened on 3 August 1898 in a primary school in Zapadni Vračar with about 3,500 exhibits, and donations from educational institutions in Czechia, Austria-Hungary, Germany, France, Russia, Belgium, Romania and Bulgaria built up a fund of 5,000 dinars. The collections were destroyed in both world wars, yet the museum was renewed and has been housed in the Realka since 1969.

buildings.description: Built on Kosovska Street in 1908 to a design by Branko Tanazević, this was the first building in Serbia conceived and erected expressly for a telephone exchange. Tanazević married the asymmetry of the facades and the ribbed dome of the Secession with polychrome ceramic ornament of Serbian-Byzantine origin, giving the Morava school's vocabulary a more contemporary reading. In 1925 the same architect added a third storey.
buildings.history: The first stage on Kosovska Street was finished in 1908: a two-storey block by Branko Tanazević, planned from the outset around the needs of a telephone exchange. In 1925 the same architect added a third storey, bringing the building to its present height. Tanazević was among the leading advocates of the Serbian style revival, and here he applied Serbian-Byzantine forms with unusual consistency, recasting the Morava school's ornament in a modern key. The Secession still shows in the asymmetrical facade composition and in the ribbed dome, while ceramic ornament supplied the colour. The result is regarded both as the country's first building of its kind and as a distinctive authorial work of Belgrade architecture.

buildings.description: Apartment building for Dr Zdravko Đurić, long known as the Swissair house after the Swiss airline that once kept its offices here. A year after completion it won recognition for the best facade and became a model for architects of the modern school.
buildings.history: The house was built in 1934 to Branislav Kojić’s design for Dr Zdravko Đurić. The ground floor was given over to shops with large display windows, while the upper floors were handled more freely, with corner balconies and a vertical row of round windows. A year later the building was recognised for the best facade and became a model for Belgrade’s modern architects; it is counted among the anthology pieces of mature interwar modernism.

buildings.description: Town villa of Milan Piroćanac, lawyer, writer, co-founder of the Progressive Party and prime minister under King Milan Obrenović; his house was a stage for a good part of Belgrade’s political life at the end of the 19th century. Three literary associations work here today: the translators, the Serbian Literary Society and the Serbian Writers’ Association.
buildings.history: The house went up around 1884 for Milan Piroćanac, then one of the leading figures in Serbian politics. The design is attributed to Jovan Ilkić and belongs to the academicism of the day with neo-Renaissance detail. The building later served the needs of diplomatic missions. Today it holds the Association of Literary Translators of Serbia, the Serbian Literary Society and the Association of Serbian Writers.

buildings.description: Head office of PRIZAD, the privileged export joint-stock company, built after a competition held in 1937. Since the 1960s the building has housed Tanjug, the Telegraph Agency of the New Yugoslavia; the architect was Bogdan Nestorović.
buildings.history: The building went up in 1938–1939 for the privileged export joint-stock company, after a competition held in 1937. Bogdan Nestorović set the monumental volume so that its circular plan is cut into the plot between three streets, which made the house an urban landmark of this part of town. From the 1960s it has been the seat of Tanjug, the Telegraph Agency of the New Yugoslavia.

buildings.description: The Kraljica Marija elementary school on Prvomajska Street in Zemun was built in 1901 to serve the lower folk school of Franzental, an old Zemun suburb settled largely by Germans. Until 1918 the classrooms held the German elementary school; afterwards the building passed to the school that still bears the name Kraljica Marija. The single-storey block, raised on a high ground floor, was designed on a representative scale in the Neo-Renaissance manner and is regarded as the finest example of historicist architecture outside Zemun's old core. It also stands as a record of how elementary schooling developed across the city.
buildings.history: The building went up in 1901 for the lower folk school of Franzental, an old Zemun suburb whose residents were largely German. It is a single-storey house on a high ground floor, and its composition and ornament follow one consistent historicist programme in the Neo-Renaissance manner, with no detail left to chance. German classes were held here until 1918, when the building passed to the Kraljica Marija school. The change of institution gave the house a new role in the town's public life, and under that name it is known still. For Zemun it remains both a record of how elementary schooling developed and the best example of the historicist approach outside the old core.

buildings.description: Home of Dr Lazar Paču, finance minister and one of the most influential figures in the Radical Party, who lived here from 1890 to 1915. In July 1914, standing in for Nikola Pašić at the foreign ministry, Paču received Austria-Hungary’s ultimatum to Serbia.
buildings.history: The house was built in the 1880s, and Lazar Paču lived in it from 1890 until his death in 1915. He studied medicine in Zurich and Berlin and, with Pera Todorović, launched the socialist journal Straža in Novi Sad. He went on to serve as a municipal doctor in Belgrade, head of the state monopolies and a member of the State Council, and became one of the most influential members of the Radical Party’s main board. As finance minister he influenced the reorganisation of Serbia’s financial service and a series of French loans for armaments and railways.
